## PROHIBITION OF SALES TO EEA RETAIL INVESTORS

The Notes described in this offering memorandum are not intended to be offered, sold or otherwise made available to and should not be offered, sold or otherwise made available to any retail investor in the EEA. For these purposes, a retail investor means a person who is one (or more) of: (i) a retail client as defined in point (11) of Article 4(1) of Directive 2014/65/EU, as amended ("MiFID II"); or (ii) a customer within the meaning of Directive (EU) 2016/97, where that customer would not qualify as a professional client as defined in point (10) of Article 4(1) of MiFID II. Consequently, no key information document required by Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014, as amended (the "EU PRIIPs Regulation"), for offering or selling the securities described in this offering memorandum or otherwise making them available to retail investors in the EEA has been prepared and therefore offering or selling the securities described in this offering memorandum or otherwise making them available to any retail investor in the EEA may be unlawful under the EU PRIIPs Regulation.

The Notes described in this offering memorandum are not intended to be offered, sold, distributed or otherwise made available to and should not be offered, sold, distributed or otherwise made available to any retail investor in the United Kingdom ("UK"). For these purposes, a retail investor means a person who is not a professional client, as defined in point (8) of Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) No 600/2014 as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 ("EUWA"). The interest rate on the Notes will be notified to the Superintendency of the Securities Market of the Republic of Panama (the "SMV") and the Latin American Stock Exchange ("Bolsa Latinoamericana de Valores, S.A.", or "Latinex") after determination thereof. The Issuer is a direct subsidiary of Group Energy Gas Panama Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada, a limited liability company organized under the laws of Panama (the "HoldCo") and jointly owned by InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas Ltd. ("InterEnergy"), and AES Panamá S. de RL. ("AES Panamá"), affiliates of InterEnergy Group Ltd., and AES Corporation, respectively (collectively, the "Sponsors"). As part of a corporate reorganization or restructurings, the Issuer will be permitted to merge with HoldCo, with the Issuer remaining as the surviving entity.

The Notes will be direct, unconditional and general obligations of the Issuer and together with all other Senior Debt (as defined below) and any future Permitted Pari Passu Secured Indebtedness (as defined below), will rank (i) pari passu in right of payment with all other existing and future unsubordinated obligations of the Issuer (other than obligations preferred by statute or by operation of law) and (ii) effectively senior in right of payment to any unsecured obligations of the Issuer to the extent of the value of the collateral securing the Notes (subject to any priority rights of such unsecured obligations pursuant to applicable law). Upon the repayment in full of the Existing Facilities (as defined below), the Notes will be secured by a first-priority security interest in the Collateral (as defined below). See "Description of the Notes—Security—Overview."

The Notes may be redeemed, at the Issuer's option, in whole or in part, on any date prior to three years prior to the Maturity Date, at a redemption price based on a "make-whole" premium and, on or after such date, at the redemption prices set forth in this offering memorandum, in each case, plus accrued and unpaid interest and any additional amounts related thereto, to, but not including the date of redemption. The Issuer also may redeem the Notes at its option, in whole but not in part, at 100% of their principal amount, plus accrued and unpaid interest to the date of redemption and any additional amounts then due and payable, upon the occurrence of any specified events affecting taxation of the Notes. See "Description of the Notes—Optional Redemption with Make-Whole Amount," "Optional Redemption with Make-Whole Amount" and "Redemption for Changes in Withholding Taxes."

The Issuer will be required to redeem the Notes in whole or in part at a redemption price equal to 100% of the outstanding principal amount of the Notes being redeemed, plus accrued and unpaid interest to the redemption date and any additional amounts (excluding any premium), upon the receipt of proceeds in connection with (i) the occurrence of certain events of loss and condemnation, (ii) the termination of PPAs (as defined below), (iii) certain asset sales and (iv) Material Project Document Claims (as defined below). See "Description of the Notes Redemption of the Notes—Mandatory Redemption" and "Certain Covenants—Limitations on Asset Sales."

Upon the occurrence of a change of control resulting in a ratings decline described herein, the Issuer will be required to offer to purchase the Notes at a purchase price equal to 101% of the portion of the outstanding principal balance represented by the Notes to be repurchased, plus all accrued and unpaid interest thereon, to but excluding the purchase date, plus any additional amounts. See "Description of the Notes—Repurchase upon a Change of Control."

# ENFORCEMENT OF CIVIL LIABILITIES

The Issuer is a sociedad anónima organized under the laws of Panama.

Substantially all of the Issuer’s directors, administrators and executive officers reside outside the United States, all of their assets are located outside the United States, and certain of the experts named in this offering memorandum also reside outside the United States. As a result, it may not be possible for investors to effect service of process within the United States upon these persons, including with respect to matters arising under the federal securities laws of the U.S., or to enforce against the Issuer or them in U.S. courts judgments predicated upon the civil liability provisions of the federal securities laws of the United States. However, the Issuer has appointed Cogency Global Inc., with offices currently located at 122 East 42nd Street, 18th Floor, New York, NY 10168, as its authorized agent in connection with the Notes and the Indenture, upon which process may be served in any suit or proceeding arising out of or relating to the foregoing that may be instituted against the Issuer in any federal or state court located in the County of New York, State of New York.

We have been advised by our Panamanian counsel that no treaty exists between the United States and Panama for the reciprocal enforcement of foreign judgments and that there is doubt as to the enforceability, in original actions in Panamanian courts, of liabilities predicated solely on the U.S. federal securities laws and as to the enforceability in Panamanian courts of judgments of U.S. courts obtained in actions predicated upon the civil liability provisions of the federal securities laws of the U.S. We have also been advised by our Panamanian counsel that a judgment of a court outside Panama, including but not limited to judgments of U.S. courts, may only be recognized and enforced by the courts of Panama if the Supreme Court of Panama validates the judgment by the issuance of a writ of exequatur. Any final money judgment rendered by any foreign court will be recognized, conclusive and enforceable in the courts of Panama without reconsideration of the merits, provided that the Fourth Chamber of General Affairs (Sala Cuarta de Negocios Generales) of the Supreme Court of Panama shall, for purposes of issuing a writ of exequatur ordering such enforcement, confirm that: (i) such foreign court grants reciprocity to the enforcement of judgments of the courts of Panama, that is the foreign court would in similar circumstances recognize a final judgment of the courts of the Republic of Panama; (ii) such judgment was issued by a competent court of the foreign jurisdiction (Panamanian courts have exclusive jurisdiction on matters of real estate located in Panama); (iii) the party against whom the judgment was rendered, or its agent, was personally served (with service by mail being insufficient) in such action within such foreign jurisdiction; (iv) the judgment arises out of a personal action against the defendant; (v) the obligation in respect of which the judgment was rendered is lawful in Panama and does not contradict the public policy of Panama; (vi) the foreign judgment, in accordance with the laws of the country where it was rendered, is final and is not subject to appeal; (vii) the judgment is properly authenticated by diplomatic or consular officers of Panama or pursuant to the 1961 Hague Convention Abolishing the Requirement of Legalization of Foreign Public Documents; and (viii) a copy of the final judgment is translated into Spanish by a licensed translator in Panama. See “Risk Factors—Risks relating to the Notes and the Collateral—It may be difficult to enforce civil liabilities against us or our administrators and executive officers and controlling persons.”

Forward-looking statements are only our current expectations and are based on our management’s belief and assumptions and on information currently available to our management. Therefore, actual outcomes and results may differ materially from these expressed or implied in such forward-looking statements.

By their very nature, forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied in the forward-looking statements as a result of various factors, including, but not limited to, those identified under the caption “Risk Factors.” These factors include:

- reliance on transmission assets and energy infrastructure and services that we do not own or control;
- the accuracy of the assumptions, estimates, projections and forward-looking statements included in the financial model presented in the Independent Engineer’s Report included elsewhere in this offering memorandum;
- the accuracy of assumptions and estimates used in the preparation of the Independent Consultants’ Reports included elsewhere in this offering memorandum, including the projections presented therein;
- extensive government legislation and regulations that apply to our business and the electricity generation business;
- our limited operating history;
- failure to comply with our obligations under our PPAs or any contractual disputes with significant customers;
- operational disruptions and infrastructure limitations, including as a result of mechanical malfunctions or similar events;
- our ability to contract all of our uncontracted generation capacity under long-term PPAs or in the spot market;
- our ability to adapt to changes in applicable governmental regulations, rules, principles or practices by legislative, legal, regulatory, governmental and environmental bodies governing tax, accounting and environmental matters in Panama and other countries;
- future economic conditions in the regional, national and international markets, including but not limited to regional and national wholesale electricity markets;
- extraordinary events affecting our operations, including unexpected system failures, strikes, emergency safety measures, military or terrorist attacks, organized crime, weather conditions and natural disasters;
- our ability to carry out marketing and sales plans, as well as manage changes in business strategy, operations or development plans;
- our ability to attract and retain qualified management and other personnel;

# PRESENTATION OF FINANCIAL AND OTHER INFORMATION

## Currencies and Exchange Rates

Unless otherwise specified herein or the context otherwise requires, in this offering memorandum references to “Central America” are to the region formed by the countries of Panama, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica, together; references to “Panama” are to the Republic of Panama; references to the “Panamanian government” are to the Government of Panama; references to the “United States” or the “U.S.” are to the United States of America; references to “U.S.$” or “U.S. dollars” are to the lawful currency of the United States, which since 1904 is also legal tender in and the functional currency of Panama and references to the “Balboa” are to the official monetary unit of Panama, which serves only as coinage, and has been pegged at parity with the U.S. dollar since 1904. The Balboa/U.S. dollar exchange rate has been fixed at B/.1.00 to U.S.$1.00 since the Balboa was first introduced in 1904, and has always circulated alongside U.S. dollars in the Republic of Panama. Other than coins with a value of B/. 1.00 or less, there are no circulating Balboa bills. Currency conversions contained in this offering memorandum should not be construed as representations that Balboas have been, could have been or could be converted into U.S. dollars at the indicated or any other rate of exchange.

## Financial Statements

This offering memorandum contains audited consolidated financial statements of the Parent Company as of and for the years ended December 31, 2025, 2024 and 2023 and the related notes thereto, which have been audited by PricewaterhouseCoopers Panamá, S.R.L., a member firm of PricewaterhouseCoopers (the “audited consolidated financial statements”). Our audited consolidated financial statements and related notes included in this offering memorandum have been prepared in U.S. dollars and in accordance with IFRS Accounting Standards (“IFRS”) as issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (“IASB”).

Separate financial statements of the Issuer have not been included in this offering document because the Issuer is the sole consolidated subsidiary of the Parent Company and its financial position, results of operations, and cash flows are fully reflected in the Parent Company’s consolidated financial statements. As the Issuer is the sole operating entity and revenue-generating entity of the Parent Company, the financial condition and results of operations of the Parent Company effectively represent those of the Issuer.

In addition, following the consummation of the Corporate Reorganization (as defined below), the Issuer and the Parent Company will be consolidated into a single entity, with the Issuer as the surviving entity. Given that the Issuer is the only subsidiary and asset of the Parent Company, the financial statements included in this offering memorandum are expected to remain comparable to those following such Corporate Reorganization.

Accordingly, investors should refer to the Parent Company’s consolidated financial statements, which provide and, following the Corporate Reorganization will continue to provide, a comprehensive view of the Issuer’s financial position and performance.

## Non-IFRS Financial Measures

This offering memorandum presents EBITDA information for convenience of investors. The Issuer calculates EBITDA for any period, as total comprehensive income for the period plus the sum of (a) total income tax, (b) finance cost, net and (c) depreciation and amortization. EBITDA is a supplemental measure of financial performance that is not required under, or presented in accordance with, IFRS. EBITDA is presented because the Issuer believes that some investors find it to be a useful tool for measuring a company’s financial performance. EBITDA should not be considered as an alternative to, in isolation from, or as a substitute for analysis of the Issuer’s financial condition or results of operations, as reported under IFRS. Other companies in the Issuer’s industries may calculate EBITDA differently than the Issuer has for purposes of this offering memorandum, limiting EBITDA’s usefulness as a comparative measure.

## Rounding

Rounding adjustments have been made to figures included in this offering memorandum. Unless otherwise stated or the context otherwise requires, all financial information in this offering memorandum is rounded to the

nearest one-tenth of one million U.S. dollars, and percentage figures included in this offering memorandum are rounded to the nearest one-tenth of one percent. As a result, numerical figures shown as totals in some tables may not be an arithmetic aggregation of the figures that preceded them.

## Market and Other Information

This offering memorandum contains and refers to information and statistics regarding the Panamanian electricity industry. This market data was obtained from independent public sources, including publications and materials from participants in the electricity industry and from governmental entities such as the Ministry of Economy and Finance (Ministerio de Economía y Finanzas), the National Secretary of Energy (Secretaria Nacional de Energía), the Office of the Comptroller (Contraloría General de la República), the National Dispatch Center (Centro National de Despacho), the Electricity Transmission Company (Empresa de Transmisión Eléctrica, S.A.), the National Authority of Public Services (Autoridad Nacional de los Servicios Públicos or ASEP) and the Environment Ministry (Ministerio de Ambiente), among others. Some data are also based on the Issuer's estimates, which are derived from the Issuer's review of internal reports, as well as independent sources. Although these sources are believed to be reliable, the Issuer has not independently verified, and does not guarantee the accuracy and completeness of this information.

See "Terms Used in this Offering Memorandum" for a description of terms referred to in this offering memorandum, including certain technical terms commonly used in the electricity generation industry in Panama.

# SUMMARY

This summary highlights information presented in greater detail elsewhere in this offering memorandum. This summary is not complete and does not contain all the information you should consider before investing in the Notes. You should carefully read this entire offering memorandum before investing, including “Risk Factors,” “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations,” “Business” and the consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in the offering memorandum. See “Presentation of Financial and Other Information” for information regarding the audited consolidated financial statements, definitions of technical terms and other introductory matters.

# Overview

We are engaged in the generation and supply of electricity in Panama. We own and operate Generadora Gatún, a 670 MW natural gas-fired combined cycle power plant with 640 MW in net capacity, located on Telfers Island near Colón, adjacent to the Panama Canal (the “Facility” or the “Project”). The gas turbines of the Facility began to supply energy and capacity into the National Interconnected System in October 2024, and the steam turbine became fully operational in May 2025, increasing the Facility’s efficiency and reaching commercial operation in July 2025.

We supply electricity to the National Interconnected System, which serves the country’s energy demand across industrial, commercial, and residential sectors. International interconnections link the National Interconnected System with neighboring countries through the Panama’s participation in the MER, where generators and demands located in any of the member countries can freely decide whether to carry out their energy purchase / sale transactions in the MER or in their own domestic markets. The six participant countries are Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama, Nicaragua and Guatemala. See “The Panama Electricity Market.”

The Panamanian electricity market is primarily supported by a mix of hydropower, natural gas, and other thermal generation sources, with growing integration of renewable energy. The Facility is the largest natural gas power plant in Panama and Central America, strengthening the country’s energy security and facilitating the transition to a more diversified generation mix. Additionally, the Panamanian power system operates under a competitive wholesale market model, managed by the CND and regulated by the ASEP. The state-owned transmission company, ETESA, plays a key role in system planning and the expansion of the transmission network. Panama also stands out as a strategic energy hub in the region, with international interconnections to Costa Rica and prospects for strengthening integration with Colombia. In recent years, long-term energy auctions have been promoted to encourage investment in renewable generation, particularly solar and wind, as part of the national energy transition strategy toward a cleaner, more resilient, and sustainable energy matrix.

We sell the electric power generated by us to the Distribution Companies through long-term PPAs for a capacity of up to 550 MW. Our capacity is 62.50% contracted for the first four years of operations and 85.90% contracted for years five through 20 under the PPAs, in each case, based on firm capacity, leaving additional opportunities for the Company to enter into additional PPAs or sell excess energy in the spot market. We have PPAs with EDECHI, EDEMET and ENSA, which collectively serve 83% of the Panamanian energy market and all of whose parent companies have credit rating profiles in line with those of Panama. EDECHI and EDEMET are 51.00% owned by Naturgy Energy Group (formerly, Gas Natural Fenosa) and ENSA is a 51.00% subsidiary of EPM. The Republic of Panama owns 48.30% of each of the Distribution Companies, with the remaining being owned by former employees of the Instituto de Recursos Hidráulicos y Electrificación (“IRHE”), a Panamanian government-owned utility that existed prior to the privatization of the Panamanian electricity market. The EDECHI and EDEMET PPAs are for the supply of 40MW and 200MW, respectively, during the first four years and 55 MW and 275 MW, respectively, for the remaining 16 years. The ENSA PPA is for the supply of 160 MW during the first four years and 220 MW for the remaining 16 years. Each of these PPAs has a tenor of 20 years, commencing from October 2024 and include certain “pass-through” provisions that allow us to transfer or share certain of our generation costs to our customers. The PPAs provide for a fixed capacity payment component (the “Capacity Revenue”) and a partially fixed energy payment indexed to Henry Hub (the “Energy Revenue”). As a result, we believe our long-term PPAs provide a very stable source or recurring cash flow. See “—Sources of Revenue,” “Business—Main Contracts.”

For the year ended December 31, 2025, energy sales under our PPAs were 239.97 GWh to EDECHI, 1,063.80 GWh to EDEMET, and 838.26 GWh to ENSA, and those sales represented 10.2%, 41.5% and 33.7% of our operating

revenues, respectively. For the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024, energy sales (i) under PPAs, comprised as energy sales – contracts were U.S.$182.97 million in 2025 and U.S.$42.05 million in 2024 and as capacity sales – contracts were U.S.$94.84 million in 2025 and U.S.$23.95 million in 2024, and (ii) in the spot market were U.S.$43.50 million in 2025 and U.S.$5.15 million in 2024.

## The Facility

The Facility is strategically located within Limon Bay, 2 km south of the port city of Colon, Panama, and directly adjacent to the Atlantic entrance to the canal. The location of the Project was selected to enable easy access for global and regional LNG carriers, easy shipping of key parts to the Facility site and for its proximity to the Colón Terminal, which is only 1.2 km away. Panama is expected to become a convergence point in the new LNG trade routes, especially as LNG exports from the US Gulf of Mexico continue to increase over next few years.

The map below sets out the location of the Facility.



According to the SNE, electricity demand in Panama continues to increase, driven by sustained economic expansion and industrial growth. The country's historical reliance on hydroelectric generation has exposed the system to intermittency and hydrological variability, underscoring the need for firm, dispatchable capacity. Prior to the commencement of energy and capacity dispatch from our Facility in October 2024, Panama had only 381 MW of installed natural gas combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) capacity, all from the Colón Plant. Following the start of operations at our Facility, total installed natural gas CCGT capacity increased to 1,051 MW, reflecting the combined capacity of the Colón Plant and Generadora Gatún. Since commencing operations, the Facility has begun supplying critical firm thermal capacity to meet current and projected electricity demand, while supporting the phased retirement of older, less efficient, and higher-emitting diesel-fired generation units. As of December 31, 2025, Panama's generation mix consisted of 59.78% hydroelectric, 22.76% LNG, 2.21% bunker and diesel fuel, 9.64% solar, 5.27% wind, and 0.34% coal. In this context of rising demand, increasing system firming needs, and a shifting generation mix toward natural gas, the SNE's September 2025 announcement of a potential 2025-2029 PPA tender schedule—including a tender with a firm capacity component in which natural gas-fired plants such as our Facility may be required to participate—signals a regulatory framework aligned with the system's growing need for reliable thermal capacity.

## Sources of Revenue

The Facility derives all of its revenue from the sale of electricity through firm capacity and energy supply PPAs, which account for 86.00% of our total revenue, as well as from merchant sales in the Panamanian spot market, which account for the remaining 14.00%. The Facility’s primary customers are Panama’s three energy distribution companies: EDEMET (owned by Naturgy Energy Group, which has a long-term debt rating of Baa2 by Moody’s, BBB by S&amp;P and BBB by Fitch), EDECHI (also owned by Naturgy), and ENSA (which has a long-term debt rating of AAA(pan) by Fitch Ratings) and is owned by EPM (a state-owned company in Colombia, which has long-term debt rating of Baa3 by Moody’s and BB by Fitch). As of December 31, 2025 and 2024, the revenue derived from the PPAs with the Distribution Companies represented 86.00% and 93.00% of our total revenues, respectively. Rating agencies continuously assess rating levels and there can be no assurance that the rating level or outlook of the Facility’s primary customers will remain constant for any given period of time or that a rating level will not be lowered or withdrawn entirely by the credit rating agency if, in its judgment, circumstances in the future so warrant.

For the year ended December 31, 2025, we derived 86.00% of our total revenues from the PPAs with Distribution Companies, which revenues represented 57.00% Energy Revenues and 29.00% Capacity Revenues. The remaining 14.00% corresponded to energy sales in the spot market.

For the year ended December 31, 2024, we derived 93.00% of our total revenues from the PPAs with the Distribution Companies, which revenues represented 59.00% Energy Revenues and 34.00% Capacity Revenues. The remaining 7.00% corresponded to energy sales in the spot market.

As of the date of this offering memorandum, on average 81.45% of the Facility’s firm capacity was under contract through 2044 pursuant to the PPAs with the Distribution Companies (see “Business—Main Contracts”), with the remainder expected to be sold in the spot market as merchant revenues.

## The Panamanian Electricity Market.

As of December 31, 2025, Panama had a mixed electricity system with a total installed capacity (including auto-generators) of approximately 5,120.19 MW. The electricity sector has been privatized since 1998 and is a dollarized system. Panama’s electricity system has historically relied heavily on hydroelectric power, with much of the generating capacity located in western Panama, close to the Costa Rican border, where the majority of Panama’s

hydroelectric resources are located. After facing one of its worst droughts in 2013 and 2014, the Panamanian government introduced regulatory reforms aimed at reducing the country's reliance on hydroelectric power by encouraging the development of alternative energy sources. Since then, Panama has faced persistent hydrological challenges and volatility, with below-average rainfall in both 2017 and 2018, culminating in its driest year on record in 2019. A temporary reprieve came in 2020 and 2021, when favorable rainfall boosted hydroelectric output, reduced dependence on thermal generation, and lowered overall generation costs. However, the onset of the El Niño phenomenon in 2023 and 2024 brought critically low reservoir inflows, sharply curtailing hydro generation and forcing greater reliance on fossil fuels to meet electricity demand. This shift increased price volatility in the spot market. By mid-2025, rainfall conditions had begun to normalize, and hydroelectric generation showed early signs of recovery, gradually easing pressure on the energy system.

Hydroelectric generation accounted for approximately 65.84% of Panama's electricity supply in 2015, which share declined slightly to 59.78% by the end of 2025. As of December 31, 2025, the remainder of Panama's electricity was generated from 59.78% hydroelectric, 22.76% LNG, 2.21% bunker and diesel fuel, 9.64% solar power, 5.27% wind power, and 0.34% coal. The diversification of the generation matrix in 2019 mitigated the effects of poor hydrology by stabilizing the supply of electricity and reducing spot market volatility during dry conditions. For the year ended December 31, 2025, the average spot market price was U.S.$66.33 per MWh, a 36.9% increase from an average spot price of U.S.$48.45 per MWh in 2020.

In addition, Panama participates in the MER, where generators and demands located in any of the member countries can freely decide whether to carry out their energy purchase / sale transactions in the MER or in their own domestic markets. The six participant countries are Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama, Nicaragua and Guatemala. International interconnections link the National Interconnected System with neighboring countries. Historically, Panama has been a net exporter to neighboring countries in the MER. As of the date of this offering memorandum, Panama's grid is connected with Costa Rica through the SIEPAC (a line with 200 MW capacity both ways at 230 kV) as part of the MER.

## Dispatch Priority

As a result of the efficiency and diversification that the Facility injects into the system, we are able to take advantage of the dispatch methodology in Panama. Thermal plants in the system are dispatched after hydroelectric and renewable plants, with the order within thermal plants preferring natural gas power generators over those operating with diesel or other fossil fuels. Since commencing operations, in our experience, the Colón Plant has usually been among the first three thermal plants in the system to be dispatched after hydroelectric and renewable plants. Accordingly, given that Generadora Gatún is also a natural gas combined cycle plant, it provides a relatively efficient generation source and we expect it will become one of the most efficient sources of thermal generation in the market.

Generadora Gatún and Gas Natural Atlántico, are both natural gas-fired combined-cycle thermal power plants located in Colón Province, Panama. While they share similar fuel sources and technology types, key differences in efficiency and commissioning dates influence their relative positions in the economic dispatch of Panama's electricity system.

Generadora Gatún, which began operations in 2024, is a state-of-the-art facility designed for high thermal efficiency. In contrast, Gas Natural Atlántico was commissioned in 2018 and, while also a combined-cycle plant, operates with slightly lower efficiency due to its earlier-generation technology.

Under Panama's economic dispatch model, managed by CND, generating units are prioritized based on their variable generation cost (VC). Since both plants use natural gas, their dispatch order is primarily influenced by factors such as heat rate, fuel procurement terms, and operational performance. Generadora Gatún's advanced design is expected to give it a lower VC, as compared to Gas Natural Atlántico, positioning it favorably in the dispatch queue and making it one of the most efficient thermal plants in the country.

# Key Credit Highlights

We benefit from the strength of the Facility's business and our ownership and management, which we believe

provide reliable cashflows.

## Stable economic background

Panama is a dollarized economy, located strategically in the middle of the Americas, connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans via the Panama Canal. Panama has been one of the fastest-growing economies in Latin America over the past decade, with a GDP per capita of U.S.$19,200 and an average annual GDP growth rate of 4.0% between 2015 and 2025. In 2025, growth slowed to 3.0%, primarily due to the suspension of operations at the country's largest copper mine. Nevertheless, economic activity is expected to rebound in 2026, with projected GDP growth of 4.0%, supported by strong domestic demand and the reactivation of both public and private investment. We believe these factors position Panama as an attractive destination for foreign investment in Latin America, supported by low inflation, one of the region's lowest unemployment rates, and a stable political environment—even amid recent credit rating downgrades and a split investment-grade status. Moreover, Panama's dollarized economy provides us with a stable currency base underlying our revenues and cash generated over time. These revenues and cashflows will be used to make payments on the Notes.

In addition, Panama's energy demand is projected to grow at an average annual rate of approximately 4.42% over the next 11 years, in line with the country's expected GDP growth, according to ETESA's 2022–2036 expansion plan. Given Generadora Gatún's cost-efficient profile and competitive positioning near the top of the dispatch curve, we believe the Facility is well positioned to capture a substantial share of this demand growth, supporting long-term revenue maximization and operational scalability.

## Stable cashflow profile

Our stable cash flow profile is underpinned by several structural factors: high contracted capacity, favorable power purchase agreement (PPA) terms, and the positioning of natural gas thermal plants on the dispatch curve. We believe these attributes support consistent revenue generation and are further reinforced by USD-denominated PPAs with long-term tenors extending through 2044, which together are expected to strengthen our ability to meet payment obligations on the Notes. Our capacity is 62.5% contracted for the first four years of operations and 85.9% contracted for years five through 20 under the PPAs, in each case, based on firm capacity. Up to 550 MW of the Facility's firm capacity is under contract with the Distribution Companies, leaving additional opportunities for the Company to enter into additional PPAs or sell excess energy in the spot market. The PPA price structure includes a passthrough mechanism of transmission costs, a fixed capacity component, and an energy component indexed 40% to HH Gas Price. The contracted energy volumes under the PPAs follow the Distribution Companies' load factors, which measure the shape of consumption (average demand to peak) and is a stable metric—ranging in any market in the 65-75% range and in Panama historically within the 60-70% range.

## Robust financing structure

The terms of the Notes will limit our ability to incur additional indebtedness, subject to the satisfaction of certain financial ratios. In addition, we also intend to enter into the LC Facility of approximately 5 years to enhance our ability to make payments on the Notes. As a result of these enhancements and limitations, we believe that the issuance of the Notes offered hereby provide us with a robust financing structure to support our operational ramp up while preserving cash to meet our indebtedness obligations.

Pursuant to the Indenture, we have agreed to customary negative covenants against (i) debt incurrence (unless certain debt incurrence conditions are satisfied including compliance with historical and projected debt service coverage ratios greater than 1.35:1.00, (ii) creation of liens (including liens to secure indebtedness up to a specified amount), (iii) affiliate transactions (except on an arm's-length basis), (iv) asset sales, (v) mergers and acquisitions (unless the leverage tests referred to above for debt incurrence have been satisfied), other than the Corporate Reorganization (as described below) and (vi) distributions (unless in compliance with the distribution conditions). For more information regarding the financing structure see "Description of the Notes" and "Description of the Financing Documents".

# Robust operations and maintenance arrangements and adequate gas supply strategy

We have long-term and favorable arrangements with our principal shareholders—an operation and maintenance agreement with AES Panamá and an administrative services agreement with InterEnergy Holdings UK. In addition, we have a TUA and an OCA with Costa Norte LNG Terminal, S. de R.L. an affiliate of AES Panamá. Both AES Panamá and InterEnergy Holdings UK are highly experienced and reputable counterparties, properly incentivized to perform.

Moreover, we have secured strong and favorable gas supply contract terms at a price indexed to Henry Hub through a 20-year LNG sales and purchase agreement with Total, an LNG global market leader and reputable counterparty. We believe the contractual arrangement with Total will allow us to service the PPAs while allowing adequate flexibility to adjust cargo quantities depending on the Facility's needs and dispatch, including in extreme weather events (high hydrology years) and other natural weather patterns.

The Facility also has strong control systems that increase its efficiency and improve employee safety. The Facility is certified under the OHSAS 18001 and ISO 14001 standards for integrated safety and environmental management systems. We continue to develop our strategic and operational management to allow us to efficiently plan, prioritize and achieve our business and operational objectives. We operate under strict internal financial controls and manage our working capital with a view towards financing growth while limiting excess liquidity. We continuously review and improve our internal procedures and training methods in order to improve the safety of our employees.

# Experienced management team

Our highly experienced management has extensive knowledge of and vast experience in the Panamanian energy sector, as well as a broad range of relevant experience in Central America and the Caribbean. Our officers and directors have an average of 20 years of experience in the energy industry in Panama. We believe the management team's capabilities and core understanding of both the business and the related regulatory environment, enable the team to operate efficiently and manage risk effectively.

# Strong sponsorship

We benefit from the strong and constructive relationships with our principal shareholders and their parent companies, which provide experience, management, guidance and support, and represent important political allies and business partners. The direct and indirect holder of AES Panamá's equity are AES (which owns AES Panamá's direct managing equity holder, Global Power Holdings) and the Panamanian Government. AES is a Fortune 500 global power company that seeks to provide affordable, sustainable energy in 12 countries on four continents (the Americas, Asia and Europe) through a diverse portfolio of distribution businesses as well as thermal and renewable generation facilities. As of December 31, 2025, AES managed approximately U.S.$51 billion in total assets and had revenues of U.S.$12.2 billion. AES currently distributes electricity through its various electric utility subsidiaries to over 2.6 million customers worldwide. AES also has 34.4 GW in gross capacity in operation globally. AES and its affiliates provide us with technical expertise and financial and operational management, support and training to help grow their businesses.

The indirect holder of InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas's equity is InterEnergy Group. InterEnergy Group was established in 2011 and is a developer, owner, and operator for power generation, transmission, and distribution assets in the Latin American and Caribbean region, with 2.5 GW of installed capacity across 28 operating assets in 10 countries. InterEnergy Group is an experienced sponsor in the power sector with a focus on renewable energy and energy transition. The group has been a pioneer in developing state-of-the-art energy infrastructure, including solar parks and energy storage systems, as well as expanding electric vehicle charging networks through Evergo. In Jamaica, InterEnergy Group owns almost 40% of the country's total base load capacity. In Dominican Republic, InterEnergy Group owns two generation, transmission, and distribution companies through which it became the first wind operator in 2011. In 2014, InterEnergy built the largest wind farm in the Central American and Caribbean region (Laudato Si wind farm in Panama). Other investments include solar and wind power plants in Chile, solar, wind and thermal power plants in Panama, wind generation in Uruguay, Guatemala and the Dominican Republic, solar and thermal power plants in Jamaica, and solar plants in the Cayman Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

We represent an important part of AES Panamá's and InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas' operations and long-term commitment to supply power in Panama. In furtherance of this commitment, both AES Panamá and InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas have made extensive capital expenditures to develop, operate and manage the Facility. In addition, in pursuing their corporate strategy, which implements the strategic goals (green growth, customer centricity, new business models and new technologies) of both AES and the InterEnergy Group, through their investment in Generadora Gatún, they have positioned themselves well for continued growth and increased their importance to the Panamanian energy market, and by extension, to the Panamanian government, AES Panamá's majority equity holder. As operator of the Colón Facilities, the only LNG power plant and terminal in Panama, prior to the commencement of operations at our Facility, AES Panamá has advanced AES's strategic goals of incorporating new technologies and new business models by expanding its combined generation portfolio to include LNG and establishing a new revenue stream from storage capacity sales. In addition, through the construction of Generadora Gatún, AES Panamá and InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas have contributed significantly to the diversification and reliability of the Panamanian generation matrix, and the reduction and stabilization of spot market prices. We believe that these contributions have further increased their strategic importance to the Panamanian government, aligning their interests with those of their equity holders. Neither AES Panamá nor InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas are guarantors of the Notes.

## Business Strategy

As Panama's largest natural gas-fired power plant, we believe that Generadora Gatún, has significant opportunities to strengthen its market position, enhance efficiency, and expand into new areas of growth.

## Increasing market positioning and expansion in Central America and the Caribbean

Expanding its market reach beyond Panama presents a significant growth opportunity for our business. One strategic approach is leveraging Panama's interconnection with the SIEPAC to export electricity to countries experiencing supply gaps, such as Guatemala, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Honduras. The planned interconnection between Panama and Colombia is progressing steadily, presenting a strategic opportunity to strengthen our regional positioning and anticipate increased profitability in the future. Additionally, securing new long-term PPAs with Panama's Distribution Companies and industrial consumers can provide additional flows of stable revenue streams while reinforcing Generadora Gatún's role in Panama's energy supply.

Another area of expansion is becoming a backup energy provider for renewables, supplying dispatchable power to compensate for fluctuations in hydro, wind, and solar generation. With Panama's industrial and commercial energy demand growing, Gatún can also position itself as the primary energy supplier for major industries, including port operations, logistics hubs, and free trade zones in Colón and the Panama Canal area. Strengthening relationships with ETESA and major industrial clients will be crucial in ensuring that Generadora Gatún remains an integral part of Panama's evolving energy infrastructure.

## Continued focus on optimization of operations and efficiency improvements

Maximizing operational efficiency and minimizing costs will be critical for our long-term competitiveness in the Panamanian energy market. One of the key strategies is to enhance the efficiency of the Facility's combined-cycle technology by implementing advanced digital monitoring systems, including AI-driven predictive maintenance. These tools can help optimize turbine performance, reduce unplanned downtime, and extend the life of critical assets. Additionally, fuel optimization will play a crucial role in controlling costs, requiring strategic long-term LNG procurement contracts linked to Henry Hub or other competitive benchmarks to ensure price stability.

Beyond fuel efficiency, participating in Panama's wholesale energy market can provide additional revenue streams by allowing us to sell excess power during peak pricing periods and balance generation with real-time demand fluctuations. The Facility can also position itself as a key provider of grid stability services, offering fast-ramping capacity to help manage fluctuations in intermittent renewable generation. Further, investing in carbon capture technologies and emissions reductions can align the Facility with Panama's sustainability goals, ensuring compliance with evolving regulatory frameworks while improving its environmental impact.

Sargent &amp; Lundy has prepared the Independent Engineer Report and consented to the inclusion of a copy of such report as Annex A to this offering memorandum. Sargent &amp; Lundy is an independent international consulting firm that provides technical consulting services covering, among other industries, the energy and utilities sector. The Independent Engineer Report summarizes Sargent &amp; Lundy's analysis, provides an overview of the Facility, a review of its material agreements and historical performance, an assessment as to the reasonableness of the Company's maintenance and operating costs, maintenance plan, as well as an environmental and permit review and assessment. It also includes the financial model. Sargent &amp; Lundy and its affiliates do not approve or endorse, directly or indirectly, any product, service, or Notes offered by the Issuer.

Key Findings

Sargent &amp; Lundy performed a site visit to observe the conditions of the Facility during the week of May 13, 2025 through May 15, 2025, and on January 28, 2026. The Independent Engineer Report's key findings are as follows:

- Sargent &amp; Lundy conducted a site visit to Generadora Gatún combined cycle power plant on January 28, 2026, to independently review the unit #1 gas turbine generator (GTG1) rotor incident, repair, and return to service, and assess recurrence risk for the affected unit #1 and sister unit #2 gas turbine generator (GTG2) and steam turbine generator (STG). Based on a detailed review of event chronology, diagnostic testing, and the fast-track rotor rewind and reinstallation performed under the EPC Contractor POSCO's EPC / original equipment manufacturer (OEM) warranty claim framework, Sargent &amp; Lundy found that GTG1 has been restored to a reliable operational state, with full field rewind, slot-end blending, and enhanced monitoring in place, and that current operating data since its return to service support a low residual risk of recurrence.

Source: 260211 Gatun - GE RCA Report 20260205 R07.pdf

- Sargent &amp; Lundy stated that, while the final root cause has not yet been conclusively determined, the two root causes with the highest probability (Leading and Mild-Probability) have been identified and corrective action implemented. The fact that GE continues to evaluate the remaining "Low Probability" root causes is merely to confirm that they can be discarded. Therefore, it was Sargent &amp; Lundy's technical opinion that the residual risk of recurrence is low, as supported by the actual operating data, since GTG1 was declared available by CND on January 13, 2026.

- In conclusion, Sargent &amp; Lundy's comprehensive technical due diligence review confirmed that the Plant is well-positioned for successful refinancing and ongoing operations. ## Independent Energy Market Consultant Report

Estudios Energéticos Consultores has prepared the Independent Energy Market Consultant Report and consented the inclusion of a copy of such report as Annex B to this offering memorandum. Estudios Energéticos Consultores is an independent international consulting firm that provides energy market consulting services covering, among other industries, the energy and utilities sector. The Independent Energy Market Consultant Report summarizes Estudios Energéticos Consultores’ analysis and opinions, provides an overview of the Facility, a market study, regulatory and prospective analysis of the Panamanian wholesale electricity market, including electricity price forecasts in the short, mid and long-term markets. Estudios Energéticos Consultores and its affiliates do not approve or endorse, directly or indirectly, any product, service, or Notes offered by the Issuer.

## Key Findings

Subject to the information and qualifications contained and assumptions made in the Independent Energy Market Consultant Report, the Independent Energy Market Consultant has expressed the following main findings:

- The Central American region is characterized by peak demands in a range of between 840 MW in Nicaragua to 2122 MW in Guatemala, with El Salvador as a middle size country with a peak demand of 1194 MW. The installed capacity in the countries of the Regional Market (“MER”) lies between 1600 and 4500 MW. Overall, the electricity generation is predominantly renewable (hydroelectricity and non-conventional renewable energy), but with significant differences among countries: the thermal generation ranges from almost 5% in Costa Rica to 45% in Nicaragua and Honduras.
- In recent years the MER has been one of the regional integration axes, allowing for energy exchanges among interconnected countries in Central America. According to the Ente Operador Regional (EOR), as of May 2025 the MER had 318 agents registered, Guatemala with 113, Panama with 73, El Salvador with 84, Nicaragua with 44 and Costa Rica and Honduras with only two local agents each. In 2024, the energy purchases positioned Nicaragua first, El Salvador second and Costa Rica third.
- It is observed that these technologies are becoming increasingly competitive in the region, consistent with the worldwide trend.
- In the last decade, Panama’s economy has been very stable with high growth rates (8% average growth from 2004 to 2014, 5% from 2014 to 2017 and about 3% in 2018-2019). The projection for the next two years is around 3% and remains relatively high around 4% for the following years (IMF estimates).
- Panama, similar to the rest of the Central American countries, is not an oil producer, for this reason all its fuel consumption is imported from the international market. In this context, energy market spot prices tend to follow prices of commodities worldwide.
- Panama’s energy market is a very mature and competitive market, operating as deregulated since 1999. Foreign investment is a probe of market credibility.
- Commercially speaking, the wholesale electricity market (WEM) consists of two markets, a relatively small one accounting for opportunity exchanges (spot market) and another for long-term contracts.
- Distribution Companies must contract 100% of the demand in advance.
- Panama is a country committed to achieve a cleaner energy matrix. As such initiatives for energy transition and innovation plans have been set in place.

11

- Similar to other countries in the region, the main contributor to the electricity production is by far hydroelectric power plants. Although, in this case, LNG has a main role as well. In 2024, the new 670 MW LNG CCGT power plant was commissioned (first stage of 440MW).
- Renewables energies have a relative medium impact in the generation matrix. In the future, new non-conventional renewable energy sources are expected to keep entering the matrix, especially solar photovoltaic.
- Regarding demand, Panama has a strong commercial demand, mainly from the service sector.
- Finally, in Panama both transmission and distribution are considered natural monopolies by the Panamanian government and are therefore regulated. Transmission is wholly performed by Empresa de Transmisión Eléctrica S.A. (ETESA), which is a state-controlled company.

For additional information about the Independent Consultants’ Reports, including certain information about the financial model, see “Third-Party Financial Projections.”

## Recent Developments

### Rotor Outage

In July 2025, we experienced a partial unplanned outage that lasted 176 days due to a rotor failure in one of the gas turbine generator units. As a result of this failure, we immediately initiated a warranty claim under the EPC Contract and worked with GE generator specialists who conducted several on-site and off-site diagnostic tests, as well as an investigation to determine the cause of the equipment failure. The investigation concluded that the most likely cause of the rotor failure in the gas turbine generator was the result of small metal fragments left inside the generator during the original manufacturing process. The total revenue losses associated with this outage are estimated at up to U.S.$5.27 million, representing the amount being claimed under our business interruption insurance policy (which is subject to a 60-day deductible). Although we have submitted a claim under our business interruption insurance in respect of such losses, as of the date of this offering memorandum, we cannot ascertain or provide any assurances that we will recover all or any part of such loss from our insurance coverage claim. Notwithstanding the duration of the outage, we believe its impact on Generadora Gatún’s results of operations was limited, primarily due to prevailing dispatch conditions during the outage period, including a seasonally high hydroelectric contribution (with 2025 being a particularly wet year), which reduced reliance on thermal generation.

Despite our attempts to create redundancy and protocols to reduce systemic risks of equipment failure, we cannot guarantee that any or all of our power generation or other ancillary equipment at our Facility will not malfunction again or become otherwise unavailable to generate electricity or support the ancillary functions for the Facility for an extended period of time. Although we rely on a combination of monitoring systems, EPC warranties, and a long-term service agreement with the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) to maintain operational integrity and reduce the risk of forced outages, unforeseen equipment failures, technical issues, or infrastructure degradation may still occur. Any such extended malfunction or unavailability would have an adverse effect on our results of operations. See “Risk Factors—Risks Relating to Our Business—Operational disruptions and infrastructure limitations could adversely affect our ability to meet contractual obligations and impact our financial performance.”

### Acquisition of the AES Sponsor

On March 1, 2026, AES entered into an Agreement and Plan of Merger (the “Merger Agreement”), by and among AES Corporation, Horizon Parent, L.P., (“Horizon Parent”) a Delaware limited partnership, and Horizon Merger Sub, Inc., a Delaware corporation and wholly owned subsidiary of Horizon Parent (“Horizon Sub”). Pursuant to the Merger Agreement, on the terms and subject to the conditions set forth therein, Horizon Sub will merge with and into AES (the “Horizon Merger”), with AES continuing as the surviving corporation in the merger. Horizon Parent is jointly controlled by investment vehicles affiliated with one or more funds, accounts or other entities managed or advised by Global Infrastructure Management, LLC and the EQT Infrastructure VI fund. The Horizon Merger is currently expected to close in late 2026 or early 2027, subject to satisfaction or waiver (to the extent permitted by law) of all closing conditions.

# Corporate Reorganization

Following the consummation of the offering of Notes as described in this offering memorandum, we intend to effect the Corporate Reorganization of our business in order to simplify our corporate structure. See “Summary—Corporate Structure.” To effect the Corporate Reorganization, a merger agreement and corporate authorizations of the Issuer and HoldCo will be registered with the Public Registry, and thereafter, made public by the Issuer as a communication of relevant matter in compliance with SMV Rule No. 3-2008 (as modified) and Rule No. 5-2005 (as modified). We expect the net effect of the Corporate Reorganization to be a more simplified and efficient corporate structure that is tied more closely to our underlying operating asset—Generadora Gatún. To allow us to implement the Corporate Reorganization efficiently, the covenants in the indenture relating to the Notes and in the LC Facility Agreement, including covenants relating to restricted payments and investments, will contain broad exceptions to allow the Corporate Reorganization. However, we do not expect the Corporate Reorganization to affect the terms of the Notes or the Collateral, including any restrictions to be imposed on us pursuant to the terms of the Notes or the Collateral.

# The Issuer

The Issuer was incorporated on January 19, 2015 under the laws of Panama. Since March 31, 2021, the Issuer is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Parent Company, a Panamanian limited liability company. The Parent Company is owned by InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas (51%) and AES Panamá (49%). Pursuant to a shareholders’ agreement each of the sponsors has the right to appoint three members to the Parent Company’s board of directors. The Parent Company is the sole shareholder of all of the Issuer’s share capital. The ultimate parent of InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas is InterEnergy Group, and the ultimate parents of AES Panamá are The AES Corporation located in Arlington, Virginia (USA) and the Republic of Panama.

In the ordinary course of business, the Issuer engages in a variety of transactions with certain of its affiliates, primarily for the purchase, at fair market prices negotiated on an arm’s-length basis, of goods or services that may also be provided by other suppliers. For more details, see “Related Party Transactions”.

# Our Principal Shareholders

## InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas

InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas owns a 51% interest in us. InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas’ indirect parent company, InterEnergy Group, was established in 2011 and is a developer, owner, and operator for power generation, transmission, and distribution assets in the Latin American and Caribbean region, with 2.5 GW of installed capacity across 28 operating assets in 10 countries. InterEnergy Group is an experienced sponsor in the power sector with a focus on renewable energy and energy transition. In Jamaica, InterEnergy Group owns almost 40% of the country’s total base load capacity. In Dominican Republic, InterEnergy Group owns two generation, transmission, and distribution companies through which it became the first wind operator in 2011. In 2014, InterEnergy built the largest wind farm in the Central American and Caribbean region (Laudato Si wind farm in Panama). Other investments include solar and wind power plants in Chile, solar, wind and thermal power plants in Panama, wind generation in Uruguay, Guatemala and the Dominican Republic, solar and thermal power plants in Jamaica, and solar plants in the Cayman Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands. As of December 31, 2025, InterEnergy Group, through its Panamanian subsidiaries, supplies 19.98% of Panama’s electricity generation.

## AES Panamá

AES Panamá owns a 49% interest in us. AES Panamá is owned 50.50% by the Republic of Panama, 0.40% by minority shareholders and 49.10% by AES through its wholly owned subsidiary AES Global Power Holdings. Through AES Global Power Holdings, AES currently owns an interest in and operates a large portfolio of electricity generation and LNG assets in Panama. AES Panamá currently operates 5 hydroelectric power plants, 1 wind farm and 7 solar plants, amounting to an installed capacity of 612 MW. AES Panamá also operates facilities in Colón and Changuinola, resulting in a combined generation portfolio that amounts to 1,216 MW, making AES Panamá the largest generation sponsor in Panama both by installed capacity and energy generation. As of December 31, 2025, all AES assets in Panama supply 30% of the country’s electricity generation.

|  Use of Proceeds | The Issuer intends to use the proceeds of this issuance of Notes (i) to pay transaction fees and expenses accrued in connection with the issuance of the Notes and the LC Facility; (ii) to repay in full and cancel the loans outstanding under the Existing Facilities, including, in each case, related interest, breakage costs, premia, fees, costs and other expenses; (iii) to the pro rata payment of all fees and moneys then due and payable to any of the agents under the Financing Documents relating to services rendered in their respective capacities as agents, in each case in accordance with the Financing Documents; (iv) to fund the Notes Debt Service Reserve Account and the O&M Reserve Account in the manner described in “Description of the Notes—Disposition of Issue Date Proceeds”; and (v) to the extent of any remaining funds, on the Issue Date, to make a capital reduction and an intercompany loan to the Holding Company, and to deposit any remaining fund to the Distribution Suspense Account for use in connection with the Corporate Reorganization. “Use of Proceeds” and “Description of the Notes—Disposition of Issue Date Proceeds.”  |

priority of such accounts see “Description of the Notes—Accounts,” “—Cash Waterfall,” and “—Summary of Invasion of Accounts Procedure.”

The Issuer will agree under the Indenture to comply with certain negative covenants, which will significantly limit its ability to, among other things:

- incur, guaranty or refinance certain debt, other than Permitted Indebtedness and Permitted Pari Passu Secured Indebtedness;
- make distributions or restricted payments;
- grant, create, incur, assume or suffer to exist any liens, other than Permitted Liens;
- make investments, other than Permitted Investments;
- enter into any agreement or arrangement with any affiliate;
- change the nature of its business or project;
- sell, assign, convey, transfer, lease or otherwise dispose of its properties and assets substantially as an entirety;
- consolidate, merge, liquidate, dissolve, change legal form, materially amend constitutional documents, form or own any subsidiaries, other than in connection with the Corporate Reorganization; and
- enter into sale and lease-back transactions.

Certain Affirmative Covenants

All of these restrictions and limitations are subject to a number of significant qualifications and exceptions. See “Description of the Notes—Certain Covenants of the Issuer.”

The Issuer will agree under the Indenture to comply with certain affirmative covenants, including requirements to, among other things:

- preserve and maintain corporate existence and legal form;
- comply with all applicable laws (including any environmental laws);
- exercise commercially reasonable efforts to maintain a rating of the Notes by at least two Rating Agencies;
- maintain insurance coverage in such amounts and covering such risks as set forth in the Financing Documents;
- obtain and maintain in full force and effect all material Governmental Approvals required under Applicable Law to be obtained or maintained by it in connection with the operation of the Project and the performance of its obligations under the Material Project Documents and under

21

the Notes, the Indenture and the other Financing Documents;

- keep and maintain the Project and property;
- maintain proper books of record and account;
- deliver an operating budget;
- apply the proceeds from the sale of the Notes as set forth in “Use of Proceeds”;

(i) perform and observe all terms and provisions of the Material Project Documents to be performed or observed by it, (ii) maintain the Material Project Documents to which it is a party in full force and effect, and (iii) exercise all its rights, discretion and remedies, if any, under the Material Project Documents to which it is a party in accordance with their terms and in a manner consistent with (and subject to) the Issuer’s obligations under the Indenture and the Security Documents, in each case of clauses (i) through (iii) above, except to the extent that failure to do any of the foregoing could not, individually or in the aggregate, reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect;

- undertake all actions that are necessary to enable each of the Collateral Agent and the Panamanian Trustee, on behalf of the Secured Parties, to exercise and enforce its rights, powers, remedies and privileges under the Security Documents;

- prepare, give, execute, deliver, file and/or record any notice, financing statement, continuation statement, public deed, instrument or agreement necessary under Applicable Law to maintain, preserve or perfect any Lien granted under the Security Documents; and

- permit the exercise of inspection rights by the holders, the Indenture Trustee and the Collateral Agent.

All of these covenants are subject to a number of significant qualifications, thresholds and exceptions. See “Description of the Notes—Certain Covenants of the Issuer.”

Transfer Restrictions ……………………………………………………………… The Issuer has not and will not register the Notes under the Securities Act, or the securities laws of any other jurisdiction (other than Panama). The Notes are subject to restrictions on transfer and may

only be offered in transactions exempt from or not subject to the registration requirements of the Securities Act. See “Transfer Restrictions.”

Form and Denominations... The Notes will be issued in registered form only, without interest coupons, in denominations of U.S.$ 200,000 and integral multiples of U.S.$ 1,000 in excess thereof. The Notes will be initially registered in the name of DTC or its nominee and deposited with the Indenture Trustee as custodian for DTC.

Listing... The Notes will be registered with the Panamanian Superintendency of Capital Markets (Superintendencia del Mercado de Valores de Panamá) and will be listed on the Bolsa Latinoamericana de Valores (Latin American Stock Exchange or “Latinex”).

Application will be made for the listing of and quotation for the Notes on the Official List of the SGX-ST.

Based on the analysis of the financial model, the Independent Engineer concludes as follows:

- Overall, the financial model provided for review is reasonable and appropriate. The major technical and operational assumptions are consistent with the terms in the contractual documents reviewed by Sargent &amp; Lundy.
- Sargent &amp; Lundy finds the projected heat rate based and availability factor values to be comparable to other units of comparable size and technology.
- Sargent &amp; Lundy finds the capital costs for the maintenance and the LTSA to be adequately accounted for in the financial model with a total of U.S.$143 million not including capital expenditures to build the plant.
- Sargent &amp; Lundy finds the projected technical O&amp;M costs are increasing, with an average annual inflation rate of 2.69% from 2025 through 2044, with average technical O&amp;M costs of U.S.$27.03/kW-yr.
- Sargent &amp; Lundy finds that the revenue projection and provisions of the PPA appear to be adequately formulated within the financial model, and all assumptions used for forecasting variable energy revenue are reasonable for the Project.
- Sargent &amp; Lundy’s review of the debt service coverage ratio finds that the Project projections appear to be in good financial health with a strong cash flow generation relative to debt service obligations and a manageable level of leverage.
