# RISK FACTORS

An investment in the Notes involves risk. You should carefully consider the risks and uncertainties described below and the other information in this offering memorandum before making an investment in the Notes. Our business, financial condition or results of operations could be materially adversely affected by any of these risks. The risks described below are not the only ones facing us or investments in Panama in general. Additional risks not presently known to us or that we currently deem immaterial may also impair our business operations.

This offering memorandum also contains forward-looking statements that involve risks and uncertainties. Our actual results could differ materially from those anticipated in these forward-looking statements as a result of certain factors, including the risks faced by us as described below and elsewhere in this offering memorandum.

## Risks Relating to Our Business

**Failure to perform under our PPAs or their early termination will result in reduced revenue and could materially adversely affect our results of operations and ability to make payments on the Notes.**

Our principal asset is the Facility and the PPAs pursuant to which we derive our revenues. As a result, in order to make payments on the Notes, we are dependent upon the cash flows produced from the PPAs. These PPAs are subject to termination prior to expiration in certain circumstances, including default by us.

If a PPA is terminated, it may be difficult for us to secure a new PPA on acceptable terms or timing, if at all. The price received under subsequent arrangements may be reduced significantly and there may be a delay in securing a new PPA until a significant time after the PPA is terminated which could materially and adversely affect our ability to make payments on the Notes.

**It may be difficult for us to fulfill our contractual obligations and we may need to purchase energy from other generation companies at the prevailing spot market price which may be higher than the price at which we sell energy under our PPAs.**

We are entirely dependent on one asset, the Facility, and the three Distribution Companies as our customers to generate substantially all of our revenues. Our electricity generation production depends upon our ability to maintain the working order of the Facility and its component equipment, and the Facility being called for dispatch based on the merit order. If the electricity dispatched from the Facility is less than the level that we have contracted to provide or sell under our PPAs, we must purchase the difference in the spot market or through back-up (reserve) agreements from other generators (if applicable), in order to fulfill our obligations under our PPAs. If the Facility experiences availability issues that require us to purchase energy in the spot market, this could negatively impact our results of operations because the replacement costs can be substantially higher than the average price at which we sell under our PPAs.

However, in the event of energy rationing measures we may not be able to purchase in the spot market or through back-up agreements the electricity resulting from the production deficit of the Facility, in which case we would be subject to penalties of up to seven (7) times the price of the electricity we are required to deliver under the applicable PPA. Failure to have available the required amount of capacity could subject us to penalties of up to three (3) times the price of the capacity we are required to deliver under the applicable PPA. For purposes of determining shortages in firm capacity requirements, the CND verifies the average weekly capacity availability for each generation company. For further information see "Business—Main Contracts—PPAs".

Conversely, during periods when the actual generation of the Facility is higher than our contracted energy, we may be able to sell the excess energy into the market at the then-current spot price. If higher demand leads to increased dispatch and higher spot prices, revenues from such excess energy would increase accordingly.

Spot prices for energy can be affected by a number of factors that are beyond our control, such as weather conditions, seasonality, reductions in electricity usage, new market entrants, transmission congestion and new regulations. Fuel prices also affect the spot price for electricity because the spot price is set using the highest variable cost thermal unit to be dispatched to meet the system demand on an hourly basis, and the variable cost of thermal units depends heavily on the price of the fuel used to run them. Similarly, spot prices respond to the number of individual

generation technologies available in a specific market. The Panamanian power market is characterized by a limited number of large generation companies, each representing a significant share of system capacity and peak demand. As a result, market dynamics can be more sensitive to technological shifts or changes in operating performance at the major generation assets.

Moreover, our three PPAs with the Distribution Companies incorporate fuel indexations in their contracted energy price calculation. If the price of the fuel used to operate drops below the reference price used to calculate the payments we receive for the contracted energy under the related PPAs or if the spot price of replacement energy drops below the contract price of the energy we sell, we would not be entitled to payments for contracted energy, which may negatively impact the results of our operations.

**A portion of our generation capacity is not currently contracted under long-term power purchase agreements and is subject to economic dispatch based on merit order, which may result in lower or more volatile revenues.**

As of the date of this offering memorandum, the Facility's capacity is 62.50% contracted for the first four years of operations and 85.90% contracted for years five through 20 under the PPAs with the Distribution Companies, in each case, based on firm capacity. The associated contracted energy volumes total approximately 2,226.25 GWh and 3,146.63 GWh per year, respectively for the first four years of operations and for years five through 20 under the PPAs, respectively. The remaining 14.00% of the Facility's net capacity is not currently contracted under long-term PPAs and is subject to economic dispatch pursuant to Panama's merit order framework. As a result, revenues from this portion of our generation are subject to fluctuations in spot market prices and dispatch levels, which depend on system demand, fuel prices, generation costs of other market participants, and other market dynamics.

While under current Panamanian regulations the Facility is entitled to receive at least its production cost for energy dispatched into the spot market, revenues may be adversely affected if spot prices fall below expectations, if the Facility is dispatched less frequently than anticipated, or if market reforms modify dispatch protocols or compensation mechanisms. Although we intend to monetize uncontracted capacity through spot market sales and/or the execution of new PPAs, there can be no assurance that we will be able to do so on favorable terms or at all. As a result, a small portion of our revenues may remain exposed to market-based pricing and dispatch volatility, which could adversely affect our results of operations.

**Our business may be negatively affected by increases in fuel prices or the imposition of new regulatory costs that we are unable to pass on to our customers pursuant to the cost pass through provisions of our PPAs.**

Our business may be adversely affected by increases in fuel prices or the imposition of new regulatory costs that we are unable to pass on to our customers under the cost pass-through provisions of our PPAs. Fuel prices have historically been subject to significant volatility driven by geopolitical developments, changes in global supply and demand, and disruptions to trade routes. The heightened geopolitical tensions involving the United States and Venezuela in the beginning of 2026, the ongoing conflicts between Israel and militant groups in the Middle East and the recent outbreak of war in the Middle East between Iran and the U.S. and Israel, including Iran's strikes against energy infrastructure and other targets in various Middle Eastern countries, and related disruption of shipping in the Persian Gulf and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, have resulted in a sharp increase in fuel prices, concerns that the supply of crude oil, petroleum products and LNG may be significantly constrained for some period of time and led to supply shortages and severe volatility in global oil and natural gas markets. In addition, the conflict in Ukraine, and the economic sanctions imposed by the EU, U.S. and other countries in response to Russian action, is also disrupting energy production and trade patterns. These ongoing conflicts may impact various costs of operating our business, such as LNG-related costs from our long term purchase agreement or in the spot market, which have increased with higher fuel prices. The situations in the Middle East due to war between Iran and the U.S. and Israel and in Ukraine, and the global responses, continue to evolve and their respective impact on energy supply and demand, energy prices and LNG tanker operations remains subject to considerable uncertainty, which could adversely impact our business, results of operations and financial condition. There is no assurance that these conditions will stabilize or that additional sanctions, trade restrictions, or retaliatory measures will not further disrupt fuel supply or increase costs.

Although our PPAs currently include price adjustment mechanisms designed to pass through certain cost increases, including through a formula that references average monthly Henry Hub prices, there is no guarantee that these mechanisms will fully capture the magnitude of potential increases or that they will remain enforceable under

31

all circumstances. Moreover, our ability to negotiate or enforce such provisions in future PPAs depends on our market position and regulatory environment.

Moreover, although we have entered into a long-term gas supply agreement intended to mitigate our exposure to volatile fuel prices by securing more predictable fuel supply terms, if market prices diverge significantly from contract pricing, or if broader economic or political pressures arise, our counterparty may be unwilling or unable to perform its contractual obligations, whether due to economic disincentives or operational constraints. In such case, we may be forced to procure fuel on the spot market at significantly higher prices, which could materially reduce our margins and negatively impact our business, financial condition and results of operations.

**Operational disruptions and infrastructure limitations could adversely affect our ability to meet contractual obligations and impact our financial performance.**

Our ability to generate revenue depends on the continued availability, reliability, and adequate maintenance of the Facility. Planned outages are scheduled based on projected operating hours using commercial generation modeling, while unplanned outage assumptions are derived from industry benchmarks and the Facilities' expected performance. Additionally, our equipment, even if maintained in accordance with good practices, is subject to operational failure, including events that are beyond our control, and may require unplanned expenditures to operate efficiently. Unplanned outages of our Facility, including extensions of scheduled outages due to mechanical failures, as well as other problems such as equipment malfunctions at the Facility or any ancillary facilities or support structures, occur from time to time and are an inherent risk of our business. Unplanned outages typically increase operation and maintenance expenses and may reduce our revenues or require us to incur additional costs. For example, in July 2025, we experienced a partial unplanned outage that lasted 176 days due to a rotor failure in one of the gas turbine generator units. As a result of such failure, we immediately initiated a warranty claim under the EPC Contract and worked with GE generator specialists who conducted several on-site and off-site diagnostic tests. The EPC Contractor and the equipment vendor completed the repairs and returned the equipment to reliable and continuous operation. Additionally, an investigation was conducted to determine the cause of the equipment failure. The investigation concluded that the most likely cause of the rotor failure in the gas turbine generator was the result of small metal fragments left inside the generator during the original manufacturing process. The total revenue losses associated with this outage are estimated at up to U.S.$5.27 million, representing the amount being claimed under our business interruption insurance policy (which is subject to a 60-day deductible). Although we have submitted a claim under our business interruption insurance in respect of such losses, as of the date of this offering memorandum, we cannot ascertain or provide any assurances that we will recover all or any part of such loss from our insurance coverage claim. For further information see "Summary—Independent Consultants' Reports—Independent Engineer Report".

In addition, despite our attempts to create redundancy and protocols to reduce systemic risks of equipment failure, we cannot guarantee that any or all of our power generation or other ancillary equipment at our Facility will not malfunction again or become otherwise be unavailable to generate electricity or support the ancillary functions for the Facility for an extended period of time. Although we rely on a combination of monitoring systems, EPC warranties, and a long-term service agreement with the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) to maintain operational integrity and reduce the risk of forced outages, unforeseen equipment failures, technical issues, or infrastructure degradation may still occur. Any such extended malfunction or unavailability would have an adverse effect on our results of operations.

Furthermore, adverse weather events, sabotage, or other disruptions could impair the operation or maintenance of our facilities, potentially delaying or reducing availability and output. If we fail to meet the required availability or delivery levels under our PPAs, other than in cases of force majeure, we could face reduced revenues, penalties, or even termination of such contracts. While we may mitigate certain risks through the purchase of replacement capacity in the short-term market, such alternatives may not be reliably available on acceptable terms or in sufficient quantities. Any of these events could materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

32

We are entirely dependent on one asset, the Facility, and three Distribution Companies customers to generate substantially all of our revenues.

We are dependent on our sole asset, the Facility, and three Distribution Companies, to generate substantially all of our revenue. We have entered into a total of three PPAs with EDEMET, EDECHI and ENSA with term of 20 years, which commenced in October 2024 and are set to expire in 2044. Revenues derived from these long-term agreements constitute a significant portion of our revenues and are expected to continue to constitute substantially all of our revenues for the foreseeable future. Accordingly, we are dependent on the Distribution Companies' continued willingness and ability to timely meet their respective contractual obligations to us. The PPAs are in general subject to:

- early termination provisions for the failure of a party to perform its obligations under the agreement;
- suspension or termination provisions for force majeure events beyond the control of the parties; and
- standard liability limitations with no specific limit.

There can be no assurance that the Distribution Companies will fulfill their obligations under the applicable PPAs, or that they will remain solvent. EDEMET and EDECHI are owned by Naturgy Energy Group, which has long-term credit ratings of Baa2 (Moody's), BBB (S&amp;P) and BBB (Fitch), and ENSA is owned by Empresas Públicas de Medellín (EPM) and is rated BB+ (stable) by Fitch Ratings. Any deterioration in the financial condition or creditworthiness of the Distribution Companies—including a downgrade, negative outlook, or withdrawal of their credit ratings, or, in the worst case, a failure to remain solvent—could impair their ability to meet their payment obligations under their agreements with us. This, in turn, could materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, prospects and our liquidity, including our ability to make payments on the Notes as well as meet general, administrative other operating expenses. Credit ratings are subject to ongoing review by the relevant rating agencies, and there can be no assurance that the current ratings or outlooks assigned to the Distribution Companies' controlling groups will remain in effect for any period of time or that they will not be downgraded or withdrawn in the future.

Our business requires substantial capital expenditures for ongoing maintenance and environmental requirements.

Responding to ongoing and unexpected maintenance requirements of our energy generation, transmission and transportation facilities may require incremental capital expenditures in the future. Furthermore, we may need to invest significant capital to modernize our existing facilities in order to comply with new emissions standards and other regulatory requirements. See "Overview of the Panamanian Electricity Industry—Environmental Regulation." Although our budget includes provisions for maintenance capital expenditures, if such expenditures increase significantly and we are unable to finance any such capital expenditures or we are required to use funds for such capital expenditures that would otherwise have been used to grow our business, our business could be adversely affected.

The Facility has a limited operating history.

The Facility is the sole asset and source of revenues of our business and we do not currently intend to develop or acquire any other assets. We have a very limited history of operations upon which an investor could evaluate our company. The financial statements included in this offering memorandum are our Parent Company's audited consolidated financial statements as of and for the years ended December 31, 2025, 2024 and 2023. However, the Facility began supplying energy and capacity into the National Interconnected System in October 2024 and achieved full commercial operation on July 24, 2025. In addition, despite our short operating history, we experienced a 176-day outage from July 21, 2025 through January 13, 2026. See “—Operational disruptions and infrastructure limitations could adversely affect our ability to meet contractual obligations and impact our financial performance.” Accordingly, our limited operational history makes it difficult to effectively evaluate our future prospects and may increase the risk that we will not be successful. Furthermore, the limited historical financial information available with respect to the Facility may make it difficult to assess our financial position and operating results for the dates and periods presented. You should consider our business and prospects in light of the risks and difficulties we may encounter in the market.
