**We may not be able to generate sufficient cash flows to meet our debt service obligations.**

The obligations to make payments of principal, premium, if any, and interest on the Notes will be solely our obligations. None of the Sponsors or any of their respective affiliates (other than us) or their respective incorporators, stockholders, members, directors, managers or officers will guarantee the payment of the Notes.

Our ability to make scheduled payments on, or to refinance, our obligations with respect to our indebtedness, including the Notes, will depend on our financial and operating performance, which in turn will be affected by general economic conditions and by financial, competitive, regulatory and other factors beyond our control. We cannot assure you that the Facility will generate sufficient cash flow or that future sources of capital will be available to us in an amount sufficient to enable us to service our indebtedness, including the Notes, or to fund our other liquidity needs. If we are unable to generate sufficient cash flow to satisfy our debt obligations, we may have to undertake alternative financing plans, such as refinancing or restructuring our debt, selling assets, reducing or delaying capital investments or seeking to raise additional capital.

We cannot assure you that any refinancing would be possible, that any assets could be sold or, if sold, of the timing of the sales and the amount of proceeds that may be realized from those sales, or that additional financing could be obtained on acceptable terms, if at all. The Indenture that will govern the Notes will restrict our ability to dispose of assets and use the proceeds from the disposition and may also restrict our ability to raise debt or equity capital to be used to repay other indebtedness when it becomes due. We may not be able to consummate those dispositions or

51

to obtain proceeds in an amount sufficient to meet any debt service obligations then due. Our inability to generate sufficient cash flows to satisfy our debt obligations, or to refinance our indebtedness on commercially reasonable terms, would materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, prospects and our ability to repay the Notes.

If we cannot make scheduled payments on our debt, we will be in default and holders of the Notes could declare all outstanding principal and interest to be due and payable, causing a cross-acceleration or cross-default under other debt agreements, and we could be forced into insolvency, liquidation or restructuring proceedings.

**Certain restrictive covenants contained in the Indenture governing the Notes will limit our operating and financial flexibility in operating our business.**

The Indenture governing the Notes will contain restrictive affirmative and negative (including in relation to indebtedness) and other covenants that limit or prohibit, among other things, the manner in which we may structure or operate our business, including by limiting our ability to:

- incur indebtedness;
- make restricted payments and investments;
- create liens;
- sell assets;
- enter into transactions with affiliates; and
- create subsidiaries.

See “Description of the Notes—Certain Covenants of the Issuer.” As a result of these covenants, we will be limited in the manner in which we conduct our business, and we may be unable to engage in favorable business opportunities.

**The Notes will be secured only to the extent of the value of the assets that have been granted as security for the Notes.**

If there is an event of default on the Notes, the holders of the Notes will be secured only to the extent of the value of the Collateral underlying their security interest. To the extent that the claims of the holders of the Notes exceed the value of the assets securing the Notes and other obligations, those claims will rank equally with the claims of the holders of all other existing and future senior unsecured indebtedness ranking equally in right of payment with the Notes. As a result, if the value of the assets pledged or hypothecated as security for the Notes is less than the value of the claims of the holders of the Notes, those claims may not be satisfied in full before the claims of certain unsecured creditors are paid. Furthermore, upon enforcement against any collateral or in insolvency, the claims of the holders of the Notes to the proceeds of such enforcement will rank equal in right of payment with the claims of the lenders and other holders of any future senior indebtedness secured by the Collateral. As a result, holders of the Notes will receive less from the proceeds of the Collateral in an enforcement action or insolvency proceeding than if they were not required to share proceeds. See “—The rights of the holders of Notes with respect to the Collateral are subject to the terms of the Intercreditor Agreement and the other Security Documents, which may materially limit the rights of the holders of the Notes to take enforcement actions, including with respect to the Collateral securing the Notes.”

No appraisal of the value of the Collateral has been made in connection with this offering and the fair market value of the Collateral may be subject to fluctuations based on factors that include, among others, general economic conditions, industry conditions and similar factors. The amount to be received upon a sale of the Collateral would be dependent on numerous factors, including, but not limited to, the actual fair market value of the Collateral at such time, the timing and the manner (including the possibility of the Collateral or portions thereof being sold together or as an operating business) of the sale and the availability of prospective buyers. By its nature, some of the assets that comprise the Collateral may be illiquid and may have no readily ascertainable market value or any other comparable

value at all. We cannot assure you that the Collateral can be sold and, even if saleable, the timing of its liquidation and the value to be derived therefrom are uncertain. In the event of a foreclosure, liquidation, bankruptcy or similar proceeding, the Collateral may not be sold in a timely or orderly manner, and the proceeds from any sale or liquidation of this Collateral may not be sufficient to repay the obligations under the Notes.

Panamanian securities markets are influenced, to varying degrees, by economic and market conditions in other countries, especially those in Latin America and other emerging markets. Emerging markets like Panama are subject to greater risks than more developed markets, and financial turmoil in any emerging market could disrupt business in Panama and adversely affect the price of the Notes. Moreover, financial turmoil in any important emerging market country may adversely affect prices in stock markets and prices for debt securities of issuers in other emerging market countries as investors move their money to more stable, developed markets. There can be no assurance that the value of the Notes will not be negatively affected by events in other emerging markets or the global economy in general.

Rights of holders of Notes in the Collateral may be materially adversely affected by insolvency proceedings under Panamanian Law.

The right of the Collateral Agent to repossess and dispose of the Collateral securing the Notes upon acceleration is likely to be significantly impaired if any reorganization or liquidation proceedings under Panama's insolvency law are commenced by or against us prior to or possibly even after the Collateral Agent has repossessed and disposed of the Collateral. Under applicable insolvency laws, a secured creditor, such as the Collateral Agent, is typically prohibited for a specified period from repossessing its security from a debtor during any reorganization proceedings in an insolvency case, or from disposing of security repossessed from a debtor, without insolvency court approval. Moreover, applicable insolvency law generally permits the debtor to continue to retain and to use Collateral and the proceeds, products, rents or profits of the Collateral, even though the debtor is in default under the applicable debt instruments, provided that the secured creditor is given "adequate protection." The meaning of the term "adequate protection" may vary according to circumstances and applicable law, but it is intended in general to protect the value of the secured creditor's interest in the Collateral and may include cash payments or the granting of additional security, if and at such time as the court in its discretion determines, for any diminution in the value of the Collateral as a result of the stay of repossession or disposition or any use of the Collateral by the debtor during the pendency of the insolvency case. In view of the broad discretionary powers of an insolvency court, it is impossible to predict how long payments under the Notes could be delayed following commencement of an insolvency case, whether or when the Collateral Agent would repossess or dispose of the Collateral, and whether or to what extent holders of the Notes would be compensated for any delay in payment or loss of value of the Collateral through the requirements of "adequate protection". Furthermore, in the event the insolvency or other applicable court determines that the value of the Collateral is not sufficient to repay all amounts due on the Notes, the holders of the Notes would have an "undersecured claim," with respect to any outstanding amount not guaranteed by the Collateral, which means that they would have a secured claim to the extent of the value of the Collateral and an unsecured claim for the difference. Moreover, during any reorganization proceeding, the accrual of any interest (other than those attributable to claims secured by the Collateral or other secured claims) in reorganization proceedings shall remain suspended until a reorganization plan is approved. For further information relating to insolvency proceedings, see "Overview of the Panamanian Electricity Industry—Insolvency Regime".

The Intercreditor Agent, the Collateral Agent, the Panamanian Trustee or the Indenture Trustee may fail or refuse to act under the Indenture, the Intercreditor Agreement or other security documents for the Notes if they are not provided with adequate security and/or indemnification.

Under the Indenture, the Intercreditor Agreement and certain Security Documents, the failure to provide adequate security or indemnification to the Collateral Agent, the Intercreditor Agent, the Panamanian Trustee or the Indenture Trustee, as applicable, as satisfactory to the Collateral Agent, the Intercreditor Agent, the Panamanian Trustee or the Indenture Trustee, as applicable, will justify such agent's failure or refusal to act under such documents. To the extent that a security and/or indemnification provided by us is not satisfactory to the Collateral Agent, the Intercreditor Agent, the Panamanian Trustee or the Indenture Trustee, as applicable, for the exercise of any right or remedy under the Indenture, the Intercreditor Agreement or the applicable Security Documents, as applicable, that may cause the Collateral Agent, the Intercreditor Agent, the Panamanian Trustee or the Indenture Trustee to incur liability or expense (including any enforcement or collection proceeding resulting from an Event of Default under the Indenture), the holders of the Notes will be required to provide such agent with security and/or indemnification

54

satisfactory to such agent against any and all liability and expense that may be incurred by such agent by reason of taking or continuing to take action under the Indenture, the Intercreditor Agreement or such Security Documents. Failure by the holders of Notes to provide such security and/or indemnification may result in the Collateral Agent, the Intercreditor Agent, the Panamanian Trustee or the Indenture Trustee failing or refusing to act under the Indenture, the Intercreditor Agreement or the Security Documents, which could have a material adverse effect on the rights of the holders of Notes under the Notes or with respect to the Collateral.

## The Collateral securing the Notes may be diluted under certain circumstances.

The Collateral may secure Additional Notes, issued or entered into, in the future in certain circumstances, subject to, restrictions on and conditions to any such issuance contained in the Indenture. In addition, the Collateral is shared with the LC Lenders on a pari passu basis. The rights of holders of Notes to the Collateral could be diluted by any such increase in the indebtedness secured by the Collateral. See “Description of the Notes—Further Issues” and “—Security.”

## The covenants in the Indenture will contain broad exceptions to allow the Corporate Reorganization, which could allow us to take actions which may not be in the interests of the holders of the Notes.

Following the Issue Date, we intend to undertake the Corporate Reorganization in order to simplify our corporate structure by consolidating and merging with the Holding Company. To allow us to implement the Corporate Reorganization efficiently, the covenants in the Indenture, including the covenants relating to restricted payments and investments, will contain broad exceptions to allow the Corporate Reorganization. See “Description of the Notes—Disposition of Issue Date Proceeds” and “—Certain Covenants of the Issuer—Disposition of Issue Date Proceeds.” While we do not expect that the Corporate Reorganization would affect any of the restrictions to be imposed on us or the Collateral pursuant to the terms of the Notes, it is possible that these exceptions may allow us to take actions as part of the Corporate Reorganization which may not be in the interests of the holders of the Notes. Any such actions could have a material adverse effect on our ability to repay the Notes and on your investment in the Notes.

## The Indenture will not be qualified under the Trust Indenture Act and the obligations of the Indenture Trustee are limited.

The Indenture will not be qualified as an indenture under the Trust Indenture Act of 1939 (the “Trust Indenture Act”), and the Indenture Trustee will not be required to qualify as a trustee under the Trust Indenture Act. Thus, the holders of the Notes will not have the benefit of the protection of the Trust Indenture Act with respect to the Indenture or the Indenture Trustee. The protections generally afforded to the holder of a security issued under an indenture that has been qualified under the Trust Indenture Act include: (i) disqualification of the indenture trustee for “conflicting interests,” as defined in the Trust Indenture Act; provisions preventing a trustee that is also a creditor of the Co-Issuers from improving its own credit; (ii) position at the expense of the security holders immediately prior to or after a default under such indenture; (iii) the requirement that the indenture trustee deliver reports at least annually with respect to certain matters concerning the indenture trustee and the securities; and (iv) unanimous voting thresholds for certain amendments.

## Application of existing tax laws, rules and regulations is subject to interpretation by taxing authorities and our positions with respect to the tax treatment of the Notes, the Corporate Reorganization and other complex matters may be subject to disagreement by Tax authorities.

We may be subject to certain taxes in numerous jurisdictions, including Panama. While we may rely on consultations with outside accounting and tax experts in computing our obligations under tax laws, rules and regulations, we are required to take various tax accounting and reporting positions on complex matters, including for example, the tax treatment of the Notes and the Corporate Reorganization, that are not entirely free from doubt and for which we have not received rulings from the governing authorities. We are also subject to intercompany transfer pricing laws.

Tax authorities in Panama or in any other applicable jurisdiction may disagree with the positions we have taken or intend to take regarding the tax treatment or characterization of any of our transactions, such as the tax treatment or characterization of our indebtedness, existing and future intercompany loans or the deduction of interest

55

expenses. Although we believe our tax positions, including those with respect to the Corporate Reorganization, are reasonable, we cannot assure you that the applicable taxing authorities will agree with our positions.

If any applicable tax authorities were to successfully challenge the tax treatment or characterization of any of our intercompany transactions, including the Corporate Reorganization, it could result in the disallowance of deductions, a limitation on our ability to deduct interest expenses, the imposition of withholding taxes, the application of penalties and accrued interest on intercompany loans or internal deemed transfers or other consequences that could have a material and adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations, which could in turn adversely affect our ability to fulfill our obligations under the Notes or cause the market price of the Notes to decline.

## Our obligations under the Notes will be subordinated to statutory preferences.

Under Panamanian law, our obligations under the Notes are subordinated to specified statutory preferences for payment of claims, including claims for wages, social security, certain insurance claims, taxes, court fees and expenses, and other separately secured claims. In the event of our liquidation, these preferences will have priority over any other claims, including claims by any holder in respect of the Notes and, as a result, holders of Notes may be unable to recover amounts due under the Notes, in whole or in part.

## Our ability to amend, waive or modify the terms of the Notes may affect your rights.

We, together with the Indenture Trustee, may amend, modify, or supplement the terms of the Notes and the related documents, or waive certain provisions, as permitted under the governing documents. Some amendments and waivers may be made without noteholders' consent—such as those intended to correct errors, cure ambiguities, or comply with legal or regulatory requirements—while others that could materially affect noteholders' rights if approved by the required specified percentage of noteholders.

The terms and conditions of the Notes and/or the documentation covering this Issue may be subject to modification or waiver in accordance with the terms of the Section labeled "Description of the Notes—Security" and "Amendment, Supplement and Waiver." The modification of terms of a public offering is regulated by special regulations, namely, Agreement No. 4-2003 of April 11, 2003.

Any such amendments, waivers, or modifications—could affect the value of the Notes and the noteholders' rights under the Indenture and Security Documents.

## Changes in tax laws or their interpretation could adversely affect the tax treatment of the Notes.

The tax treatment of interest on the Notes and any capital gains realized from their sale or other disposition is based on current laws, regulations, and interpretations. We cannot guarantee that these tax rules, or the official interpretation of them, will remain unchanged for the life of the Notes. Changes in tax legislation, tax treaties, administrative guidance, or court decisions—whether enacted by governmental authorities in our jurisdiction or in other relevant jurisdictions—could result in higher taxes, the elimination of tax benefits, or the imposition of additional reporting or withholding obligations.

Any such changes could reduce noteholders' after-tax return on the Notes, decrease the market value of their investment in the Notes, or require investors to take additional steps to comply with revised tax rules. Investors should consult their own tax advisors about the potential impact of future tax law changes on their individual situations.

# MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

The following discussion and analysis are derived from and should be read together with our historical financial statements and the notes thereto included elsewhere in this offering circular. The following discussion includes certain forward-looking statements. For a discussion of important factors, including the continuing development of our business, actions of regulatory authorities and competitors and other factors which could cause actual results to differ materially from the results referred to in the forward-looking statements, see “Cautionary Language Regarding Forward-Looking Statements” and “Risk Factors.”

## Overview

We are engaged in the generation and supply of electricity in Panama. We own and operate Generadora Gatún, a 670 MW natural gas-fired combined cycle power plant with 640 MW in net capacity, located on Telfers Island near Colón, adjacent to the Panama Canal (the "Facility" or the "Project"). The gas turbines of the Facility began to supply energy and capacity into the National Interconnected System in October 2024, and the steam turbine became fully operational in May 2025, increasing the Facility's efficiency and reaching commercial operation in July 2025.

We supply electricity to the National Interconnected System, which serves the country's energy demand across industrial, commercial, and residential sectors. International interconnections link the National Interconnected System with neighboring countries through the Panama's participation in the MER, where generators and demands located in any of the member countries can freely decide whether to carry out their energy purchase / sale transactions in the MER or in their own domestic markets. The six participant countries are Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama, Nicaragua and Guatemala. See "The Panama Electricity Market."

The Panamanian electricity market is primarily supported by a mix of hydropower, natural gas, and other thermal generation sources, with growing integration of renewable energy. The Facility is the largest natural gas power plant in Panama and Central America, strengthening the country's energy security and facilitating the transition to a more diversified generation mix. Additionally, the Panamanian power system operates under a competitive wholesale market model, managed by the CND and regulated by the ASEP. The state-owned transmission company, ETESA, plays a key role in system planning and the expansion of the transmission network. Panama also stands out as a strategic energy hub in the region, with international interconnections to Costa Rica and prospects for strengthening integration with Colombia. In recent years, long-term energy auctions have been promoted to encourage investment in renewable generation, particularly solar and wind, as part of the national energy transition strategy toward a cleaner, more resilient, and sustainable energy matrix.

We sell the electric power generated by us to the Distribution Companies through long-term PPAs for a capacity of up to 550 MW. Our capacity is 62.50% contracted for the first four years of operations and 85.90% contracted for years five through 20 under the PPAs, in each case, based on firm capacity, leaving additional opportunities for the Company to enter into additional PPAs or sell excess energy in the spot market. We have PPAs with EDECHI, EDEMET and ENSA, which collectively serve 83% of the Panamanian energy market and all of whose parent companies have credit rating profiles in line with those of Panama. EDECHI and EDEMET are 51.00% owned by Naturgy Energy Group (formerly, Gas Natural Fenosa) and ENSA is a 51.00% subsidiary of EPM. The Republic of Panama owns 48.30% of each of the Distribution Companies, with the remaining being owned by former employees of the Instituto de Recursos Hidráulicos y Electrificación ("IRHE"), a Panamanian government-owned utility that existed prior to the privatization of the Panamanian electricity market. The EDECHI and EDEMET PPAs are for the supply of 40MW and 200MW, respectively, during the first four years and 55 MW and 275 MW, respectively, for the remaining 16 years. The ENSA PPA is for the supply of 160 MW during the first four years and 220 MW for the remaining 16 years. Each of these PPAs has a tenor of 20 years, commencing from October 2024 and include certain "pass-through" provisions that allow us to transfer or share certain of our generation costs to our customers. The PPAs provide for a fixed capacity payment component (the "Capacity Revenue") and a partially fixed energy payment indexed to Henry Hub (the "Energy Revenue"). As a result, we believe our long-term PPAs provide a very stable source or recurring cash flow. See "Sources of Revenue," "Business—Main Contracts."

For the year ended December 31, 2025, our total energy sales under our PPAs were 239.97 GWh to EDECHI, 1,063.80 GWh to EDEMET, and 838.26 GWh to ENSA, and those sales represented 10.2%, 41.5% and 33.7% of our

operating revenues, respectively. For the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024, energy sales (i) under PPAs, comprised as energy sales – contracts were U.S.$182.97 million in 2025 and U.S.$42.05 million in 2024 and as capacity sales – contracts were U.S.$94.84 million in 2025 and U.S.$23.95 million in 2024, and (ii) in the spot market were U.S.$43.50 million in 2025 and U.S.$5.15 million in 2024.

## Principal Factors Affecting Our Results of Operations

### The Panamanian Electricity Sector

We believe the Panamanian government, the largest equity holder of AES Panamá, considers the electricity sector as vitally important to the continued economic growth of Panama. As our principal shareholders are leading electricity generation conglomerates in Panama and given that, as of the date of this offering memorandum, the government is an equity holder in the Distribution Companies and AES Panamá's majority equity holder, we believe the Panamanian government is committed to our success and understands the importance of generation assets to the Panamanian power sector. Accordingly, we believe the Panamanian government has an interest in the continued success of AES Panamá and InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas and thus our success and that of the Panamanian electricity sector.

### Long-term Contracts and the Spot Market

The Facility derives all of its revenue from the sale of electricity through firm capacity and energy supply PPAs, which account for 86.00% of our total revenue, as well as from merchant sales in the Panamanian spot market, which account for the remaining 14.00%. The Facility's primary customers are Panama's three energy distribution companies: EDEMET (owned by Naturgy Energy Group, which has a long-term debt rating of Baa2 by Moody's, BBB by S&amp;P and BBB by Fitch), EDECHI (also owned by Naturgy), and ENSA (which has a long-term debt rating of AAA(pan) by Fitch Ratings) and is owned by EPM (a state-owned company in Colombia, which has long-term debt rating of Baa3 by Moody's and BB by Fitch). As of December 31, 2025 and 2024, the revenue derived from the PPAs with the Distribution Companies represented 86.00% and 93.00% of our total revenues, respectively. Rating agencies continuously assess rating levels and there can be no assurance that the rating level or outlook of the Facility's primary customers will remain constant for any given period of time or that a rating level will not be lowered or withdrawn entirely by the credit rating agency if, in its judgment, circumstances in the future so warrant.

For the year ended December 31, 2025, we derived 86.00% of our total revenues from the PPAs with Distribution Companies, which revenues represented 57.00% Energy Revenues and 29.00% Capacity Revenues. The remaining 14.00% corresponded to energy sales in the spot market.

For the year ended December 31, 2024, we derived 93.00% of our total revenues from the PPAs with the Distribution Companies, which revenues represented 59.00% Energy Revenues and 34.00% Capacity Revenues. The remaining 7.00% corresponded to energy sales in the spot market.

As of the date of this offering memorandum, approximately 81.30% of the Facility's installed capacity (670 MW) is committed through 2044 pursuant to the PPAs with the Distribution Companies (see "Business—Main Contracts"), with the remainder expected to be sold in the spot market as merchant revenues.

# Transmission Charges and Adjustments

The transmission charges that we pay to ETESA for use of and connection to the transmission system and the integrated operation service include fixed charges and variable charges. ETESA sets the amount of variable transmission charges on an annual basis depending on the cost of transmission that ETESA expects to incur when a plant connects to the system. See “Overview of the Panamanian Electricity Industry—Transmission.” Each year, ETESA reviews the transmission charges actually paid by generation companies in the previous year against the actual cost of transmission in that year, and it applies adjustments. If actual charges paid exceed the actual cost of transmission, ETESA applies compensation adjustments in favor of the applicable generation company, and if the actual cost of transmission exceeds the actual charges paid, it applies compensation adjustments in favor of ETESA. These compensation adjustments can affect our transmission costs and costs of electricity sales.

# Fuel Costs and Variable Margins

Our fuel costs mainly derive from purchases of natural gas under a contract with Total pursuant to an LNG sale and purchase agreement, with pricing linked to the Henry Hub Natural Gas benchmark as determined based on the New York Mercantile Exchange (“NYMEX HH”). Generally, we pass through these supply costs to our off-takers pursuant to the PPAs. In addition, we also incur fuel costs in connection with any additional energy dispatched and sold in the spot market.

# Panamanian Economic Conditions

Our results of operations and financial condition depend on the Panamanian economy, inflation rates, interest rates, regulation, taxation, social instability, political unrest and other developments in or affecting Panama. In the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023, Panama’s economy registered real growth of 2.7% and 7.2%, respectively. If the growth of the Panamanian economy continues to slow, it could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition. Due to the small size and limited focus of the Panamanian economy, adverse developments in Panama (even developments affecting a single activity) could have a more pronounced effect than in a larger, more diversified economy.

# Fees Payable under Management and Administrative Agreements

We have entered into various agreements with our principal shareholders. Under the Original O&amp;M Agreement with AES Latin America, we agreed to pay AES Latin America monthly management services fees as follows: U.S.$45,833 increasing to U.S.$91,667 after the date the Facility became available for dispatch, in each case, adjusted annually for inflation. Similarly, under the Original ASA with InterEnergy Holdings UK, we agreed to pay InterEnergy Holdings UK monthly fees for administrative services, as follows: approximately U.S.$5,000 per month until the final notice to proceed under the underlying EPC Contract, U.S.$58,333 per month from the final notice to proceed under the EPC Contract until the available dispatch date, and U.S.$83,333 per month after the available for dispatch date. Under these agreements we pay for personnel costs incurred by AES Latin America and InterEnergy Holdings UK for rendering such services to us.

On or about the Issue Date, the Original O&amp;M Agreement and the Original ASA will be terminated and replaced by the New O&amp;M Agreement and the New ASA, respectively. The New O&amp;M Agreement and the New ASA will have an initial term of five years unless earlier terminated or extended by the mutual consent of both parties and their respective terms are otherwise substantially the same as under the Original O&amp;M Agreement and Original ASA, as the case maybe, except that the applicable services fee under (a) the New O&amp;M Agreement will be a fixed monthly service of U.S.$106,545.35, subject to annual CPI-based adjustments and (b) the New ASA will be fixed quarterly services fee of U.S.$319,636.05, subject to annual CPI-based adjustments.

We account for payments made pursuant to these agreements as in the statement of comprehensive income as management fees. As a result, the level of activity at the Facility and the commencement of operations has impacted and could continue to impact our Operating, general and maintenance expenses.

For additional information on these agreements, see “Related Party Transactions.”

Unplanned Outage and Equipment Failure

In July 2025, we experienced a partial unplanned outage that lasted 176 days due to a rotor failure in one of the gas turbine generator units. As a result of this failure, we immediately initiated a warranty claim under the EPC Contract and worked with GE generator specialists who conducted several on-site and off-site diagnostic tests, as well as an investigation to determine the cause of the equipment failure. The investigation concluded that the most likely cause of the rotor failure in the gas turbine generator was the result of small metal fragments left inside the generator during the original manufacturing process. The total revenue losses associated with this outage are estimated at up to U.S.$5.27 million, representing the amount being claimed under our business interruption insurance policy (which is subject to a 60-day deductible). Although we have submitted a claim under our business interruption insurance in respect of such losses, as of the date of this offering memorandum, we cannot ascertain or provide any assurances that we will recover all or any part of such loss from our insurance coverage claim. Notwithstanding the duration of the outage, we believe its impact on Generadora Gatún's results of operations was limited, primarily due to prevailing dispatch conditions during the outage period, including a seasonally high hydroelectric contribution (with 2025 being a particularly wet year), which reduced reliance on thermal generation. Unplanned outages of this nature may affect plant availability and could adversely impact our operating results and cash flows in future periods. See "Summary—Recent Developments" and "Risk Factors—Risks Relating to Our Business—Operational disruptions and infrastructure limitations could adversely affect our ability to meet contractual obligations and impact our financial performance."

## Electricity sales

Electricity sales for the year ended December 31, 2025 were U.S.$321.68 million, an increase of U.S.$250.53 million, or 77.88%, from U.S.$71.15 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to the first full year of sales under the PPAs, compared to a partial year in 2024 following the commencement of operations in October 2024.

## Operating costs and expenses

Total operating costs and expenses for the year ended December 31, 2025 were U.S.$264.72 million, an increase of U.S.$202.32 million from U.S.$62.40 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. Our operating costs consist primarily of electricity purchases, fuel costs, depreciation and amortization, operating, maintenance, and transmission costs and General and administrative expenses, as described below.

## Electricity purchases

Electricity purchases for the year ended December 31, 2025 were U.S.$45.49 million, an increase of U.S.$21.98 million, or 48.32%, from U.S.$23.51 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to higher dispatch volumes during 2025 and the associated purchases required to manage system conditions and meet delivery obligations.

## Fuel costs

Fuel costs for the year ended December 31, 2025 were U.S.$151.39 million, an increase of U.S.$124.13 million, or 81.99%, from U.S.$27.26 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to the first full year of the Facility's operations in 2025, with an increase in generation of 1,963.26 GWh to 2,511.32 GWh for the year ended December 31, 2025 from 588.06 GWh for the year ended December 31, 2024, which in turn resulted in higher LNG consumption relative to the partial operating period in 2024.

## Depreciation and amortization

Depreciation and amortization expense for the year ended December 31, 2025 was U.S.$41.82 million, an increase of U.S.$32.75 million, or 78.31%, from U.S.$9.07 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to the recognition of depreciation for a full year of operations in 2025, including the impact of the depreciation of power plant assets placed in service in 2025 following the commencement of operations and the amortization of intangible assets related to acquired PPAs and amortization of right of use assets in accordance with IAS 16, IAS 38 and IFRS 16, compared to a partial-year depreciation profile in 2024.

## Operating, maintenance, and transmission costs

Operating, maintenance and transmission costs for the year ended December 31, 2025 were U.S.$16.14 million, an increase of U.S.$15.13 million, or 93.74%, from U.S.$1.01 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to the ramp-up of operations during 2025, mainly (i) transmission charges paid to ETESA under the interconnection agreement, representing regulated tolls for the use of the national transmission grid associated with dispatch of energy and capacity under the PPAs, (ii) fixed and variable operating and maintenance expenses, including plant staffing, technical services, maintenance contracts, spare parts, consumables and plant support services, incurred throughout the full operating year and (iii) security services and site

support costs, including utilities, insurance-related operational services and logistical support required for continuous plant operation.

## General and administrative expenses

General and administrative expenses for the year ended December 31, 2025 were U.S.$9.88 million, an increase of U.S.$8.33 million, or 84.31%, from U.S.$1.55 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to the first full year of operations in 2025 mainly due to (i) a U.S.$3.77 million increase in personnel expenses, related to compensation of corporate and plant administrative staff, including salaries, social security contributions, labor benefits, thirteenth-month bonuses and accrued severance obligations; (ii) a U.S.$0.65 million increase in professional services, including legal, audit, tax advisory and regulatory compliance services, as well as administration fees payable under the Original ASA, (iii) a U.S.$1.61 million increase in office maintenance and related expenses, including utilities, office services, and general corporate infrastructure costs associated with the our headquarters in Panama City; and (iv) an increase in other administrative costs, including bank fees, travel and transportation, IT services, insurance-related administrative expenses and other recurring corporate costs.

## Other (expenses) income

Other expenses for the year ended December 31, 2025 were U.S.$60.02 million, an increase of U.S.$46.32 million, from U.S.$13.70 million for the year ended December 31, 2024, primarily as a result of the net effect of finance costs and other income as described below.

## Finance cost, net

Finance cost, net, for the year ended December 31, 2025 was of U.S.$69.20 million, an increase of U.S.$54.78 million, or 79.16%, compared to U.S.$14.42 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to the transition from the construction phase to the operational phase of the Facility, mainly due to (i) interest of U.S.$49.52 million under the Existing Project Loan and U.S.$12.82 million under the Existing HoldCo Loan, (ii) U.S.$10.71 million in amortization of deferred financing costs, including upfront and arrangement fees and (iii) U.S.$5.23 million in interest accruals related to accounts payable for intangible asset acquisitions. This increase was partially offset by (i) U.S.$13.26 million in derivative earnings associated with interest rate hedging instruments and (ii) interest income from restricted and operating cash accounts.

## Other income, net

Other income, net, for the year ended December 31, 2025 was of U.S.$9.18 million, an increase of U.S.$8.46 million, or 92.16%, compared to U.S.$0.72 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to U.S.$38.16 million in non-core revenue from gas sales, partially offset by U.S.$29.02 million in the cost of gas sold, resulting in a net positive contribution reflected in other income, net.

## Net loss

Our net loss for the year ended December 31, 2025 was U.S.$8.64 million, an increase in loss of U.S.$2.25 million, or 26.04%, compared to a net loss of U.S.$6.39 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to higher income tax expense to U.S.$5.58 million in 2025 from U.S.$1.44 million in 2024, due to improved operating performance from a full year of operations as described above, which resulted in a net loss before tax of U.S.$3.06 million in 2025, compared to a net loss before tax of U.S.$4.95 million in 2024.

## Other comprehensive income (loss)

Other comprehensive loss for the year ended December 31, 2025 was U.S.$23.61 million, a decrease of U.S.$33.42 million or 141.55% from U.S.$9.81 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This decrease was primarily attributable to movements in the fair value of interest rate swaps designated as cash flow hedges of the Existing Project Loan, mainly due to shifts in market interest rate expectations and discount curves, resulting in unfavorable mark-to-market adjustments.

# Cash Flows

## Cash Flows from Operating Activities

Our net cash provided by operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2025 was U.S.$75.85 million, as compared to U.S.$4.49 million in net cash provided by operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2024. This increase was primarily attributable to the first full year of commercial operations in 2025, compared to a partial operating year in 2024, resulting in stabilized electricity sales under PPAs, normalization of working capital balances, improved fuel procurement efficiency and steady-state cash flow from operations.

Our net cash provided by operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 was U.S.$4.49 million, as compared to U.S.$2.57 million in net cash used in operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2023. This reversal was primarily attributable to the transition from the development and construction phase of our Facility to operational readiness, following the commencement of our dispatch of energy and capacity in October 2024, partially offset by an increase operating cash outflows for administrative expenses and the initial build-up of working capital.

## Cash Flows from Investing Activities

Our net cash used in investing activities for the year ended December 31, 2025 was U.S.$25.87 million, a decrease of U.S.$150.15 million or 85.30% from U.S.$176.02 million for the year ended December 31, 2024. This decrease was primarily attributable to the substantial completion of construction activities in 2024 when we reflected final EPC milestone payments and commissioning-related disbursements, as compared to 2025 when investing cash flows were limited to residual capital expenditures related to post-commencement of operations and minor operational enhancements, consistent with a fully operational asset.

Our net cash used in investing activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 was U.S.$176.02 million, a decrease of U.S.$140.27 million or 44.35% from U.S.$316.29 million for the year ended December 31, 2023. This decrease was primarily attributable to lower use of restricted cash in the amount of U.S.$65.49 million and lower payments to sellers in the amount of U.S.$60.00 million made during the construction phase in 2023, partially offset by higher investment disbursements in connection with construction progress in the amount of U.S.$150.13 million.

## Cash Flows from Financing Activities

Our net cash used in financing activities for the year ended December 31, 2025 was U.S.$51.54 million, as compared to net cash provided by financing activities of U.S.$206.49 million for the year ended December 31, 2024, representing a decrease of U.S.$258.05 million or 124.96%. This variation reflects the transition from construction-phase funding to an amortizing project finance profile. Financing cash flows in 2024 were primarily driven by debt drawdowns and capital contributions, whereas 2025 reflects scheduled principal amortization, the absence of material new debt drawings and normalization of the capital structure following full operational ramp-up.

Our net cash provided by financing activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 was U.S.$206.49 million, a decrease of U.S.$112.37 million or 35.2% from U.S.$318.87 million for the year ended December 31, 2023. This decrease was primarily attributable to a U.S.$162.82 million decrease in disbursements under the Existing Facilities, partially offset by (i) a U.S.$20.65 million increase in interest paid on outstanding debt under the Existing Facilities and (ii) U.S.$70.09 million in inflows from capital contributions from our shareholders.

# Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosure about Market Risk

We are exposed to specific risks in the business environment in which we operate. These risks include exposure to derivative transactions, liquidity, interest rates, inflation, and customer credit risks arising in the normal course of business. Generally, our overall objective is to ensure that management understands, measures and monitors these various risks and take appropriate actions to minimize our exposure to such risks. Our policies for managing each of these risks are described below.

# Liquidity Risk

We have adopted liquidity risk management practices that are intended to maintain sufficient cash. We maintain short-term financing lines with financial institutions in Panama that provide them with the required operational flexibility to comply with our electricity purchases and other obligations.

# Credit Risk

We are party to bilateral contracts relating to the sale of energy and associated capacity to the Distribution Companies. We risk non-performance by our counterparties of their obligations under these contracts and agreements. This risk is partially mitigated by the existing payment guarantees issued by Distribution Companies.

75

# Commodities Risk

We are exposed to commodities risk in connection with the purchase of LNG required to operate the Facility. We pass through volatility in fuel prices to offtakers under the PPAs, partially mitigating this risk.

# Inflation Risk

Inflation in Panama is measured by the CPI variation, as computed by the National Institute of Statistics and Census (Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo) a specialized unit within the Comptroller General office, using a standard basket of goods and services. The current basket uses the 2013 price level as the basis for determining the CPI and is affected, by the prices of food staples (fruits and vegetables, basic grains such as corn, rice and beans, and others), education, furniture and other home goods, utilities, clothes, health, recreation, communications and transport

While inflation in Panama has remained relatively low in recent years, certain cost components of the Company's operations are partially linked to inflation-sensitive inputs. In particular, 40% of the energy tariff is indexed to natural gas prices, which in turn reference the EIA Henry Hub Spot Price. By contrast, capacity payments are indexed to 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds and are not linked to fuel costs or CPI variation, as they are associated with firm capacity and not fuel-based dispatch.

Although a portion of the LNG supply cost may be CPI-linked, this is not expected to have a material impact on our margins under current inflation levels. Accordingly, inflation risk is considered partially mitigated, though it may become more relevant under a sustained high-inflation scenario.

# OVERVIEW OF THE PANAMANIAN ELECTRICITY INDUSTRY

Panama has a mixed hydro-thermal electricity system with a current installed generating capacity (including auto-generators) of approximately 4,968 MW (36.62% hydroelectric, 42.93% thermal, 6.66% wind and 13.79% solar), with a peak demand of 1,915 MW, as of June 30, 2025 (the latest available data). In addition, as of June 30, 2025, the national electricity system supplied energy to 1,309,872 customers, an increase of 1.1% from June 2024. In 2019, Panama's driest year on record, approximately 47% of gross generation output came from hydroelectric facilities. Over 38.9% of the generating capacity is located in the western region of the country, close to the Costa Rican border, where the majority of Panama's hydroelectric resources are located. A 429-kilometer transmission line links these hydroelectric facilities to the load center in the Panama City-Colón corridor.

The electricity system in Panama is interconnected with those of Costa Rica, Honduras, Nicaragua, El Salvador and Guatemala. The governments of Central America have developed a regional electricity market, including an interconnected system known as the Central American Interconnection System or SIEPAC (Sistema de Interconexión de los Países de América Central). The project consists of an approximately 1,800 km transmission line across the six countries of the isthmus, from Guatemala to Panama. This 230 kV single-circuit transmission line has increased the interconnection capacity between each country to 300 MW. The regional transmission line began partial operations in 2010 and became fully operational in the middle of 2014.

Since 2017, electricity sales by Distribution Companies have been growing at an average of approximately 2.4% per year and in June 2025 totaled 4.62 TWh, of which 34.82% was residential, 47.31% was commercial, 1.63% was industrial and 16.24% was used by the public sector including street lighting. This is equivalent to a monthly consumption rate of approximately 6,781 kWh per customer (2,958 kWh for residential customers only).

## Regulatory Entities

The organizations that participate in the regulation of the electricity sector in Panama are:

- The National Energy Secretariat (Secretaría Nacional de Energía or SNE). The energy sector, including electricity, is under the jurisdiction of the SNE. The SNE is responsible for proposing a national energy policy that ensures rational, efficient and sustainable use of resources and energy. More specifically, the SNE has, as part of its duties, the primary responsibility of designing and proposing national electricity policy, with the collaboration of other government agencies such as the ASEP and the ETESA Planning Unit. As such, the SNE recommends ETESA to launch new power purchase bids to cover the supply commitments of the Distribution Companies on a short, medium and long term strategy basis.

- The National Authority of Public Services (Autoridad Nacional de los Servicios Públicos or ASEP). The ASEP is the regulator of public services, empowered with overseeing and regulating these activities. The ASEP regulates power generation, transmission, interconnection, and distribution activities in the electric power sector; approves generation and transmission programs for the National Interconnected System; and promotes competition within the different areas of the energy sector so that economically efficient and high-quality energy services are provided. Its responsibilities include: (i) regulating the electricity sector, (ii) establishing the criteria, methodologies and formulas to be followed to determine the tariffs applicable to certain public electricity services such as transmission and distribution, (iii) establishing the tariff structure for access to and use of the grids, (iv) classifying which consumers of electricity are subject to tariff regulation and (v) determining the rules for the planning and coordination of the National Interconnected System.

- ETESA. ETESA is responsible for preparing the transmission expansion plans for the National Interconnected System. ETESA is also responsible for forecasting the overall energy demand in Panama and determining ways to satisfy such demand. Utility companies are required to provide the information necessary to allow ETESA to prepare the transmission expansion plans. ETESA is also responsible for managing the procurement of new power purchase agreements on behalf of the country's three Distribution Companies. Under this system, each Distribution Company submits its expected needs to ETESA, which in turn runs a competitive bidding process for power supply.

- The National Dispatch Center (Centro Nacional de Despacho or CND). The CND is a sub-unit of ETESA. The CND is the operator of the National Interconnected System, and the market administrator. The CND responsible for planning, supervising and controlling the integrated operation of the National Interconnected System and for ensuring its safe and reliable operation. The CND is also responsible, among others, for (i) coordinating the operation of the National Interconnected System with regional dispatch centers, (ii) receiving information necessary for dispatch planning, including the generation costs for each generator, (iii) developing daily demand forecasts and managing dispatch, (iv) determining the hourly energy spot prices in the spot market and the amounts of electricity sold, (v) managing the transmission network and the auxiliary services required for the proper operation of the National Interconnected System (vi) providing settlement values on a monthly basis with respect to the division of energy between suppliers and producers and (viii) managing the commercial transactions among participants of the wholesale electricity market.

- The Environment Ministry (Ministerio de Ambiente). The Environment Ministry was created on March 28, 2015, pursuant to Law No. 8 of March 25, 2015, to replace the National Environmental Authority, which had previously been responsible for implementing environmental policy, as Panama's governing body for matters of protection, conservation, preservation and restoration of the environment and the sustainable use of natural resources. The Environment Ministry is also responsible for the design, approval and implementation of the national environmental policy and for ensuring compliance with and application of the laws and regulations that fall within its purview. The Environment Ministry is also in charge of approving the environmental impact assessments required for projects, including those related to the electricity sector.

## History

Prior to the privatization of Panama's generation and distribution sectors in 1998, the country's electricity sector was managed by the state-owned, vertically integrated utility, Instituto de Recursos Hidráulicos y Electrificación ("IRHE"). Established in 1961, IRHE's initial purpose was to provide service in areas not covered by private utilities and to promote the overall development of electricity services in Panama.

Over time, IRHE gradually assumed control of assets and operations previously held by private utilities. Starting in the mid-1970s, it significantly expanded the country's generation capacity, particularly through the development of new hydroelectric plants in western Panama. IRHE also introduced a national dispatch center to optimize system operations and facilitate electricity exchanges with the Panama Canal Commission and neighboring Central American countries.

In 1997, the Panamanian government launched a comprehensive power sector reform by initiating the privatization of IRHE. This reform was part of a broader program that included the creation of a new regulatory framework, the establishment of a wholesale electricity market, the adoption of updated tariff regulations, and the unbundling of IRHE's operations into three segments: generation, transmission, and distribution. As part of this restructuring, IRHE's generation operations were divided into four generation companies; its distribution activities were split into three geographically based companies; and its transmission operations were consolidated into a single entity.

In September 1998, the Panamanian government conducted a public auction in which it sold 51% of the shares in each Distribution Company. This was followed in November 1998 by the sale of 49% of the shares in each of the three state-owned hydroelectric generation companies and 51% of the shares in the principal thermoelectric generation company. These transactions were finalized in 1999.

The Panamanian government retained ownership of ETESA, the state-owned transmission company, which continues to operate and control the national transmission system (230kV and selected 115kV lines). Bidding requirements for privatization mandated that each consortium include a company—either directly or through an affiliate—with a minimum level of experience in electricity generation or distribution.

The legal foundation for this privatization process was established by Law No. 6 of February 3, 1997, which set the parameters for reform and the accompanying regulatory structure. Panama's wholesale electricity market

77

became operational in 1999. Under this new model, generation was opened to competition, while transmission (state-owned) and distribution (mixed ownership) were treated as regulated public services.

# The National Authority of Public Services (ASEP)

The 1996 Regulatory Entity for Public Services Law established the Ente Regulador de los Servicios Públicos, an autonomous government agency with responsibility for regulating water, telecommunications, radio and TV, electricity and natural gas. Pursuant to Decree Law No. 10 of February 22, 2006, the Ente Regulador de los Servicios Públicos was restructured and changed its name to Autoridad Nacional de los Servicios Públicos (the National Authority of Public Services or ASEP). ASEP is headed by a general administrator, whose appointment is subject to ratification by the National Assembly.

ASEP's responsibilities include:

- ensuring compliance with sector laws and regulations and applying sanctions;
- issuing concessions and licenses;
- monitoring quality of service standards;
- verifying fulfillment of expansion and system improvement targets as required by law, regulation or under the terms of specific concessions or licenses;
- promoting competition and investigating monopolistic or anti-competitive practices;
- determining efficiency criteria for evaluating the performance of regulated companies;
- establishing the principles and methodologies for tariff regulation;
- determining the information and the frequency of such information to be provided by public service providers;
- arbitrating conflicts between operators, government agencies, municipalities and consumers; and
- authorizing rights of way for the provision of public electricity services.

The ASEP is financed from various sources, including fees payable by all providers of electricity services. These fees, which are payable monthly and are not recoverable from consumers, may not exceed one percent (1%) of gross sector revenues in the preceding year on an annual basis. For each individual company, the applicable percentage is applied to revenues from regulated and non-regulated customers less amounts paid by that company to other service providers to cover energy or transmission costs. The fees stipulated by the ASEP for control, supervision and regulation are often variable amounts established annually. The 2025 fee is equivalent to 0.8130% and shall be applied to the total gross income obtained by the electricity services providers to the fiscal period corresponding to 2024. This fee was established by the ASEP through Resolution AN No. 1375-ADM of December 4, 2024.

ASEP may impose sanctions of up to U.S.$20 million, depending on the nature and severity of the violations, as detailed in the Electricity Law. Other considerations for determining the amount of the sanctions include any corrective measures taken, the degree of interruption to the electricity industry, and the complexity and time required to correct any damages. Additionally, any delays in following ASEP orders for corrective measures, or failure to take action pursuant to such order, may result in fines of up to U.S.$10,000 per day until measures are implemented. Fines are applied as discounts to consumers. Additional sanctions may include terminating a concession agreement or cancellation of licenses.

Moreover, ASEP is duly empowered to intervene the public services companies, when necessary, including for purposes of guaranteeing the efficient, continued and uninterrupted rendering of public services subject to the restrictions set out in the Electricity Law.

78

79

# The Electricity Law

The Electricity Law was introduced to improve operation efficiencies, achieve reliable and good quality service, guarantee good quality of supply through the promotion of competition and private sector participation, and keep the cost of the service at reasonable prices. Key provisions include:

- defining the duties and obligations of electricity service providers including continuity of supply and provision of open access in transmission and distribution;
- dividing the generation, transmission and distribution operations of IRHE into separate companies and establishing requirements for management and accounting separation of generation, transmission and distribution activities;
- restricting participation by Distribution Companies in generation and in transmission and by generation companies in the control of Distribution Companies;
- establishing procedures for privatization of the sector other than ETESA, the company formed to hold IRHE’s transmission assets, which was to remain wholly state-owned;
- establishing procedures for granting concessions and licenses subject to limitations on the market shares of individual generators and distributors;
- defining the role of ETESA and procedures for management of central dispatch;
- allowing Large Customers with maximum demand of over 500 kW to purchase directly from generators and other suppliers. In 2007, the ASEP reduced this threshold to 100 kW; and
- establishing principles of tariff-setting for price-regulated services.

The SNE has no authority to amend the Electricity Law or to adopt additional laws or regulations relating to the electricity industry. However, the SNE can propose and recommend changes and amendments to existing regulation, or propose new regulation, which could entail changes in existing legislation or the adoption of new legislation relating to the energy sector, including the electricity industry.

# Concessions and Licenses

Under the Electricity Law, concessions are required for the construction and operation of hydroelectric or geothermal plants and for the provision of transmission or distribution services. Concessions are awarded, through contracts, by ASEP and have the following time limits:

- Hydroelectric or geothermal generation: up to 50 years;
- Transmission: 25 years; and
- Distribution: 15 years.

Thermal, wind and solar power plants, as well as all other power plants, require licenses issued by the ASEP but, unlike hydroelectric or geothermal power plants, do not require a concession. These licenses are granted by the ASEP for a term of up to 40 years.

# System Operation

The Electricity Law provides that the operation and administration of the wholesale electricity market be managed by the CND, a unit within ETESA with separate accounting records. The wholesale electricity market in Panama is divided into the contract (PPA) market and the spot market.

The contract market includes power purchase agreements with Distribution Companies, Large Customers, or other generators or self-generators, acting as purchasers.

The regulations under the Electricity Law allow generating companies to compete in sales to Distribution Companies. The Distribution Companies are permitted to generate only fifteen percent (15%) of their annual electricity requirements.

Distribution Companies are required by law to provide contract coverage for regulated customers' contribution to the System Peak Demand (Demanda Máxima de Generación or DMG), and associated energy of their regulated customer base. The Distribution Companies are required to contract 100% of the demand of regulated customers (including Large Customers) for the next two years, 90% for the following third and fourth years, and 80% for the following fifth and sixth years. This requires Distribution Companies to accurately estimate customer's needs. Distribution Companies provide ETESA with their needs based on a month-by-month analysis submitted to the ASEP by the CND each year using forecasts supplied by the Distribution Companies (Informe Indicativo de Demanda). ETESA in turn submits a Request for Proposal to generators. ETESA administers the bid process, contract negotiations and other logistical items, and then adjudicates the Distribution Companies' PPAs to the generators selected through the bidding process. Energy purchase costs are passed through during this process.

The amount a generator may offer may not exceed its own firm capacity and any such capacity acquired from other generators under reserve contracts. For thermal plants, firm capacity is established by the CND based on net capacity and historical availability.

The capacity and associated energy contracts are not take-or-pay contracts for the energy component, as the energy component is only paid for when used. However, the Distribution Companies have unconditional long-term contractual obligations, related to the purchase of power capacity only, which is totally passed through to their customers.

The CND plans the economic dispatch of electricity from the generation units using a model that incorporates stochastic dynamic programming in order to factor into the dispatch process the opportunity cost of the water, the variable cost of thermal plants and the availability of the primary resource for renewable plants, among other factors. Therefore, dispatch is based on merit order, which allows competition between generation companies and aims to increase the quality of supply. Variables considered in determining merit include variable costs, parameters for system security, operating constraints and the operational regulations (Reglamento de Operación) approved by the ASEP.

Most electricity is sold through the contracts market, while the spot market serves to adjust the differences between generators from production / demand and contractual commitments. The spot market price by hour is determined by the variable cost of the last power plant called to dispatch to meet the demand.

Transmission losses are valued differently depending on the type of technology and following the methodology established in the commercial rules governing the electricity wholesale market (the "Commercial Rules"). These losses are charged separately to Distribution Companies based on loss factors applicable to their connection points on the National Interconnected System. See "Overview of the Panamanian Electricity Industry—Dispatch" below.

Variances between a generator's actual dispatch and contracted energy volumes are settled through the spot market. Out of merit plants dispatched by the CND to maintain real time system stability (generación obligada) receive an additional payment to cover the difference between their variable costs and the hourly spot price. The CND is also responsible for the coordination of auxiliary services (servicios auxiliares) and their remuneration through additional charges to the system. Details of the average monthly spot price in the wholesale market since January 1999, excluding capacity costs, are set out below under "The Spot Market."

## Dispatch

According to the Electricity Law, the order in which generators are dispatched must be based on maximizing efficient consumption of energy by minimizing the total cost of energy in the Panamanian power system. The system dispatch order is planned by the CND. Generators are dispatched in an order that maximizes consumption of energy while also minimizing the total cost of energy in the Panamanian power system.

80

81

# Economic Dispatch

The CND generally dispatches generating units in accordance with a merit order based on each generator's variable costs:

- In the case of thermal units, variable costs (in U.S.$/MWh) are calculated based on incremental fuel costs and non-fuel costs, such as a thermal unit's administration, operation and maintenance costs, and its facility heat rate.
- In the case of renewable variable generation, such as wind, solar or run-of-river hydroelectric facilities, variable costs are considered to be zero.
- In the case of reservoir hydroelectric facilities (e.g., Bayano), variable costs correspond to the opportunity value of water, which is computed using a dispatch model incorporating stochastic dynamic programming, or the Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming ("SDDP") model. The CND uses the SDDP model to calculate the expected thermal generation cost saved in the future by the conservation of marginal amounts of water by a hydroelectric generator, taking into account projected operations of the national interconnected power system over the medium and long term. In determining the marginal amounts of water that must be conserved by a hydroelectric generator, the SDDP model takes into account estimated rainfall in the region and the risks of dam spillage and depletion of reserves by that hydroelectric generator. When calculating the risks of dam spillage and reserve depletion, the SDDP model also considers the size of the reservoir and efficiency of the generator's turbines. Thus, although the value of water is strongly linked to the variable costs of marginal thermal generation, other factors are taken into account when determining the marginal amounts of water required to save thermal generation costs.

The planned dispatch is revised continuously by the CND in response to any changes affecting the system (e.g., demand, actual generator availability and system restrictions) that may take place throughout the day. Additionally, each week, representatives from the CND and each Panamanian thermal, wind, solar, and hydroelectric company meet to discuss the results of the dispatch model and determine the following week's dispatch order.

Transmission losses are valued as set forth below based on cost and type of plant:

- Plants with zero variable cost or reservoir hydroelectric facilities that have large storage capacity, at the monthly weighted average price of energy in their PPAs;
- Plants with zero variable cost or reservoir hydroelectric facilities that do not have PPAs registered before the ASEP for such technology, at the monthly weighted average price of energy in all the registered PPAs backed by plants using such technology; or, in case there are no PPAs backed by plants using the same technology, at the weighted average price of energy of all PPAs with zero variable costs;
- Plants with variable cost higher than zero, except for reservoir hydroelectric facilities, and that have PPAs with the Distribution Companies, at the monthly arithmetical average price of energy in their PPAs, indexed to the declared in the weekly dispatch; and
- Plants with variable cost higher than zero, except for reservoir hydroelectric facilities that do not have PPAs with the Distribution Companies, at the applicable variable cost.

# Non-economic Dispatch

The Commercial Rules allow the CND to dispatch energy based on guidelines other than the SDDP model's projections when following the economic dispatch order would jeopardize the technical and commercial security of the system. The resulting altered dispatch order may cause generators that would have normally been dispatched not to be dispatched, forcing them to buy energy on the spot market to satisfy their contractual commitments. The Commercial Rules provide for certain payments to those generators for the non-dispatched, or restricted energy, based on the difference between the spot price of the energy purchased by the restricted generators to satisfy their contractual

commitments and the variable cost assigned to such generators by the CND for the non-economic dispatch period. Under the Commercial Rules, the party causing the condition that triggers non-economic dispatch is liable for the above payments.

## The Spot Market

The Panamanian power sector is structured as a spot market with an overlay of bilateral contracts between the generation companies and the Distribution Companies. In addition, the spot market is designed to balance the supply and demand of capacity and associated energy in the wholesale electricity market. The spot market commenced operation on July 1, 1998 under the administration of ETESA and the CND. The principal function of the spot market is to allow market forces to determine the amount, mix and cost characteristics of generation facilities, and the level and shape of demand. The spot market involves transactions of energy and capacity that are not subject to contracts, and consists of the energy spot market and the capacity spot market (known as daily capacity compensations).

## Spot Market for Energy

In the case of generators, energy spot transactions correspond to the hourly differences between the actual dispatch of energy by each generator and its contractual commitments to supply energy. A generator whose dispatched energy is greater than its contractual commitments to supply energy at any given time is a seller in the Panamanian energy spot market; the reverse is true for a generator whose dispatched energy is less than its contractual commitments to supply energy. Distribution companies, generators and Large Customers who have private PPAs can purchase energy in the Panamanian energy spot market, and generators and Large Customers can sell energy in the Panamanian energy spot market.

For every hour, the energy spot price is set by the marginal cost, which is the variable cost of the last power plant called to dispatch to meet the demand. See "Overview of the Panamanian Electricity Industry—Dispatch—Economic Dispatch." above. The price in the Panamanian energy spot market for all generators is set by the costliest generator dispatched in each hourly period, which becomes the clearing price for energy. Generally, the CND calculates the price of energy using the variable cost applicable to the dispatch of the generation unit which is required by the price dispatch to cover demand. Such variable cost is equal to the demand plus the current short-term reserve of the system. The value of wind, solar and run-of-river facilities is set at zero because the wind, sun and water used to operate these facilities do not generate a variable cost. The value of reservoir facilities is set at the opportunity cost of the water maintained in the reservoir which is limited and is essentially lost once it is used. The value of thermal facilities is set by the variable cost of the fuel used to operate these facilities, making them the costliest. For more detail on the calculation of the variable cost please see "Overview of the Panamanian Electricity Industry—Dispatch—Economic Dispatch" above.

## Spot Market for Capacity

Transactions take place daily in the capacity spot market in order to match the actual available capacity of generators with the actual peak capacity requirements that each generator must meet under their outstanding supply contracts. Each day, generators must submit their offers to sell their excess capacity for the following day. The CND

must accept capacity offers in increasing price order until all capacity requirements are covered. The price for spot capacity transactions is calculated each day based on offers submitted to the CND by the generators during the prior day. Daily prices are expressed as one-thirtieth (1/30) of a monthly price (U.S.$/kW – month). The spot capacity price at which generators sell their actual available capacity is equal to the last offer accepted, which translates to the price of the highest accepted offer. The capacity spot price is capped at a regulated price of U.S.$8.96 per kW a month, as of the date of this offering memorandum.

The capacity which the market participant may have available to sell may depend on a determination of whether or not it has a shortage or surplus of capacity available. The calculation of whether or not the market participant has a shortage or surplus is made by the CND, who calculates the balance between the capacity requirement and availability of each producer participant, discounting the committed capacity for supply from the capacity made available. If the balance is negative, the producing participant has a shortage and may not participate as a seller in the market. If on the contrary it is positive, the producing participant has access to the spot market and may sell the surplus on the capacity spot market.

## Power Purchase Agreements

The dominance of hydroelectric generation and the marked seasonal variations in Panama's hydrology result in a high degree of price volatility in the energy spot market. In order to mitigate this volatility, generators can enter into long-term power purchase agreements with Distribution Companies or Large Customers for the sale of capacity and/or energy. In addition, generators can enter into alternative supply contracts with one another, which are called reserve contracts. The terms and contents of PPAs with Distribution Companies are determined through a competitive bidding process and are governed by the Commercial Rules. PPAs must include, among others, the following information: (i) identity of the contracting parties; (ii) clear rules or procedures to determine, on an hourly basis, the quantity of energy which may be requested; and (iii) the corresponding prices.

## Capacity Charge

The capacity charge is a fee paid to thermal and hydroelectric generators intended to remunerate them for the firm capacity made available to the National Interconnected System. The capacity charge provides generators with a source of fixed revenue which depends primarily on the generator's own availability. The CND can verify a generator's declared availability and the ASEP can impose sanctions if the actual availability is lower than the declared value.

If a generator's actual availability is less than the declared availability, that generator is required to pay penalties calculated as provided in the PPA.
