Because the Electricity Law sets forth this restriction regarding "concessions," which include hydroelectric and geo-thermoelectric generation, this restriction should not apply to generation "licenses" that refer to other types of generation power plants.

In order to reduce Panama's reliance on hydroelectric generation and to increase the security of supply, the Panamanian government has decided to promote alternative sources of energy, particularly thermal power. In August 2012, law No. 41-2012 was approved, introducing new incentives for natural gas power plants, including an import

tax exception, a 20-year income tax holiday, accelerated depreciation and a 5% tax credit for total direct investment. Similarly, law No. 43-2012 amended the Electricity Law to permit capacity auctions based on the energy technology used (i.e. hydroelectric, wind, coal, natural gas and bunker, among others) and incorporating natural gas as a renewable energy in order to receive the benefit of a 5% preference granted in the bid price for the auction (relative to other types of generators). Law 37-2013 establishes incentives for solar power generators. Law 44-2011 establishes incentives for wind energy generators.

## Transmission

As of December 31, 2025, the transmission system in Panama, owned and operated by ETESA, comprised approximately 2,808.8 kilometers of single and double circuit 230kV lines linking the main generation facilities to the system load center at Panama City, 312.30 kilometers of single and double circuit 115kV lines and a total of 24 substations, which are comprised of 2 substations at a 115kV level and the other 22 substations are reducing substations with a total capacity of 2,419.4 MVA at 230/115/13.8kV.

As of the date of this offering memorandum, the transmission grid consists of four transmission lines: the first transmission line is 2,885.87 km long with a capacity of 230 kV per circuit, the second transmission line is 93.85 km long with a capacity of 230 kV per circuit, the third transmission line is 272.23 km long with a capacity of 115 kV per circuit and the fourth transmission line is 40.00 km long with a capacity of 115 kV per circuit. While each of the transmission lines has different starting points in the west of the country, they mostly transverse parallel to each other through the country to the population centers in the east of the country.

ETESA is responsible for expanding and upgrading the network to meet the requirements of demand growth and system stability.

Under the Electricity Law, ETESA is tasked with continuing investment and expansion of the national grid for the transmission of electricity in the National Interconnected System, this includes the operation and building of new installations, reinforcement of the existing grid, and the preparation of the expansion plan for transmission services. Such expansion plan for the interconnected system is to be prepared by ETESA in line with quality and reliability standards and development objectives set by the SNE. This plan is based on projections of expected growth in demand and energy consumption over the next 10 years which market participants are required to submit by June 30 of each year. Compliance with the plan is mandatory for transmission projects and indicative for purposes of generation projects.

ETESA is obliged to carry out all projects included in the transmission expansion plan, as approved by the ASEP, and all related construction work must be contracted on the basis of competitive bidding.

The Electricity Law provides for open access to transmission subject to a regulated tariff for connection and use of system charges. The current tariff, which was approved by Resolution AN No. 20618-Elec of July 4, 2025 issued by ASEP, is due to remain in force until a different tariff is approved by the ASEP.

The Electricity Law provides a maximum permitted income for ETESA for the transmission services, which is determined through a regulated tariff set by the ASEP every four years, which is subject to annual adjustments to provide for economic and industry factors. The transmission tariff (ingreso máximo permitido) is designed to cover the capital, administrative, operational, maintenance costs and depreciation incurred from managing the transmission grid, based on an economically efficient basis so as to provide an expected rate of return before tax on net fixed assets

that is within a 2% range above or below the average yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury Bond in the year preceding the setting of the tariff, plus a risk premium of 7%. Every year within the tariff period, the transmission charges are inflation-adjusted and revised for compliance with authorized investment programs. Delays in such investment programs lead to a reduction in the transmission charges to ETESA until the asset comes online.

Under the current tariff structure, which will remain in effect until June 30, 2030 pursuant to recent resolutions issued by ASEP, the pre-tax rate of return (tasa de rentabilidad) for ETESA has been set at 9.6%.

Transmission tariffs do not depend on the amount of electricity transmitted, but rather are a function of ETESA’s productive assets for which generation and Distribution Companies using the electric grid are charged.

Since transmission revenues are derived from the availability of transmission assets, if ETESA experiences shortfalls in transmission capacity, ETESA must compensate for the electricity that it is not able to deliver, through fees paid to power generators and the Distribution Companies. Pursuant to Section 9.6, Mandatory Generation (Generación Obligada), of the Commercial Rules, ETESA is required to pay electricity generators for associated cost overrun to the Mandatory Generation, which is caused by a congestion in the transmission grid.

Use of system charges (wheeling fees) reflect the costs assigned to each user for the use of the main transmission system and are comprised by: a “postage stamp” (estampilla postal) tariff methodology based on installed capacity of generators and annual non-coincident peak demand and an electrical monitoring charge based on a charge per unit of energy (Costo Unitario de los Servicios Prestados en la Transmisión, or CUSPT). ETESA’s charges for the use of the system are differentiated by zone depending on the extent to which the user is close to the system load center.

Renewable energy generators with an installed capacity of up to 10MW are exempt from these charges, while renewable energy generators with an installed capacity of up to 20MW pay only for the energy produced in excess of the first 10MW of installed capacity.

## Connection Services

Connection services are provided by ETESA allowing users who do not own the assets for connection, to connect to the transmission grid. The connection services fees come from the same tariff approved by the ASEP for transmission services, however it includes as a component the fee collection carried out by ETESA for the actual connection services. The tariff also recognizes investments approved and implemented as well as the cost of wages approved and executed in connection with the connection assets only. In general, the tariff is meant to recognize and repay approved costs of providing the connection services and is not intended to provide profit to ETESA. Specifically, the connection services are calculated separately from the main transmission system.

## International Interconnections

Connection services also include connections to the Sistema de Interconexión Eléctrica de los Países de América Central (“SIEPAC”) which connects Panama with Costa Rica, Honduras, Nicaragua, El Salvador and Guatemala. The SIEPAC is owned and operated by the Empresa Propietaria de la Red, S.A. (“EPR”). In turn, ETESA owns EPR, together with certain public utility and transmission companies of the countries connected to the SIEPAC along with private shareholders (Endesa S.A. (Spain) and Interconexión Eléctrica S.A. E.S.P (Colombia)). EPR is the only other company that has received a concession by the ASEP to transmit electricity in the territory of Panama, but only with regard to its role with the SIEPAC.

Commercial operations of the MER commenced in June 2013. We expect that the MER together with the SIEPAC regional market could have a positive impact on our results of operations in the short term. For example, we could benefit from taking short positions in the MER and SIEPAC during the wet and dry seasons, respectively.

Another separate bilateral effort to build an interconnection between Panama and Colombia is also being analyzed. Interconexión Eléctrica Colombia – Panamá (ICP) is a binational company created to make design, build, and operate the electrical interconnection line between Colombia and Panama. The ICP Project will have a 300 MW transmission capacity and consists of an Electric Transmission Line High Voltage Direct Current – HVDC. The cost of the project has not been published as of the date of this offering memorandum. In 2012, ICP released the first

86

auction of rights of way, but due to various operational, environmental, financial and regulatory risks, ICP canceled the auction. As of the date of this offering memorandum, technical, environmental, economic, financing and regulatory studies are still being conducted. The development and construction of the project are expected to be delayed such that operations are not expected to begin before 2026.

## Integrated Operation Services

Integrated operation services such as grid operator and market administrator are provided by the CND and paid by market agents. The CND is a unit within ETESA (it is not a subsidiary but rather the same legal entity), which coordinates the operations and transactions that take place among the participants of the electricity wholesale market. The CND has operational autonomy and independence, while still subject to ETESA's board of directors.

The income received is on the basis of a tariff that is not related to the transmission and connection services tariff. The tariff is meant to cover the cost of administration and operation of the integrated operation services, but does not provide any profitability for ETESA.

Moreover, market agents also pay fees to the Instituto de Metereología e Hidrología de Panamá ("IHMPA"), formerly known as ETESA's Hydromet, a division of ETESA with operational autonomy and independence, which was created under Law No. 209 of 2021, and replaced ETESA's Hydromet. IHMPA is necessary for generation planning of market agents, and operates 221 meteorological stations throughout Panama to measure meteorological parameters such as pressure, temperature, extreme temperature, humidity, precipitation (quantity and intensity), wind (speed and direction), evaporation, soil temperature, insolation and solar radiation. It also operates 85 hydrometric stations to measure the river and lake levers continuously throughout the year. Its services include providing reports on the various measurements it makes.

As part of Law 209 of April 22, 2021, market agents' contribution to IHMPA is paid on a monthly basis, representing one-twelfth of the total annual amount due from market agents. The Board of Directors of IHMPA approved Resolution No. 002 on June 28, 2023, which outlines the details of this "Contribution Payable by Electric Market Agents." In order to carry out any procedures with IHMPA, market agents must be in good standing with their contribution payments.

Integrated operation service charges, which include costs associated with the CND and hydrometeorology which are currently set at U.S.$ 0.1117 per kW/month for generators and U.S.$0.2414 per kW/month for distributors and Large Customers.

The three The Distribution Companies are public-private partnerships with the state holding ownership levels of 48-49% and operating under a concession expiring in October 2028. Distribution concessions are awarded for 15-year terms. Tariffs for distributors are regulated by the ASEP.

No distributor or its shareholders may participate, directly or indirectly, in the control or operations of generation assets with an aggregate capacity representing more than 15% of its total customer demand within its

concession zone. Within this limit, distributors may only engage in generation and transmission activities, provided that there is adequate management and accounting separation. Similarly, distribution companies may engage in transmission and generation services only in off-the-grid areas.

## Value Added of Distribution

The Electricity Law states that distribution charges should be set at a level, which based on estimates at the start of the tariff period, should allow Distribution Companies to achieve revenues to cover their recognized costs of distribution or Value Added Distribution ("VAD"). These are defined as the costs which an efficient distributor operating in a concession area would incur in terms of administration, operation and maintenance (including metering, billing and customer service), standard losses and depreciation plus a reasonable return on investment. The assumption of efficiency shall be based on the recent performance of similar real companies, either foreign or domestic.

The ASEP will determine the rate of return that it considers reasonable for the Distribution Company considering its efficiency, the quality of its service, its investment program for the period of validity of the tariff rates schedule and any other factor that the ASEP deems relevant. However, the rate of return that the ASEP determines must be within a two percent (2%) range above or below the average yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury Bond in the year preceding the setting of the tariff plus an eight percent (8%) risk premium.

This rate is applied to the Distribution Company's net fixed assets in operation during the tariff period based on historic accounting values at the start of the tariff period plus the Distribution Company's efficient investment requirements during the tariff period. For the purpose of determining appropriate levels of efficiency, the ASEP is required to analyze each Distribution Company's concession zone in terms of up to five representative areas according to density, based on the recent performance of actual companies in Panama or elsewhere operating in similar areas. The ASEP determines efficiency parameters by selecting comparable companies for each representative area.

Once this rate is applied to the assets and efficient investments, the Distribution Company prepares and submits for the approval of the ASEP the tariff schedules for each service area and customer category, for the ASEP to determine the Distribution Company's maximum allowable rate to charge customers.

Under the regulatory framework established by the ASEP, every four years, the ASEP sets the maximum tariff level (Ingreso Máximo Permitido) for the VAD tariff formulas of the Distribution Companies, based on future operating and capital expenditures as estimated by ASEP. The Electricity Law establishes a market-oriented framework for the Distribution Companies, which allow these to retain the financial benefits derived from efficiency gains during each four-year tariff period.

The VAD tariff structure remains in full force and effect for a four-year period. Historically, every six months during the tariff period, the capacity and energy cost-components of the tariff are adjusted to account for variances in actual and expected energy costs, and only forty-five percent (45%) of the distribution and commercial charges are adjusted for inflation based on the Panamanian CPI for the prior two six-month periods. These energy-related component adjustments are applied starting the following six-month period. Since July 1, 2006, adjustments for variances in actual fuel prices occur on a monthly basis, rather than a semi-annual basis and are applied to the next month's bill. The generation and transmission components of the tariff are adjusted based on the actual energy purchased and the actual cost of transmission. The current VAD has been in place since October 2023 and will remain in effect through June 2026.

## Final Customer Tariffs

In addition to the VAD tariff component, the tariffs for regulated customers have a separate component that includes the weighted average cost of energy the Distribution Companies purchase from generators and in the spot market, transmission tolls paid to ETESA and public lighting energy consumption. This energy component is established by the ASEP as a pass-through of the Distribution Companies' energy costs to the customers and is adjusted every six months to reflect the actual costs of energy due to the fluctuation in fuel price and energy prices in the spot market.

The tariff system for the distribution service is composed by rules related to:

1. procedures, methodologies, formulas, structures, options, values and in general all aspects determining the collection of rates subject to regulation.

2. the subsidy system that can be awarded so that the lowest income individuals be able to pay the electric public service tariffs covering their basic needs. The regulation shall indicate the procedure for the application of the subsidies when they exist.

Panamanians or foreign residents in the territory of Panama that are senior citizens (in the case of women, age 55 and older, or in the case of men, 60 years or older), and all retirees (men aged 62 or older and women aged 57 or older), and pensioners (pensionados) receive a 25% discount on charges applied for the first 600 kWh of consumption. For any consumption above the 600 kWh threshold, retirees pay full charges.

Tariff options for customers include:

- Simple Tariff (“BTS”). The simple tariff is an energy per kW hour rate restricted to customers with low tension lines (600 V or less) and with a demand of 15 kW or below.

- Low Tension Maximum Demand Tariff (Tarifa de Baja Tensión con Demanda or “BTD”) and Low Tension Time of Use Tariff (Tarifa de Baja Tensión Horaria or “BTH”). The low tension maximum demand tariff and low tension time of use tariff are available to customers that are connected at a voltage level at or below 600 V and also have a predictable level of demand equal or higher than 15 kW. Residential customers will not be charged fees with on-demand charges unless they opt for one at their convenience. These tariffs include a capacity or demand component, an energy component and a fixed customer charge. The capacity and energy components include a generation, transmission and distribution component. The capacity charge is now based on the customer’s actual capacity and consumption.

- Medium Tension Maximum Demand Tariff (“MTD”) and Medium Tension Time of Use Tariff (“MTH”). The medium tension maximum demand tariff and the medium tension time of use tariff are available to customers that take delivery of electricity at a voltage level higher than 600 V and lower than 115 kV. These tariff charges have the same structure and operate in the same manner as the low tension maximum tariff and the low tension time of use tariff.

- High Tension Maximum Demand Tariff (“ATD”) and High Tension Time of Use Tariff (“ATH”). The high tension maximum demand tariff and the high tension time of use tariff are available to customers that take delivery of electricity at a voltage level higher than 115 kV. These tariff charges have the same structure and operate in the same manner as the low and medium tension maximum tariff and the low and medium tension time of use tariff.

In addition, Charges for public lighting charge, including a return on capital, operating and maintenance expenses and energy consumption costs are built into the customers’ regulated tariff.

Customers are allowed to change their tariff option once in a twelve-month period without incurring a penalty. From and after the second change in that period, the customer will pay a penalty in the amount of fifty percent (50%) of the connection fee.

## Purchases by Large Clients

Large customers are currently defined as those with peak demand on a site-by-site basis of over 100 kW, and can choose to buy energy directly from other sources including generators, other distributors, or from the spot market (mercado ocasional).

Pursuant to the Electricity Law, generators may sell energy to Large Customers under PPAs at freely agreed prices. Large Customers are free to purchase energy from any generator.

With respect to power purchases, Large Customers not previously connected to one of the Distribution Companies and opting to connect directly to the National Interconnected System must enter into a supply agreement

89

with a generator, in accordance with the provisions set forth in the Commercial Rules. Large Customers already connected to one of the Distribution Companies are required to pay the Distribution Company a capacity and energy charge, or alternatively, a wheeling charge covering the distribution and commercial tariff components.

Pursuant to the rules applicable to Large Customers in Panama, if a Large Customer demands less than 100Kw for four consecutive months such Large Customer will be disqualified and as such it will become a regulated consumer and will not be able to qualify again as a Large Customer for at least a year.

## Electric Energy Rationing

The variable costs resulting from energy rationing are to be simulated daily during the planning sessions with the SDDP pursuant to the Commercial Rules and the Methodology for Daily Scheduling and Criteria for Daily Start-Up and Shutdown (Metodología para la Programación Diaria y Criterios de Arraque y Parada Diarios). Those variable costs are initially simulated on the basis of a curtailment of the demand of five percent (5%) of the total national demand; the second step of those variable costs is simulated as a curtailment of ten percent (10%) of the total national demand; the third step of those variable costs is simulated as a curtailment of thirty percent (30%) of the total national demand and the fourth step of those variable costs is simulated as a curtailment of one hundred percent (100%) of the total national demand, each step has a price based on a formula included in the Methodology for Managing Electricity Supply Rationing (Metodología para Administrar Racionamiento de Suministro de Energía Eléctrica).

If emergency rationing occurs, the CND will determine the amount of energy to be rationed according to the characteristics and implications of the emergency. The Methodology for Managing Electricity Supply Rationing provides the methodology for calculating the amount of energy to be withheld in the case of programmed and emergency rationing, and sets forth the parameters for the distribution of the rationed energy to consumers. While the energy rationing is in effect, all generators under the firm capacity agreements are obligated to generate the committed energy. In other words, during energy rationing measures, contracts are no longer treated financially and such firm capacity agreements become "physical".

## Environmental Regulation

In July 1998, the Panamanian government enacted Law 41, which created the National Environmental Authority, which through Law No. 8 of March 25, 2015 was replaced by the Environment Ministry. Law No. 8 together with Law 41 and other supplemental rules also sets out the legal framework for the protection of the environment through the sustainable use of natural resources. The Environment Ministry is responsible for implementing Panama's environmental policy with the collaboration of other government entities it supervises, such as the Environmental National Council (Consejo Nacional del Ambiente) and the Environmental Consultative National Commission (Comisión Consultiva Nacional del Ambiente). The Environment Ministry has the ability to impose all applicable environmental sanctions and fines. Under Law 41, as amended by Law No. 8, the Environment Ministry may impose fines for any violation of Law 41, including the improper use of water concessions or water resources without having the applicable concession.

Pursuant to Executive Decree 1 dated March 1, 2023, as modified by Executive Decree No. 2 dated March 27, 2024, ("Executive Decree 1"), which regulates the environmental assessment studies, generation of electricity projects (as defined therein) may not be carried out in Panama without prior approval of an environmental assessment study by the Environment Ministry. Accordingly, all private and public projects must submit an environmental assessment study to the Environment Ministry for its evaluation and approval. Moreover, Executive Decree 1 establishes that an environmental expert shall perform specific tests of criteria to determine the category of environmental assessment study that will be required for the particular type of project being evaluated and identify, evaluate and establish the mitigation measures that shall be followed (which may include reforestation requirements). Additionally, article 89

of Executive Decree 1 establishes that the sponsor must deliver periodic reports regarding the follow-up of mitigation measures to the respective regional office of the Environment Ministry (where the project is located), in accordance with the respective environmental assessment study and the terms set forth in the resolution, whereby said environmental assessment study is approved.

In addition to administrative liability, Law 41, as amended by Law No. 8 also establishes civil and criminal liability for violations thereof, and Law 5 of 2005 has introduced environmental crimes into the Penal Code, including crimes against wildlife, natural resources and crimes related to approval of and compliance with environmental documentation.

## Investments Stability Act

The Panamanian government enacted Law No. 54 of July 22, 1998, which is further regulated by Executive Decree No. 9 of February 22, 1999, or the Investments Stability Act. The Investments Stability Act provides for certain stability measures in favor of companies engaged in electricity generation, distribution and transmission activities, among others, that meet certain qualifications and register with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. As of this date, the Issuer has not registered with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry to take advantage of any benefits under the Investments Stability Act.

## Insolvency Regime

Law No. 12 of May 19, 2016 (the "Panamanian Insolvency Law") replaced the former Panamanian bankruptcy regime that was constructed upon provisions dispersed throughout several codes and laws and which did not provide for the possibility of reorganization, setting out only a framework for liquidation of troubled debtors.

The Panamanian Insolvency Law, which became effective on January 2, 2017, implemented various rules to avoid the bankruptcy of individuals and companies. The Panamanian Insolvency Law resulted from an extensive consultation process with several stakeholders and is inspired by similar regimes enacted in other jurisdictions such as Chile, Argentina, Colombia, Spain and the United States of America. The Panamanian Insolvency Law's stated objective is the viability and continuation of enterprises as well as the satisfaction of credits in excess of what would have been possible under the prior regime.

The Panamanian Insolvency Law framework provides for both reorganization and liquidation proceedings. In addition, in the case of entities that render public utility services and that are under the purview of the ASEP, as in our case, the ASEP is legally authorized to take administrative control of such entities to guarantee the safety and efficiency of the national energy grid.

## Reorganization proceedings

Upon the filing of a petition to commence reorganization proceedings under the Panamanian Insolvency Law, the creation or execution of guaranties on the debtor's assets, including by means of a guaranty trust, is not permitted (other than as part of the ordinary course of business of the debtor or with the court's consent). The debtor may not transfer, convey or dispose of assets, or enter into settlement agreements or other arrangements or reworkings with respect to its outstanding obligations or ongoing litigation. Any acts performed in breach of such limitations would be null and void and the breaching party or parties would be jointly and severally liable for damages resulting therefrom.

In addition, once the insolvency court orders the commencement of reorganization proceedings, protection (protección financiera concursal) is activated. Pursuant to such protection, inter alia, creditors (including secured parties) may not file any action against the debtor or foreclose on its assets. Moreover, any proceeding seeking the foreclosure of collateral granted by the debtor is suspended. Nevertheless, a debtor may seek to renegotiate certain executory agreements (contratos de tracto sucesivo) or, if such agreements cannot be renegotiated and the debtor can demonstrate that the costs to the debtor are onerous (taking into account the cost of replacing such services), request that the court overseeing the reorganization terminate such agreements. All relevant statutes of limitations

92

are also suspended. As an exception, secured creditors may petition the court to commence or continue the proceeding, as the Panamanian Insolvency Law grants courts the power to authorize the proceedings where the foreclosure of the underlying assets will not affect the operations of the company or the viability of reaching a reorganization agreement.

All contracts entered into by the debtor remain valid during the period of insolvency protection, but payment of interest on unsecured debt obligations is suspended.

## Liquidation proceedings

Notwithstanding the ASEP’s authority to intervene, if creditors holding at least 2/3 of the outstanding claims with the right to vote (i.e., holders of claims that have been recognized by the insolvency court) do not approve a reorganization agreement, the debtor would likely be forced into liquidation.

Upon the issuance of the court decision declaring the commencement of liquidation proceedings, the debtor ceases to have the right to manage its assets, as that right and power is conferred upon an appointed liquidator that represents the interests of the creditors. At the same time, the court decision would suspend all creditors’ rights to individually foreclose on the debtors, except for secured creditors who may continue with actions seeking the foreclosure of their collateral with the authorization of the court. Further, interest would cease to accrue on unsecured credits and secured creditors may only enforce payment of accrued interest up to the value of their collateral. Pursuant to Articles 85 and 178 of the Panamanian Insolvency Law, secured credits are not included within the liquidation proceedings unless the secured creditor waives its privilege or, following the foreclosure of the collateral, the credit is not fully satisfied. As a result, a secured creditor in a liquidation proceeding is generally free to apply the proceeds raised upon the foreclosure of its mortgage, pledge or other security interest up to the amounts owed and secured thereby. In fact, a secured creditor usually does not need to return those proceeds to the estate (unless there is an excess) or wait until the completion of the insolvency proceeding to receive them.

In the event of a court order instructing for liquidation, the following would apply to the Company and its assets:

- As of the effectiveness of the liquidation order: (a) the Company would not be able to administer or dispose of its assets (except for assets not subject to embargo or attachment) and, as from that moment, such powers would pass on to the creditors, represented by the court-appointed liquidator; (b) all of the Issuer’s obligations would become due and payable and no further interest shall accrue on such obligations; and (c) the statute of limitations applicable to liabilities payable by it would be suspended.

- Certain executory agreements (contratos de tracto sucesivo) such as lease agreements could be terminated subject to the prior delivery of any statutory or agreed upon notice. Any payment or contract entered into by the Company following the issuance of the liquidation order would be null and void and any payment it would have to be made directly to the liquidator.

- The following acts could be voidable for the benefit of the liquidation estate if executed after the liquidation order or within the year prior to the date of the liquidation order (declaratoria de liquidación): (a) any action or agreement of the Company that lacks consideration (título gratuito) and those agreements that are entered into for excessive of consideration (título oneroso); (b) the constitution of a pledge, mortgage, or any other action entered into to secure obligations previously contracted or to grant a preference over other obligations; (c) payment (either with cash, assignment, transfer) of debts that are not considered past-due or the payment of debts already overdue; and (d) modifications to the articles of incorporation (pacto social) or the bylaws (estatutos) of the Company. Any action or agreement of the Company that lacks consideration (título gratuito) in favor of a shareholder, administrator, director, manager, officer, legal representative, liquidator or attorney-in-fact could be voidable if executed within the four-year period counted as from the date of insolvency set forth by the court in the liquidation order (declaratoria de liquidación).

93

- Any actions or agreements where there is a simulation of fraud, or a misrepresentation by the parties; and any disposal of assets with or without consideration if made with the intention of subtracting the asset or its value from reach of the creditors, could be declared null and void by the court irrespective of their date of execution, and without being able to argue statute of limitations.

However, as mentioned above, pursuant to Article 284 of the Panamanian Constitution, the ASEP has the power to intervene electricity market participants in order to guarantee efficiency in the rendering of public services, subject to the restrictions set out in the law. This power is further defined and regulated by Article 4 of the Panamanian Electricity Law and Executive Decree No. 24 of 2006. Accordingly, in the event that the ASEP deems that, for instance, the failure of an energy generation company poses a substantial risk to the national energy grid, the ASEP may take administrative control of such company with the goal of guaranteeing the continued, efficient and uninterrupted availability of power on the national grid.

Pursuant to Article 5 of the Panamanian Insolvency Law, once the ASEP takes administrative control of a company, insolvency proceedings may not be commenced against the company and all ongoing proceedings must be suspended. To that end, within two days from the date on which the ASEP takes administrative control of such company, the ASEP must serve notice upon insolvency courts. Pursuant to Articles 3 and 5 of Executive Decree No. 24 of 2006, the ASEP's administrative control may last for 90 days, which term may be extended if ASEP does not achieve its objective within the 90-day period. Nevertheless, given the relatively recent enactment of the new Panamanian Insolvency Law, there are not sufficient precedents available to determine how this process will operate in practice in every case.

# BUSINESS

## Overview

We are engaged in the generation and supply of electricity in Panama. We own and operate Generadora Gatún, a 670 MW natural gas-fired combined cycle power plant with 640 MW in net capacity, located on Telfers Island near Colón, adjacent to the Panama Canal (the "Facility" or the "Project"). The gas turbines of the Facility began to supply energy and capacity into the National Interconnected System in October 2024, and the steam turbine became fully operational in May 2025, increasing the Facility's efficiency and reaching commercial operation in July 2025.

We supply electricity to the National Interconnected System, which serves the country's energy demand across industrial, commercial, and residential sectors. International interconnections link the National Interconnected System with neighboring countries through the Panama's participation in the MER, where generators and demands located in any of the member countries can freely decide whether to carry out their energy purchase / sale transactions in the MER or in their own domestic markets. The six participant countries are Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama, Nicaragua and Guatemala. See "The Panama Electricity Market."

The Panamanian electricity market is primarily supported by a mix of hydropower, natural gas, and other thermal generation sources, with growing integration of renewable energy. The Facility is the largest natural gas power plant in Panama and Central America, strengthening the country's energy security and facilitating the transition to a more diversified generation mix. Additionally, the Panamanian power system operates under a competitive wholesale market model, managed by the CND and regulated by the ASEP. The state-owned transmission company, ETESA, plays a key role in system planning and the expansion of the transmission network. Panama also stands out as a strategic energy hub in the region, with international interconnections to Costa Rica and prospects for strengthening integration with Colombia. In recent years, long-term energy auctions have been promoted to encourage investment in renewable generation, particularly solar and wind, as part of the national energy transition strategy toward a cleaner, more resilient, and sustainable energy matrix.

We sell the electric power generated by us to the Distribution Companies through long-term PPAs for a capacity of up to 550 MW. Our capacity is 62.50% contracted for the first four years of operations and 85.90% contracted for years five through 20 under the PPAs, in each case, based on firm capacity, leaving additional opportunities for the Company to enter into additional PPAs or sell excess energy in the spot market. We have PPAs with EDECHI, EDEMET and ENSA, which collectively serve 83% of the Panamanian energy market and all of whose parent companies have credit rating profiles in line with those of Panama. EDECHI and EDEMET are 51.00% owned by Naturgy Energy Group (formerly, Gas Natural Fenosa) and ENSA is a 51.00% subsidiary of EPM. The Republic of Panama owns 48.30% of each of the Distribution Companies, with the remaining being owned by former employees of the Instituto de Recursos Hidráulicos y Electrificación ("IRHE"), a Panamanian government-owned utility that existed prior to the privatization of the Panamanian electricity market. The EDECHI and EDEMET PPAs are for the supply of 40MW and 200MW, respectively, during the first four years and 55 MW and 275 MW, respectively, for the remaining 16 years. The ENSA PPA is for the supply of 160 MW during the first four years and 220 MW for the remaining 16 years. Each of these PPAs has a tenor of 20 years, commencing from October 2024 and include certain "pass-through" provisions that allow us to transfer or share certain of our generation costs to our customers. The PPAs provide for a fixed capacity payment component (the "Capacity Revenue") and a partially fixed energy payment indexed to Henry Hub (the "Energy Revenue"). As a result, we believe our long-term PPAs provide a very stable source or recurring cash flow. See "Sources of Revenue," "Business—Main Contracts."

For the year ended December 31, 2025, our total energy sales under our PPAs were 239.97 GWh to EDECHI, 1,063.80 GWh to EDEMET, and 838.26 GWh to ENSA, and those sales represented 10.2%, 41.5% and 33.7% of our operating revenues, respectively. For the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024, energy sales (i) under PPAs, comprised as energy sales - contracts were U.S.$182.97 million in 2025 and U.S.$42.05 million in 2024 and as capacity sales - contracts were U.S.$94.84 million in 2025 and U.S.$23.95 million in 2024, and (ii) in the spot market were U.S.$43.50 million in 2025 and U.S.$5.15 million in 2024.

# The Facility

The Facility is strategically located within Limon Bay,  $2\mathrm{km}$  south of the port city of Colon, Panama, and directly adjacent to the Atlantic entrance to the canal. The location of the Project was selected to enable easy access for global and regional LNG carriers, easy shipping of key parts to the Facility site and for its proximity to the Colón Terminal, which is only  $1.2\mathrm{km}$  away. Panama is expected to become a convergence point in the new LNG trade routes, especially as LNG exports from the US Gulf of Mexico continue to increase over next few years.

The map below sets out the location of the Facility.



According to the SNE, electricity demand in Panama continues to increase, driven by sustained economic expansion and industrial growth. The country's historical reliance on hydroelectric generation has exposed the system to intermittency and hydrological variability, underscoring the need for firm, dispatchable capacity. Prior to the commencement of energy and capacity dispatch from our Facility in October 2024, Panama had only  $381\mathrm{MW}$  of installed natural gas combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) capacity, all from the Colón Plant. Following the start of operations at our Facility, total installed natural gas CCGT capacity increased to  $1,051\mathrm{MW}$ , reflecting the combined capacity of the Colón Plant and Generadora Gatún. Since commencing operations, the Facility has begun supplying critical firm thermal capacity to meet current and projected electricity demand, while supporting the phased retirement of older, less efficient, and higher-emitting diesel-fired generation units. As of December 31, 2025, Panama's generation mix consisted of  $59.78\%$  hydroelectric,  $22.76\%$  LNG,  $2.21\%$  bunker and diesel fuel,  $9.64\%$  solar,  $5.27\%$  wind, and  $0.34\%$  coal. In this context of rising demand, increasing system firming needs, and a shifting generation mix toward natural gas, the SNE's September 2025 announcement of a potential 2025-2029 PPA tender schedule—including a tender with a firm capacity component in which natural gas-fired plants such as our Facility may be required to participate—signals a regulatory framework aligned with the system's growing need for reliable thermal capacity.

## Technology

## CCGT Technology

The Facility employs proven technology supplied and installed by industry leaders qualified to deliver fully performant CCGT facilities. The Facility is equipped with a 2x2x1 combined cycle block with a nominal net capacity of 640 MW and expected heat rate of 6,585 Btu/kWh (guaranteed heat rate at full capacity at High Heating Value). GE Power, which is a subsidiary of General Electric, supplied the power island equipment for the Facility.

The CCGT utilizes a GE 7F.05 power block that consists of two GE 7F.05 gas turbine (GT) generators, two GE unfired triple-pressure-reheat heat recovery steam generators (HRSGs), and one two casing triple-pressure-reheat steam turbine (ST) generator STG-D600, together making up the "Power Island". For 30 years this design has been successfully constructed and operated at a number of sites around the world—there are 27 GE 7F.05s currently in operation, and another 61 on order. The 7F 5-Series is an upgraded fifth generation 7F combustion turbine, providing increased output and efficiency, faster startup and ramp rates, and a better turn down capability than its predecessors. The 7F.05 operates at a comparable firing temperature to the 7FA.04, though higher-temperature materials from other lines of GE's combustion turbines have been incorporated into the first and second stages of the turbine section, which is expected to result in longer life and reduced wear costs. Improved cooling, sealing, and clearances are used to improve efficiency. The main cooling system uses seawater from Limon Bay on the Caribbean Sea. A pumping station is located near the plant site on the coast. The Independent Engineer confirmed that the basic control system design is conventional and uses proven technologies.

The main cooling system utilizes seawater drawn from Limon Bay on the Caribbean Sea. Demineralized water is used as make-up water for the steam cycle that drives the steam turbine generator. This demineralized water will be produced on-site through a water treatment system that processes seawater. A pumping station located near the plant site on the coast supplies the necessary seawater for both cooling and treatment processes.

# Transmission

The Facility is connected to the 230-kv Panamanian transmission grid via two interconnection points.

- The Facility interconnects to the existing AES Colon transmission line through a two-circuit 230 kV transmission line of c.  $700\mathrm{m}$  (the "Gatún-Colon T-Line"). The substation, a gas insulated switchgear (GIS) type, is connected to the Sabanitas substation via a  $230\mathrm{kV}$  double circuit line.
- The Facility also interconnects to the Sabanitas substation via a dedicated single circuit transmission line of c.  $16\mathrm{km}$  (the "Gatún-Sabanitas T-Line").

Both lines are part of the country's short-term transmission expansion plan and are operated by ETESA.

In addition, as part of its transmission plan, and to accommodate the additional capacity that the Facility provides to the market, ETESA has built a  $46\mathrm{km}$  double circuit  $230\mathrm{kV}$  transmission line between the Sabanitas substation and the new Panama III substation in Panama City (the "Sabanitas-Panama III T-Line"), with a capacity of 1,000 MVA and which became operational in January 2025.

## Key Credit Highlights

We benefit from the strength of the Facility's business and our ownership and management, which we believe provide reliable cashflows.

## Stable economic background

Panama is a dollarized economy, located strategically in the middle of the Americas, connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans via the Panama Canal. Panama has been one of the fastest-growing economies in Latin America over the past decade, with a GDP per capita of U.S.$19,200 and an average annual GDP growth rate of 4.0% between 2015 and 2025. In 2025, growth slowed to 3.0%, primarily due to the suspension of operations at the country's largest copper mine. Nevertheless, economic activity is expected to rebound in 2026, with projected GDP growth of 4.0%, supported by strong domestic demand and the reactivation of both public and private investment. We believe these factors position Panama as an attractive destination for foreign investment in Latin America, supported by low inflation, one of the region's lowest unemployment rates, and a stable political environment—even amid recent credit rating downgrades and a split investment-grade status. Moreover, Panama's dollarized economy provides us with a stable currency base underlying our revenues and cash generated over time. These revenues and cashflows will be used to make payments on the Notes.

In addition, Panama's energy demand is projected to grow at an average annual rate of approximately 4.42% over the next 11 years, in line with the country's expected GDP growth, according to ETESA's 2022-2036 expansion plan. Given Gatún's cost-efficient profile and competitive positioning near the top of the dispatch curve, we believe

the Facility is well positioned to capture a substantial share of this demand growth, supporting long-term revenue maximization and operational scalability.

## Stable cashflow profile

Our stable cash flow profile is underpinned by several structural factors: high contracted capacity, favorable power purchase agreement (PPA) terms, and the positioning of natural gas thermal plants on the dispatch curve. We believe these attributes support consistent revenue generation and are further reinforced by USD-denominated PPAs with long-term tenors extending through 2044, which together are expected to strengthen our ability to meet payment obligations on the Notes. Our capacity is 62.5% contracted for the first four years of operations and 85.9% contracted for years five through 20 under the PPAs, in each case, based on firm capacity. Up to 550 MW of the Facility's firm capacity is under contract with the Distribution Companies, leaving additional opportunities for the Company to enter into additional PPAs or sell excess energy in the spot market. The PPA price structure includes a passthrough mechanism of transmission costs, a fixed capacity component, and an energy component indexed 40% to HH Gas Price. The contracted energy volumes under the PPAs follow the Distribution Companies' load factors, which measure the shape of consumption (average demand to peak) and is a stable metric—ranging in any market in the 65-75% range and in Panama historically within the 60-70% range.

## Robust financing structure

The terms of the Notes will limit our ability to incur additional indebtedness, subject to the satisfaction of certain financial ratios. In addition, we also intend to enter into the LC Facility of approximately 5 years to enhance our ability to make payments on the Notes. As a result of these enhancements and limitations, we believe that the issuance of the Notes offered hereby provide us with a robust financing structure to support our operational ramp up while preserving cash to meet our indebtedness obligations.

Pursuant to the Indenture, we have agreed to customary negative covenants against (i) debt incurrence (unless certain debt incurrence conditions are satisfied including compliance with historical and projected debt service coverage ratios greater than 1.35:1.00, (ii) creation of liens (including liens to secure indebtedness up to a specified amount), (iii) affiliate transactions (except on an arm's-length basis), (iv) asset sales, (v) mergers and acquisitions (unless the leverage tests referred to above for debt incurrence have been satisfied), other than the Corporate Reorganization (as described below) and (vi) distributions (unless in compliance with the distribution conditions). For more information regarding the financing structure see "Description of the Notes" and "Description of the Financing Documents".

## Robust operations and maintenance arrangements and adequate gas supply strategy

We have long-term and favorable arrangements with our principal shareholders—an operation and maintenance agreement with AES Panamá and an administrative services agreement with InterEnergy Holdings UK. In addition, we have a TUA and an OCA with Costa Norte LNG Terminal, S. de R.L. an affiliate of AES Panamá. Both AES Panamá and InterEnergy Holdings UK are highly experienced and reputable counterparties, properly incentivized to perform.

Moreover, we have secured strong and favorable gas supply contract terms at a price indexed to Henry Hub through a 20-year LNG sales and purchase agreement with Total, an LNG global market leader and reputable counterparty. We believe the contractual arrangement with Total will allow us to service the PPAs while allowing adequate flexibility to adjust cargo quantities depending on the Facility's needs and dispatch, including in extreme weather events (high hydrology years) and other natural weather patterns.

The Facility also has strong control systems that increase its efficiency and improve employee safety. The Facility is certified under the OHSAS 18001 and ISO 14001 standards for integrated safety and environmental management systems. We continue to develop our strategic and operational management to allow us to efficiently plan, prioritize and achieve our business and operational objectives. We operate under strict internal financial controls and manage our working capital with a view towards financing growth while limiting excess liquidity. We continuously review and improve our internal procedures and training methods in order to improve the safety of our employees.

# Strong sponsorship

We benefit from the strong and constructive relationships with our principal shareholders and their parent companies, which provide experience, management, guidance and support, and represent important political allies and business partners. The direct and indirect holder of AES Panamá’s equity are AES (which owns AES Panamá’s direct managing equity holder, Global Power Holdings) and the Panamanian Government. AES is a Fortune 500 global power company that seeks to provide affordable, sustainable energy in 12 countries on four continents (the Americas, Asia and Europe) through a diverse portfolio of distribution businesses as well as thermal and renewable generation facilities. As of December 31, 2025, AES managed approximately U.S.$51 billion in total assets and had revenues of U.S.$12.2 billion. AES currently distributes electricity through its various electric utility subsidiaries to over 2.6 million customers worldwide. AES also has 34.4 GW in gross capacity in operation globally. AES and its affiliates provide us with technical expertise and financial and operational management, support and training to help grow their businesses.

The indirect holder of InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas’s equity is InterEnergy Group. InterEnergy Group was established in 2011 and is a developer, owner, and operator for power generation, transmission, and distribution assets in the Latin American and Caribbean region, with 2.5 GW of installed capacity across 22 operating assets in 10 countries. InterEnergy Group is an experienced sponsor in the power sector with a focus on renewable energy and energy transition. The group has been a pioneer in developing state-of-the-art energy infrastructure, including solar parks and energy storage systems, as well as expanding electric vehicle charging networks through Evergo. In Jamaica, InterEnergy Group owns almost 40% of the country’s total base load capacity. In Dominican Republic, InterEnergy Group owns two generation, transmission, and distribution companies through which it became the first wind operator in 2011. In 2014, InterEnergy built the largest wind farm in the Central American and Caribbean region (Laudato Si wind farm in Panama). Other investments include solar and wind power plants in Chile, solar, wind and thermal power plants in Panama, wind generation in Uruguay, Guatemala and the Dominican Republic, solar and thermal power plants in Jamaica, and solar plants in the Cayman Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

We represent an important part of AES Panamá’s and InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas’ operations and long-term commitment to supply power in Panama. In furtherance of this commitment, both AES Panamá and InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas have made extensive capital expenditures to develop, operate and manage the Facility. In addition, in pursuing their corporate strategy, which implements the strategic goals (green growth, customer centricity, new business models and new technologies) of both AES and the InterEnergy Group, through their investment in Generadora Gatún, they have positioned themselves well for continued growth and increased their importance to the Panamanian energy market, and by extension, to the Panamanian government, AES Panamá’s majority equity holder. As operator of the Colón Facilities, the only LNG power plant and terminal in Panama, prior to the commencement of operations at our Facility, AES Panamá has advanced AES’s strategic goals of incorporating new technologies and new business models by expanding its combined generation portfolio to include LNG and establishing a new revenue stream from storage capacity sales. In addition, through the construction of Generadora Gatún, AES Panamá and InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas have contributed significantly to the diversification and reliability of the Panamanian generation matrix, and the reduction and stabilization of spot market prices. We believe that these contributions have further increased their strategic importance to the Panamanian government, aligning their interests with those of their equity holders. Neither AES Panamá nor InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas are guarantors of the Notes.

# Business Strategy

As Panama’s largest natural gas-fired power plant, we believe that Generadora Gatún, has significant opportunities to strengthen its market position, enhance efficiency, and expand into new areas of growth.

103

# Increasing market positioning and expansion in Central America and the Caribbean

Expanding its market reach beyond Panama presents a significant growth opportunity for our business. One strategic approach is leveraging Panama's interconnection with the SIEPAC to export electricity to countries experiencing supply gaps, such as Guatemala, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Honduras. The planned interconnection between Panama and Colombia is progressing steadily, presenting a strategic opportunity to strengthen our regional positioning and anticipate increased profitability in the future. Additionally, securing new long-term PPAs with Panama's Distribution Companies and industrial consumers can provide additional flows of stable revenue streams while reinforcing Generadora Gatún's role in Panama's energy supply.

Another area of expansion is becoming a backup energy provider for renewables, supplying dispatchable power to compensate for fluctuations in hydro, wind, and solar generation. With Panama's industrial and commercial energy demand growing, Generadora Gatún can also position itself as the primary energy supplier for major industries, including port operations, logistics hubs, and free trade zones in Colón and the Panama Canal area. Strengthening relationships with ETESA and major industrial clients will be crucial in ensuring that Generadora Gatún remains an integral part of Panama's evolving energy infrastructure.

# Continued focus on optimization of operations and efficiency improvements

Maximizing operational efficiency and minimizing costs will be critical for our long-term competitiveness in the Panamanian energy market. One of the key strategies is to enhance the efficiency of the Facility's combined-cycle technology by implementing advanced digital monitoring systems, including AI-driven predictive maintenance. These tools can help optimize turbine performance, reduce unplanned downtime, and extend the life of critical assets. Additionally, fuel optimization will play a crucial role in controlling costs, requiring strategic long-term LNG procurement contracts linked to Henry Hub or other competitive benchmarks to ensure price stability.

Beyond fuel efficiency, participating in Panama's wholesale energy market can provide additional revenue streams by allowing us to sell excess power during peak pricing periods and balance generation with real-time demand fluctuations. The Facility can also position itself as a key provider of grid stability services, offering fast-ramping capacity to help manage fluctuations in intermittent renewable generation. Further, investing in carbon capture technologies and emissions reductions can align the Facility with Panama's sustainability goals, ensuring compliance with evolving regulatory frameworks while improving its environmental impact.

# The Issuer

The Issuer was incorporated on January 19, 2015 under the laws of Panama. Since March 31, 2021, the Issuer is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Parent Company, a Panamanian limited liability company. The Parent Company is owned by InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas (51%) and AES Panamá (49%). Pursuant to a shareholders' agreement each of the sponsors has the right to appoint three members to the Parent Company's board of directors. The Parent Company is the sole shareholder of all of the Issuer's share capital. The ultimate parent of InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas is InterEnergy Group, and the ultimate parents of AES Panamá are The AES Corporation located in Arlington, Virginia (USA) and the Republic of Panama.

In the ordinary course of business, the Issuer engages in a variety of transactions with certain of its affiliates, primarily for the purchase, at fair market prices negotiated on an arm's-length basis, of goods or services that may also be provided by other suppliers. For more details, see "Related Party Transactions".

# Our Principal Shareholders

## InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas

InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas owns a 51% interest in us. InterEnergy Power &amp; Gas' indirect parent company, InterEnergy Group, was established in 2011 and is a developer, owner, and operator for power generation, transmission, and distribution assets in the Latin American and Caribbean region, with 2.5 GW of installed capacity across 22 operating assets in 10 countries. InterEnergy Group is an experienced sponsor in the power sector with a focus on renewable energy and energy transition. In Jamaica, InterEnergy Group owns almost 40% of the country's total base load capacity. In Dominican Republic, InterEnergy Group owns two generation, transmission, and

distribution companies through which it became the first wind operator in 2011. In 2014, InterEnergy built the largest wind farm in the Central American and Caribbean region (Laudato Si wind farm in Panama). Other investments include solar and wind power plants in Chile, solar, wind and thermal power plants in Panama, wind generation in Uruguay, Guatemala and the Dominican Republic, solar and thermal power plants in Jamaica, and solar plants in the Cayman Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands. As of December 31, 2025, InterEnergy Group, through its Panamanian subsidiaries, supplies 19.98% of Panama's electricity generation.

## AES Panamá

AES Panamá owns a 49% interest in us. AES Panamá is owned 50.50% by the Republic of Panama, 0.40% by minority shareholders and 49.10% by AES through its wholly owned subsidiary AES Global Power Holdings. Through AES Global Power Holdings, AES currently owns an interest in and operates a large portfolio of electricity generation and LNG assets in Panama. AES Panamá currently operates 5 hydroelectric power plants, 1 wind farm and 7 solar plants, amounting to an installed capacity of 612 MW. AES Panamá also operates facilities in Colón and Changuinola, resulting in a combined generation portfolio that amounts to 1,216 MW, making AES Panamá the largest generation sponsor in Panama both by installed capacity and energy generation. As of December 31, 2025, all AES assets in Panama supply 30% of the country's electricity generation.

# Gas Strategy

The Gas Supply Arrangements for the Project involve three key agreements: (a) the LNG Sale and Purchase Agreement dated as of November 16, 2021 between TotalEnergies Gas &amp; Power Limited and the Issuer (the "LNG SPA"), (b) the LNG Terminal Use Agreement dated as of November 16, 2021 (the "TUA") between Costa Norte LNG Terminal S. de R.L. and the Issuer and (c) the Second Amended and Restated Operations Coordination Agreement dated as of November 16, 2021 (the "OCA") among Costa Norte LNG Terminal S. de R.L., the Issuer and the other parties thereto.

LNG supply is secured from Total Gas &amp; Power Limited, a subsidiary of Total, under the 20-year LNG SPA at a price indexed to Henry Hub. The LNG SPA includes cargo cancellation flexibility in case of lower/higher than expected dispatch. In addition to the LNG SPA, under the TUA with the Colón Terminal we have capacity for delivery, storage, and regasification at the Colón Terminal. Finally, through the OCA, we coordinate the scheduling and inventory of the LNG supple with the other Colón Terminal customers.

109

# Water Supply

The Facility supplies all water via a pumping station near the plant site on the coast and an associated desalinization plant. Seawater is pumped from Limón Bay on the Caribbean Sea and used for the main cooling system. For raw water, the seawater from the Limón Bay is pumped into a storage tank and then sent to the desalinization and demineralization treatment systems and utilized for the steam cycle and for general use including service and fire protection. The Facility's potable water meets WHO standards and is also provided by the desalinization plant and used for drinking, restrooms, eye wash, and emergency shower systems. Approximately 5% of pumped seawater is fed into the desalinization system. There are separate storage tanks and pumps within the Facility for raw water and potable water.

# Seasonality

Although prices in the National Interconnected System are influenced by hydrological conditions, this volatility has moderated with the increased participation of thermal generation—such as that provided by the Facility—which serves as a price cap during dry periods. However, we do not believe our operations are materially affected by seasonality as our PPA counterparties are Distribution Companies that operate year-round, with relatively stable daily demand that is generally not subject to seasonal fluctuations.

# Maintenance and Repair

The achievement of operational excellence is core to our overall business strategy. We strive to be a leader in the energy sector by providing safe, sustainable and competitive energy for our customers and the market. In this regard, we have implemented an asset management strategy to ensure adequate execution of our operation and maintenance activities. Our asset management strategy considers a systematic process of developing, operating, maintaining and disposal assets in a cost-effective manner.

Our asset management strategy is based on the following key fundamentals:

- Long- and short-term asset planning;
- Maintenance strategy based on predictive, preventive and corrective activities according to original equipment manufacturer's recommendations and industry best practices;
- Cost effective supply chain management;
- Long term services agreement for main equipment maintenance and operation;
- Continuous improvement, failure analysis and root cause analysis;
- Risk assessment of our critical activities;
- Asset performance monitoring and O&amp;M metrics; and
- Human resources development.

# Environmental and Sustainability

## Environment

We are subject to Panamanian environmental, health, and safety laws and regulations, including the Category III Environmental Impact Assessment and the Approval Resolution No. DEIA-IA-051-2021 issued by the Environment Ministry on August 24, 2021. These resolutions include the Environmental Management Plan, which establishes mitigation and control measures related to air quality, noise and vibrations, water resources, the protection of terrestrial wildlife, aquatic ecosystems, and waste management. We implement the corresponding actions to comply with all laws and regulations in accordance with the fundamental environmental aspects focused on the environmental impacts produced by thermal energy generators, in our case, using natural gas as fuel source.

As part of our ecological compensation plans, we continue monitoring the relocation of seagrass and invertebrates in Limón Bay. We have also restored 7.00 hectares of mangroves and associated species in the Punta Galeta Protected Landscape, both in the city of Colón.

To verify environmental compliance, periodic assessments (audits) are conducted by an external auditor on behalf of the Environment Ministry. The results of these audits were satisfactory.

As such, we believe we are in compliance in all material respects with these laws and regulations.

## Community

As part of our commitment to sustainable development, we continuously seek to implement programs in the communities in our areas of influence that promote learning about efficient resource management to stimulate the economic development of these communities.

In 2023, we furthered our initiatives, including our “Colón 4.0”, which provides local communities the opportunity to learn about computer and other technological resources needed in an increasingly digital world. We also support the community with youth outreach programs such as and “Fútbol con Corazón” through which we have restored public and school playgrounds throughout the Colón region and funded youth sports programs.

## Safety

Our safety management program is focused on occupational safety, with an emphasis on risk prevention for our employees, contractors, and the communities where we operate. We regularly conduct a range of activities to maintain and continually improve our safety and health standards. These include job safety analysis evaluations, work permit management, health campaigns, and safety trainings—particularly around risk assessment and hazardous energy control. On-site inspections are also carried out periodically to ensure active implementation and ongoing enhancement of our safety practices.

## Employees and Human Resources

Our team consists of directors, officers, employees, professionals and technicians. Our team is fundamental to our success, and we strive to maintain an organization that rewards competitive, engaged and qualified employees and offers them an opportunity for development and advancement. Certain personnel that serve the Facility are employed by AES Panamá and InterEnergy Group pursuant to various agreements, such as the O&amp;M Agreement, the ASA and the TUA, among others. See “Related Party Transactions”.

In promotion of long-term company sustainability and professional development, we develop and train our employees to be able to appropriately face present and future challenges. In order to effectively and efficiently operate our generation plants and administer our business, we seek to stimulate and retain our personnel while strengthening our team with suitable individuals that have the potential to take on new projects and successfully replace existing professionals. Within this framework, in recent years, we have focused our efforts on developing the skills of our existing and recently hired employees to be able to fill positions at the plants of some of our related companies.

We seek to maintain an amenable work atmosphere and encourage communication between team leaders and the professionals they supervise.

## Insurance

We maintain extensive insurance coverage for the possible risks to which our assets are subject, including possible claims that may arise in the course of its operations. For this purpose, we take out corporate insurance policies that mainly include:

(i) All Risks Material Damage, which covers machinery breakdown and loss of profits that could occur as a consequence of a stoppage of operations in the Facility, due to various circumstances. This coverage covers all assets owned by us, as well as other assets of insurable interest. This coverage has a maximum indemnification limit of U.S.$800 million per event (combined single limit material damage and business interruption coverage). These policies have deductibles of U.S.$2 million per claim except for Gas turbine/Steam turbine/HRSG/Main transformers for which the deductible is U.S.$2.5 million per claim.

(ii) General Liability, which covers possible damages to third parties caused during operations, with limits of up to U.S.$35 million for any event.

Our insurance coverage is underwritten by top-tier large reinsurance companies. We do not anticipate difficulties in renewing our insurance policies and believe that the insurance coverage that we maintain is reasonable in amount and consistent with industry standards. For more information, see "Risk Factors—Risks Relating to Our Business—We are not able to insure against all potential risks and our insurance, guarantee and warranty coverage may not be adequate."

## Competition

Generation companies in Panama compete on the basis of availability, cost and price. In the energy spot market, generators compete on the basis of availability and variable cost, and in the PPA market on the basis of bid prices for capacity and energy. These two markets are the relevant markets for our revenues and we believe we have a strong position in each of these markets pursuant to our PPAs and the Facility's full capacity. ## Legal Proceedings

On December 30, 2025, AES received a complaint filed in Virginia state court by Sinolam LNG Terminal, S.A. and Sinolam Smarter Energy LNG Power Co. (collectively, "Plaintiffs") against the AES, AES Latin America, AES Panamá, AES Colon Holdings, S. de R.L., Costa Norte LNG Terminal S. de R.L., Gas Natural del Atlantico S. de R.L., InterEnergy Holdings UK (a third party), and the Holding Company (collectively, "Defendants"). In their complaint, the Plaintiffs allege that the Defendants interfered with the Plaintiffs' efforts to develop an LNG-fired power plant and an LNG terminal in Panama. The Plaintiffs appear to seek recovery of alleged lost profits totaling about U.S.$4 billion, alleged out-of-pocket damages, interest, statutory damages, and other relief from the Defendants. As of the date of this offering memorandum, no proceedings have yet to commence in connection with the suit. AES believes that it has meritorious defenses to the claims asserted against it and will defend itself vigorously in this lawsuit; however, there can be no assurances that it will be successful in its efforts.

# CORPORATE GOVERNANCE

On November 11, 2003, the SMV approved Accord No. 12-2003 (as amended from time to time) by means of which the guides and principles of corporate governance are recommended for all issuers registered before SMV. Subsequently, on February of 2004, the Board of Directors of Latinex approved the principles of disclosure of corporate governance practices for registered issuers.

The adoption of these recommendations is not mandatory; nevertheless, issuers that are registered with the SMV are required to publicly reveal whether or not they are adopted. Our Board of Directors has taken into consideration and has partially adopted those principles that are considered appropriate and applicable to the nature, structure and course of our business, taking into account the characteristics of the Facility and our ownership structure.

Pursuant to literal C, Section IX of article 7 of Rule No. 2-2010 (which establishes the procedure for the filings of securities registration and of termination of registrations, with the SMV), as amended, restated or replaced, whereby the SMV establishes a procedure for filing requests for securities registration or termination of registration before the SMV, we have adopted the following principles and procedures of corporate governance:

- The Board of Directors is responsible for the supervision of the activities of the Project, exercising oversight over management and strategic matters.
- Decisions adopted in meetings of the Board of Directors and shareholders meetings are documented in writing through minutes. The minutes will reflect the discussions that take place during the meetings and are prepared, approved and signed in the corresponding meeting. They are later kept in places designated for recordkeeping.
- We have adopted information and communication policies information sharing and disclosure among management, directors, shareholders and, where applicable, third parties.
- The members of the Board of Directors must disclose any conflict of interest in any matter submitted for their consideration, in accordance with our internal governance rules.
- We maintain appropriate accounting records that reasonably reflect our financial position.
- Our assets are protected and we have procedures for the prevention and detection of fraud and other irregularities.
- We maintain internal control mechanisms designed to ensure the orderly and efficient conduct of our business, including controls over financial reporting and risk management.
- Our Board of Directors works through different specialized committees, focused on audit, compliance, compensation and corporate governance functions among other matters.
- Our management maintains regular meetings to implement, monitor, and execute our business strategy and operational plans, in accordance with the objectives approved by the Board of Directors.
