## Price Stabilization and Short Positions

In connection with the offering of the Notes, the Initial Purchasers may engage in overallotment, stabilizing transactions and syndicate covering transactions. Overallotment involves sales in excess of the offering size, which creates a short position for the Initial Purchasers. Stabilizing transactions involve bids to purchase the Notes in the open market for the purpose of pegging, fixing or maintaining the price of the Notes. Syndicate covering transactions involve purchases of the Notes in the open market after the distribution has been completed in order to cover short positions. Stabilizing transactions and syndicate covering transactions may cause the price of the Notes to be higher than it would otherwise be in the absence of those transactions. If the Initial Purchasers engage in stabilizing or syndicate covering transactions, they may discontinue them at any time.

## Chile

The Notes being offered will not be registered under the Chilean Securities Market Law (Ley de Mercado de Valores) in the Chilean Securities Registry (Registro de Valores) or in the Foreign Securities Registry (Registro de Valores Extranjeros) both kept by the Chilean Financial Market Commission (“CMF”) and, therefore, the Notes are not subject to the oversight of the CMF. As unregistered securities in Chile, we are not required to disclose public information about the Notes in Chile. Accordingly, the Notes cannot and will not be publicly offered to persons in Chile unless they are registered in the corresponding Chilean Securities Registry. The Notes may only be offered in Chile in circumstances that do not constitute a public offering under Chilean law or in compliance with Rule No. 336 of the CMF. Pursuant to the Chilean Securities Market Law, a public offering of securities is an offering that is addressed to the general public or to certain specific categories or groups thereof. Considering that the definition of public offering is quite broad, even an offering addressed to a small group of investors may be considered to be addressed to a certain specific category or group of the public and therefore be considered public under applicable law and, as such, subject to registration in Chile. However, pursuant to the Chilean Securities Market Law and Rule 336 of the CMF, the Notes may be privately offered in Chile to certain “qualified investors” identified as such by Rule 336 (which in turn are further described in Rule No. 216, dated June 12, 2008, issued by the CMF as amended).

Rule 336 requires the following information to be provided to prospective investors in Chile:

1. Date of commencement of the offer of the Notes in Chile: , 2026.
2. The offer of the Notes is subject to Rule 336.
3. The offering of the Notes is not registered with the Securities Registry (Registro de Valores) of the CMF nor with the foreign securities registry (Registro de Valores Extranjeros) of the CMF and as such:

a. The Notes are not subject to the oversight of the CMF; and
b. The Issuer of the Notes are not subject to the obligation to make publicly available information about the Notes in Chile.

4. The Notes may not be subject to public offering in Chile unless and until they are registered with the relevant Securities Registry of the CMF.

Los Valores se ofrecen privadamente en Chile de conformidad con las disposiciones de la Ley N° 18.045 de Mercado de Valores, y la Norma de Carácter General N° 336 de 27 de junio de 2012 (“NCG 336”) emitida por la Comisión para el Mercado Financiero (“CMF”).

En cumplimiento de la NCG 336, la siguiente información se proporciona a los potenciales inversionistas residentes en Chile.

1. La oferta de estos valores en Chile comienza el día de 2026.
2. La oferta se encuentra acogida a la NCG 336.
3. La oferta versa sobre valores que no se encuentran inscritos en el Registro de Valores ni en el Registro de Valores Extranjeros que lleva la CMF, por lo que:

a. Los valores no están sujetos a la fiscalización de la CMF; y

252

b. El emisor de los valores no está sujeto a la obligación de entregar información pública sobre los valores ofrecidos.

4. Los valores no podrán ser objeto de oferta pública en Chile mientras no sean inscritos en el Registro de Valores correspondiente.

# TRANSFER RESTRICTIONS

## General

The Notes have not been registered, and will not be registered, under the Securities Act or any state securities laws, and the Notes may not be offered or sold except pursuant to an effective registration statement or pursuant to transactions exempt from, or not subject to, registration under the Securities Act. Accordingly, the Notes are being offered and sold only:

- to qualified institutional buyers (as defined in Rule 144A) pursuant to Rule 144A under the Securities Act; and
- outside of the United States, to certain persons, other than U.S. persons, in offshore transactions meeting the requirements of Regulation S under the Securities Act.

## Purchasers’ Representations and Restrictions on Resale and Transfer

Each purchaser of Notes (other than the Initial Purchasers in connection with the initial issuance and sale of Notes) and each owner of any beneficial interest therein will be deemed, by its acceptance or purchase thereof, to have represented and agreed as follows:

(1) it is purchasing the Notes for its own account or an account with respect to which it exercises sole investment discretion and it and any such account is either (a) a qualified institutional buyer and is aware that the sale to it is being made pursuant to Rule 144A or (b) a non-U.S. person that is outside the United States;

(2) it acknowledges that the Notes have not been registered under the Securities Act or with any securities regulatory authority of any state and may not be offered or sold within the United States or to, or for the account or benefit of, U.S. persons except as set forth below;

(3) it understands and agrees that Notes initially offered to qualified institutional buyers will be represented by a Global Note and that Notes offered outside the United States pursuant to Regulation S will also be represented by a Global Note;

(4) it will not resell or otherwise transfer any of such Notes except (a) to us or any of our subsidiaries, (b) within the United States to a qualified institutional buyer in a transaction complying with Rule 144A under the Securities Act, (c) outside the United States in compliance with Rule 903 or Rule 904 of Regulation S under the Securities Act, (d) pursuant to an exemption from registration under the Securities Act (if available) or I pursuant to an effective registration statement under the Securities Act, in each case in accordance with all applicable securities laws of the states of the United States and other jurisdictions;

(5) it agrees that it will give to each person to whom it transfers the Notes notice of any restrictions on transfer of such Notes;

(6) it acknowledges that prior to any proposed transfer of Notes (other than pursuant to an effective registration statement) the holder of such Notes may be required to provide certifications relating to the manner of such transfer as provided in the indenture, including with respect to Notes sold or transferred pursuant to Rule 144A or Regulation S;

(7) it acknowledges that the trustee, registrar or transfer agent for the Notes may not be required to accept for registration or transfer of any Notes acquired by it, except upon presentation of evidence satisfactory to us that the restrictions set forth herein have been complied with;

(8) it acknowledges that we, the Initial Purchasers and other persons will rely upon the truth and accuracy of the foregoing acknowledgements, representations and agreements and agrees that if any of the acknowledgements, representations and agreements deemed to have been made by its purchase of the Notes are no longer accurate, it will promptly notify us and the Initial Purchasers; and

(9) if it is acquiring the Notes as a fiduciary or agent for one or more investor accounts, it represents that it has sole investment discretion with respect to each such account and it has full power to make the foregoing acknowledgements, representations and agreements on behalf of each account.

# EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

## INTRODUCTION

Generadora de Gatún S.A. (Owner), with shareholders InterEnergy Group (51%) and AES Panama SRL (49%) has engaged Sargent &amp; Lundy (S&amp;L) as the Independent Engineer to conduct a technical due diligence review in support of the refinancing of the Generadora de Gatún Power Plant (Project). The facility is a 640 megawatt-net (MW-net) / 670 MW-gross natural gas-fired power plant located in Colón, Panama. The Project operates in a combined-cycle configuration with two gas turbines (GT), two heat recovery steam generators (HRSG), and one steam turbine (ST). Sargent &amp; Lundy's technical due diligence evaluates the facility's condition at the end of its construction phase, to ensure compliance with design specifications, applicable standards, and contractual obligations.

Key areas of evaluation included a site visit to visually observe and assess the Project's physical condition and its expected remaining life, as well as an assessment observing if the adequate operation &amp; maintenance (O&amp;M) practices were being performed. The Gatún combined-cycle plant is operating and available for dispatch in accordance with the Centro Nacional de Despacho (CND) [41], and officially declared its Substantial Completion and commercial operation date (COD) on May 22, 2025 [43]. Evaluation also included a review of key agreements such as the power purchase agreements, interconnection agreement, fuel supply agreements, liquified natural gas (LNG) sale purchase agreement, generation permits, environmental &amp; social compliance, and the updated financial model in respect of technical inputs, operating expenditures, major maintenance, capital expenditures, and counterparties experience in complying with their respective contracts (sponsors, suppliers, operators etc.).

At the end of 1st Quarter of 2025, Generadora de Gatún S.A. reported an overall construction progress of 99.84%, declaring Mechanical Completion on February 22, 2025 [2]. The Project has been in partial commercial operation since October 1, 2024, generating 400 MW in simple cycle with gas turbines GT-1 and GT-2 to fulfill commitments under the three purchase power agreements (PPAs) with the offtakers [3]. During late 2024 and the first quarter of 2025, the Project successfully completed several steam-side system tests as part of the start-up and commissioning of the steam turbine and balance of plant. This led to the combined-cycle performance test, which was completed on May 19, 2025. As mentioned above, the Project was declared available by the CND on May 30, 2025 [41], and declared Substantial Completion on May 22, 2025. As an added note, when GT1 and/or GT2 are out of service for minor maintenance and during the combined-cycle steam power plant system testing, Generadora Gatún purchased energy at spot prices to fulfill its contracts.

# SITE VISIT, CONDITION ASSESSMENT, AND REMAINING TECHNICAL LIFE

Sargent &amp; Lundy conducted a site visit to the Generadora de Gatún power plant on May 13–15, 2025, to visually assess its current physical condition and evaluate the expected remaining technical life of the assets. This assessment included an analysis of the design, technology, site characteristics, major equipment, interconnection, fuel supply, and water supply. The visual inspection focused on various systems within the plant, particularly the major power block equipment, which includes two GTs, two HRSGs, and one ST, as well as the cooling tower, auxiliary systems, balance of plant equipment, firefighting equipment, buildings, supporting infrastructure, and the seawater intake and discharge system. Figure ES-1 shows a general plant layout of the Project, highlighting the major power block equipment, the seawater intake and discharge systems, as well as the LNG regasification plant which is seen in the background at AES Colón.

The plant and equipment were designed in accordance with industry codes and standards, the specific design criteria for the Project site, and other requirements outlined in the technical specifications of the engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) Contract. Each plant system, unless specified otherwise, was designed to provide a useful life of at least twenty-five (25) years, exceeding the 20-year term of the PPAs that commenced on October 1, 2024. Following the anticipated declaration of commercial operation on July 31, 2025, the plant will be subject to a 2-year warranty period for the equipment and a 4-year warranty for hidden defects, such as those related to concrete foundations. During the site visit, the visual inspection of the equipment and structures revealed no major discrepancies or significant damage. The plant was found to be in as-new condition, with a remaining design useful life of 25 years.

# OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE ASSESSMENT

AES Latin America will provide the plant's O&amp;M management team, which will include a Plant Director, Operations Manager, and Maintenance Manager. This O&amp;M management team will oversee the Owner's staff responsible for operating and maintaining the power plant. The O&amp;M organization chart indicates there are 41 operational staff members and 18 administrative staff members dedicated to supporting the plant's operation and maintenance. S&amp;L opines that these staffing positions are sufficient to effectively manage the daily O&amp;M activities of a power plant of the type and size of Generadora de Gatún.

The combined responsibilities of the Owner and AES Latin America include site management, operations, predictive and corrective maintenance, fuel and water management, regulatory compliance, maintenance of O&amp;M manuals, and personnel management. Key tasks for the O&amp;M Management Staff involve ensuring the plant operates in line with project agreements, submitting monthly operational summaries, controlling the O&amp;M budget, recommending specialty contractors, monitoring contractor performance, and implementing safety and environmental programs.

Sargent &amp; Lundy has assessed that the staffing levels are adequate for the daily O&amp;M of the Generadora de Gatún power plant. No issues were identified during the site visit and based on observations and conversations with the O&amp;M staff, they appeared well-qualified to effectively manage the plant. While monthly and annual reports were not available for review at the time of this report, Sargent &amp; Lundy anticipates their preparation following the official transition from EPC to O&amp;M staff, with follow-up inspections planned during the operations phase.

According to the Long-Term Service Agreement (LTSA), scheduled major maintenance for the GTs will occur approximately every 32,000 FFH. Given the relatively new condition of the GTs, no significant maintenance activities are expected in the immediate future. The O&amp;M team will closely monitor turbine performance and condition through regular assessments and predictive maintenance techniques to ensure optimal functioning and timely identification of potential issues.

# REVIEW OF KEY AGREEMENTS

Sargent &amp; Lundy reviewed the three PPAs and Amendments between Generadora Gatún S.A. ("Seller") and the three distribution companies EDEMET, EDECHI and ENSA ("Buyers"). The term of the PPAs is 20-years to deliver power / energy from Seller to Buyer starting with 400 MW from October 1, 2024, through July 31, 2028, and 550 MW from August 1, 2028, through September 30, 2044. During the entire term, the capacity payment and energy price is $18.89 USD/kW-month and $0.088 USD/kWh, respectively, adjusted to the price of US treasury bonds for capacity payments and a reference indicator of the gas chosen by the Seller and which shall be used to index the price of the energy (EIA Henry Hub) [3].

The Project has been in partial commercial operation generating 400 MW in simple cycle with gas turbines GT-1 and GT-2 since October 1, 2024, to meet the three PPAs with offtakers. S&amp;L observed the power plant output screen in the control room during the combined-cycle performance test, showing an output of about 638 MW-net subject to adjustments to ambient conditions and GT output curves based on accumulated hours since October 1, 2024. Also, S&amp;L observed the real-time generation on June 16, 2025, at 6:28 PM when Gatún power plant was generating 603.89 MW (Figure ES-2). Therefore, the rated power of 640 MW-net for the Project is sufficient to comply with the 550 MW-net required PPAs capacity and energy requirements for the 20-year term.

Natural gas required by the Project will be received via a natural gas transport pipeline from the adjacent AES Colón LNG Terminal (also known as AES Costa Norte). The Project has entered into a natural gas Sales Purchase Agreement (SPA) with Total Gas &amp; Power Limited, and a Terminal Use Agreement (TUA) and Operations Coordination Agreement (OCA) with Costa Norte. The SPA, TUA and COA agreements are in executed draft form dated November 16, 2021. The agreements contain minimum and maximum amounts for fuel supply. The SPA maximum limit is adequate to support a plant annual net capacity factor up to approximately 60% during the first two years of operation, and 70% for the years after. To run at higher capacity factors Gatún has the option of requesting additional fuel supply from Total Gas or obtaining fuel from a third party.

The power plant will be operated and maintained by Generadora de Gatún S.A. ("Owner") with staff managed by AES Latin America, S. de R.L., ("O&amp;M Manager") as per the Operation and Maintenance Management Service Agreement by and between AES Latin America, S. de R.L. and Generadora de Gatún, S.A. signed on November 16, 2021. The combined Owner and AES scope includes site management; operations; predictive and corrective maintenance; managing fuel, water, and waste; maintenance of permits, licenses, and approvals; maintenance of O&amp;M manuals; and management of personnel and subcontractors. The contract specifies a fixed monthly fee of $91,667 for services, which includes three onsite management staff, off-site support personnel, and supervision of 23 onsite staff. This fee is subject to annual adjustments based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI). While this agreement establishes a predictable cost for the specified services, it does not impose a cap on the overall O&amp;M costs incurred by the Owner. The Owner remains responsible for all additional expenses including labor costs for the 23 onsite personnel employed by the Owner. Furthermore, the agreement allows for additional fees for emergency services as needed, which will be determined based on proposals. Thus, while the O&amp;M agreement provides a fixed price for specific services, it is essential to recognize that the Owner's total O&amp;M costs may vary based on other operational needs. S&amp;L opines that this arrangement of the agreement is common in the industry.

The timeline of permits granted by the National Authorities for Public Services of Panama to Generadora de Gatún, S.A. (GdG), is as follows:

**Provisional Permit:** Issued on November 18, 2020 (Resolution AN No. 19625-Elec), this permit allowed for construction and required GdG to submit documentation to obtain a Definitive Permit. The Gatún power plant has achieved Mechanical Completion as of February 2025, with only minor Punch List items remaining.

**Definitive Permit:** Granted on September 29, 2021 (Resolution AN No. 17156-Elec), this permit approved both construction and operation, establishing an original COD of September 30, 2024. It includes standard conditions such as bonds, insurance, and compliance obligations related to taxes and performance bonds, with a term of 40 years and the possibility of a 40-year extension.

**Modification to Definitive Resolution:** Issued on March 25, 2025 (Resolution No. AN No. 20082-Elec), this modification acknowledged that the Gatún plant was generating power but still had outstanding items prior to being declared ready for Commercial Operation. It allowed for testing to commence on January 15, 2025, concluding on March 30, 2025, with a revised COD of April 15, 2025. The actual performance testing began on May 17, 2025, with Substantial Completion declared on May 22, 2025 [43]. Other provisions of the original Definitive Resolution remain in effect.

S&amp;L concludes that all necessary permits are in place to ensure the successful operation of the Gatún power plant.

## ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL

Sargent &amp; Lundy received and reviewed the Monitoring and Surveillance Plan for Environmental Physical Aspects Concerning the 670 MW Combined-Cycle Thermal Power Plant for the Project. This plan details the environmental monitoring requirements for the Project during its operation and maintenance. It includes the background, objectives, and specific monitoring strategies for Generadora de Gatún. The Plan outlines testing parameters and frequencies for the following: Ambient Air Quality, Emissions from Significant Fixed Sources, Occupational Noise, Ambient Noise, Ambient Vibrations, Soil Quality, Marine Sediment Quality, Marine Water Quality, Characterization of Aquatic Fauna, and Aquatic Ecosystems. Though the Project recently entered operation and most monitoring results are not available, it is S&amp;L's opinion that the plan is comprehensive and meets general industry standards for operational environmental monitoring and compliance.

## FINANCIAL MODEL UPDATES

S&amp;L performed a review of the underlying technical assumptions and inputs within the Project's financial model, dated May 2025 [42], that was prepared for the Gatún Liquified Natural Gas Project. The intent of the review was to evaluate the reasonableness of the technical input assumptions and to determine if the financial performance forecast for the facility is achievable. Part of this review is to confirm that the financial model is consistent with the plant performance requirements of the Project agreements and the expected capability of the plant.

Overall, S&amp;L finds the financial model to adequately account for the expected technical and operational inputs for a natural-gas-fired combined-cycle project and can perform the revenue and debt calculations accurately.

- S&amp;L finds the projected heat rate and availability factor values to be comparable to other units of comparable size and technology.
- S&amp;L finds the capital costs for the maintenance and the LTSA to be adequately accounted for in the financial model with a total of $130.37 Million not including CapEx to build the plant.
- S&amp;L finds the projected technical O&amp;M costs are increasing with an average annual inflation rate of 0.90%, 2025 through 2044, with average technical O&amp;M costs of $25.34/kW-yr.

# COUNTERPARTIES ASSESSMENT

Sargent &amp; Lundy conducted a review of the experience of Generadora Gatún S.A.’s counterparties—including sponsors, suppliers, and operators—in meeting their contractual obligations, along with an assessment of their credit ratings. The counterparties are well-established, reputable companies with extensive experience in the energy sector and solid credit standings. However, a recent downgrade was noted for ETESA, the electricity transmission company of Panama. Fitch Ratings downgraded ETESA's Long-Term Foreign- and Local-Currency Issuer Default Rating (IDR) from 'BB+' to 'B' due to a delayed coupon payment. Additionally, the National Long-Term Rating and national long-term senior unsecured rating were lowered from 'AAA (pan)' to 'BB (pan).' This rating action was announced on December 3, 2024. It is important to note that ETESA is fully owned by the Government of Panama and has a legal monopoly on electricity transmission services in the country, which leads Sargent &amp; Lundy to conclude that this downgrade does not pose a risk to the Project.

In addition, Sargent &amp; Lundy conducted a comprehensive review of other key counterparties involved in the Generadora Gatún S.A. project, focusing on sponsors, major suppliers, operators, and offtakers.

The primary sponsors, InterEnergy and AES Panama SRL, are notable players in the energy sector. InterEnergy, holding a 51% stake, is a well-established private equity-backed company with a robust portfolio across various regions, showcasing a strong commitment to delivering reliable, cost-effective, and clean energy solutions. AES Panama SRL, with a 49% stake, is a subsidiary of AES Corporation, a major global energy provider. With a Long-Term IDR of 'BBB-' and a stable outlook from Fitch Ratings, AES Panama has contributed over $2.75 billion to Panama's energy landscape, reinforcing its substantial role in the local market.

The project's operational stability is further enhanced by key suppliers and contractors. POSCO E&amp;C is tasked with EPC services. As a subsidiary of POSCO Holdings, POSCO E&amp;C brings extensive international experience, having successfully completed numerous power projects. Their credit rating of 'BBB+' with a stable outlook from Fitch Ratings underscores their financial reliability.

# CONCLUSION

In conclusion, S&amp;L's comprehensive technical due diligence review confirms that the Generadora de Gatún Power Plant is well-positioned for successful refinancing and ongoing operations. The plant's physical condition, compliance with all necessary permits, and robust operational and maintenance management demonstrate its readiness to meet contractual obligations and performance expectations. With a strong commitment to environmental and social responsibility, alongside a sound financial model, Generadora de Gatún S.A. is equipped to generate reliable power while maintaining sustainability and community engagement. Overall, the Project's viability is supported by reputable counterparties and a strategic operational framework that will foster its long-term success.

# 1. INTRODUCTION

## 1.1. PLANT DESCRIPTION

Generadora de Gatún S.A. (Owner) developed, constructed, and will operate the 640 megawatt-net (MW-net) / 670 MW-gross, natural-gas-fired, combined-cycle Generadora de Gatún Power Plant (Project), located at the inlet to the Panama Canal on the Caribbean Sea near the City of Colón, Panama (Figure 1-1), whose shareholders are InterEnergy Group (51%) and AES Panama SRL (49%). Generadora de Gatún declared Mechanical Completion on February 22, 2025 [2] completed the combined-cycle performance test on May 19, 2025, and declared Substantial Completion on May 22, 2025 [43].

Figure 1-1 — Project Location

Source: Google Maps

The Project consist of two (2) GE 7FA.05 (60 Hz) gas turbine (GT) generators in combined-cycle configuration with bypass stacks firing only natural gas; two (2) heat recovery steam generators (HRSGs) without supplemental fire, multi-pressure with horizontal reheat units that contain high, intermediate, and low-pressure steam drums; and one steam turbine generator with high-pressure (HP) intermediate-pressure (IP) and low-pressure (LP) sections. All generators are water-cooled. The incorporation of bypass

The water source for all plant uses is seawater from Limon Bay on the Caribbean Sea via a supply pipeline and pumphouse. # 2. FACILITY AND TECHNOLOGY REVIEW

## 2.1. SITE

The Project site is located just outside the City of Colón on the east bank of Limon Bay, on the Panama Canal inlet from the Caribbean Sea. The site is being leased for a period of 40 years starting on September 26, 2013, with the option to purchase the land. Since the lease was under LNG Group Panama, S.A., a sublease was signed between Generadora de Gatún and LNG Group which was approved by Unidad Administrativa de Bienes Revertidos – Ministerio de Economía y Finanzas (UABR) February 19, 2021.

The Project site is located in an uninhabited area of forests and grasslands. Residential and existing industrial areas are about 1 km (0.6 miles) from the Project area. Figure 2-1 shows the land that has been obtained for the Project, and it is optimally located next to the Panama Canal. The area outlined in yellow shows the Project area.

## 2.2. TECHNOLOGY

The Project utilizes two General Electric (GE) 7F.05 gas turbines in a power block that consists of a 2x1 combined-cycle arrangement with two HRSGs and one ST. The 7F 5-Series is an upgraded fifth generation 7F combustion turbine, providing increased output and efficiency, faster start-up and ramp rates, and better turn down capability than its predecessors. Since their introduction in 1988, GE's installed fleet of more than 1000 "F-class" technology combustion turbines have reached 67 million hours of commercial operation in power plants worldwide. The wide range of power generation applications for the 7F combustion turbine include combined-cycle and simple-cycle peaking in both cyclic and base-load operation.

## 2.3. MAJOR EQUIPMENT

### 2.3.1. Combustion Turbine

The GE 7F.05 has a gross electric output rating of 225.6 MW at 60 hertz (Hz). The two GTs are rated to produce 451.2 MW without the ST in use. There are 93-7F.05s in service with over 1.4 million operating hours since the model was introduced in 2012. ## 2.3.2. Heat Recovery Steam Generators

The Project's 7F.05 power blocks are equipped with triple-pressure, horizontal design, and natural circulation HRSGs for outdoor installation. The HRSGs have a serrated finned tube design, large steam drums, and top support heat surfaces, however they are not equipped with auxiliary firing. The HRSGs use hot exhaust gas from the GTs to generate steam for the shared ST. Each HRSG is equipped with a single blowdown tank for continuous and for intermittent blowdown. The HRSGs are composed of 22 rows of tubes, including heating sections for feedwater, superheat, economizer, and aerator sections for high-pressure (HP), intermediate-pressure (IP), and low-pressure (LP) steam.

Recent design enhancements, including component thickness, improved drainage, and suspended pressure components, have improved the HRSGs' ability to handle cycling operation. Each HRSG is equipped with a desuperheater to control the steam temperature to the ST.

As a triple-pressure-level type with a reheater, the HRSGs provides HP, IP, and LP steam to the ST. A distributed control system (DCS) synchronizes operation controls of major components according to the heat balance scenarios.

## 2.3.3. Steam Turbine

The ST is manufactured by GE and equipped with two casings: an opposed-flow HP/IP section and a double-flow LP section. HP steam enters the HP turbine from the HRSG and then exhausts to the HRSG reheat section. Reheat IP steam enters the IP turbine and exhausts to the LP turbine. The LP steam exhausts into the water-cooled surface condenser. A general representation of the ST is shown in Figure 2-3.

## 2.4. INTERCONNECT

Interconnection to the electric grid is via a 20 km, 230 kV / 60Hz, double circuit transmission line from the Telfers II Gatún Power Plant switchyard to the Sabanitas substation utilizing galvanized steel towers and poles. The Project also interconnects to the Cristobal substation at the AES Colón site to create a loop using a less than 1 km transmission line.

## 2.5. UTILITIES

### 2.5.1. Fuel Gas Systems

The GE 7F.05 GT fires only natural gas on this Project. Natural gas is delivered to the power plant terminal point by Costa Norte. From the terminal point fuel gas passes through a common trip shut-off valve, metering station, gas chromatograph, and gas regulating station. Downstream of the regulating station the flow will split to the individual GT supply lines consisting of an absolute separator, flow meter, performance heater, electric start-up heater, gas scrubber, and safety shut-off valve.

A drain tank is provided for each GT to collect accumulated hydrocarbon/condensate mixture from the absolute separator and gas scrubber.

### 2.5.2. Water Supply and Treatment Systems

Limon Bay is the source of water for the Project. The water intake structure is located northwest of the plant in Limon Bay. The vast majority of the seawater is pumped directly to the cooling tower for makeup. The

## 2.5.3. Plant Water Discharge

The vast majority of plant discharge water is cooling tower blowdown (1.5 CoC) which is returned directly to Limon Bay via a pipeline. The balance of Plant discharge is from the effluent system which collects wastewater from a number of sources and treats it before discharge. This includes sanitary waste that has been collected and sent to the wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), oily wastewater that has been sent to an oil/water separator before entering the rest of the wastewater collection, and rainwater. The wastewater network is collected and enters a homogenization and discharge basin before being combined with the cooling tower blowdown flow and discharged into Limon Bay.

## 2.6. CONCLUSION

In conclusion, the design of the power plant utilizing two GE 7F.05 GTs in a 2x1 combined-cycle arrangement is deemed acceptable. This design was previously reviewed during the due diligence process conducted in 2021, and it has been confirmed through the successful operation of the Project to date. The Generadora de Gatún plant, strategically located on the east bank of Limon Bay near the Panama Canal, benefits from advanced technology, including high-efficiency gas turbines and integrated heat recovery solutions. Additionally, the plant's infrastructure, including fuel gas systems and water supply and treatment processes, has been effectively implemented to support continuous operation. Overall, the Project is currently operating successfully, demonstrating the reliability and efficiency of the systems in place. S&amp;L's observations of the current physical condition of the power plant is discussed in Section 3 of this report.

## 3.2.1.5. Condenser Cooling and Circulating Water System

The Main Cooling System and Condensing System calls for 3x50% capacity circulating water pumps (Figure 3-7) and 2x100% cooling tower makeup water pumps (Figure 3-8). This is not a conflict, as the makeup water pumps, and the circulating water pumps perform different functions.

The seawater is mixed with chemical dosing and pumped by the circulating water pumps to the condenser. After passing through the condenser, the cooling water passes into the cooling tower and continues on a loop via the circulating water pumps. A portion of the cooling tower basin water is directed to the outfall in Limon Bay via 2x100% cooling tower blowdown pumps located in the tower basin. The circulating water system includes a condenser tube cleaning system and a cooling tower plume abatement system.

The condenser is equipped with NASH condenser vacuum pump (Figure 3-9) used to remove air and non-condensable gases from the condenser. By maintaining a vacuum, it improves the efficiency of the condenser, allowing steam to condense at a lower pressure and temperature. This enhances the overall thermal efficiency of the system. Common types include liquid ring and steam jet ejector pumps. The drains from the ST and water/steam cycle are recovered in the condenser and collected in the headers or the flash tank (Figure 3-10), depending on the temperature. The drains from the HRSG will be stored in a retention tank. There is a portion of purge that flashes and may be used elsewhere. The rest will then be disposed of in the waste treatment plant.

## 3.2.1.9. Main Steam Systems

The main steam system delivers steam from the HP section of the HRSGs (Figure 3-16) to the HP turbine (Figure 3-17) and returned to the HRSG reheat sections. Steam from the reheat sections of the HRSGs is sent to the IP turbine, after which the crossover pipe transports the steam to the LP turbine. The exhaust side of the LP turbine leads to the condenser. Water and LP steam interact in the condenser as steam passes horizontally over the tubes. Circulating water makes two passes through the heat exchanger. The condenser is designed such that one half of the heat exchanger can be taken out of operation for inspection or cleaning. Makeup water may be sprayed into the steam at the condenser neck for deaeration.

# 3.2.1.10. Feedwater System

Figure 3-18 shows the boiler feedwater pumps (2x100% per HRSG) which take hot condensate from the HRSG LP drum and provide feedwater to the HP economizer and then to the HP drum to produce steam. Feedwater is also diverted to the IP economizer through an interstage bleed. Desuperheaters located throughout the steam systems control the steam temperature. The feedwater system consists of feedwater piping, HP/IP feedwater pumps, and LP economizer recirculation pumps. The feedwater system provides condensate from the ST condenser to the HRSG (Figure 3-19). The system is configured to allow maximum steam production and to function under all planned operational cases. Two fully redundant, electric-motor-driven feedwater pumps supply the HRSGs to generate steam for the HP and IP turbine sections. The specifications call for clearly defined minimum flow and pressure margins for the feedwater pumps and condensate pumps.

# Condition

The feedwater equipment observed was found to be acceptable in "as-new" conditions with no major observable issues which may affect the operation of the power plant.

# Observation

During the walkdown boiler feed pumps, condensate pumps, pipes, foundations, and structures were observed to be in good condition. No damage nor any deterioration was observed. Housekeeping was found to be acceptable, and no personnel safety hazards were observed.

## 3.2.1.11. Sea Water System

The process for the seawater intake system consists of an inlet and outfall pipe (Figure 3-20), 2 x 100% capacity traveling screens (Figure 3-21) to prevent debris from entering the intake structure where the seawater intake pumps are located (Figure 3-22). The traveling screens are equipped with a backwash system. The operation of the 2x100% intake pumps is determined by the water level in the cooling tower basin and demand from the water treatment system. According to the EPC water balance the normal seawater intake flow is 1,674 m3/hr. The pumps name plate shows a capacity of 1,750 m3/hr. The seawater intake is the only source of water for all plant systems.

The water obtained from Limon Bay is pumped to the power plant, where most of it is used as makeup for the cooling towers. The water balance also shows effluent quantities that are returned to Limon Bay (Figure 3-23). The flow rates shown in the water balance are reasonable for a combined-cycle plant of this size. The blowdown flow rate from the cooling tower (Figure 3-24) is higher than most combined-cycle plants due to the use of seawater, the warm and humid ambient air conditions, and the low-approach design temperature. Water requirements are adequately planned to accommodate different types of water quality.

## 3.2.1.12. Water Treatment Plant

The Project necessitates pure water (demineralized water) for makeup in the water/steam cycle. This is essential because the dissolved solids content in the cycle continually increases during operation, requiring periodic removal of water from the circuit (blowdown). To address this need, a water treatment plant for the production of demineralized water is essential. The Generadora de Gatún water treatment plant is equipped with two production trains, each with a net capacity of 100%, including a reverse osmosis (RO) system.

Approximately 5% of the seawater is directed through multi-media filters before entering the 2-pass RO portion of the water treatment system. The multi-media filters are equipped with a backwash system, and the filtered water is stored in a basin that feeds the two 100% trains of seawater RO for initial demineralization. The permeate provides makeup to the service water/fire water tank, which feeds the brackish water RO units. Most of the permeate (clean water) from the brackish water RO trains is directed to the electro-deionization polishing system (EDI) to be stored and used in the demineralized water system.

The remainder of the brackish water RO permeate is stored in the potable water tank, with additional treatment as needed to meet WHO standards. The service water system will utilize dedicated 2x100% capacity pumps drawing from the combined service water/firewater tank. A network of service water piping will contain hose stations located throughout the facility and will also provide water to specific users such as quenching within the HRSG blowdown tank.

The demineralized water storage tank is sized to accommodate five days of full-load operation without concurrent tank filling. In Sargent &amp; Lundy's view, this equipment is standard for water treatment systems and should adequately supply the water necessary for the proper operation of the Project.

The effluent system collects wastewater from several effluent sources and treats the effluent before discharging it. Sanitary waste is collected and sent to the wastewater treatment plant. Oily waste is sent to an oil/water separator before entering the rest of the wastewater collection. The wastewater network is collected and enters a homogenization and discharge basin before being discharged to Limon Bay. Rainwater will also be collected in the wastewater network and ultimately sent to Limon Bay.

## 3.2.1.13. Firefighting System

The fire protection system has been implemented at the facility to reduce the risk of fire. This system has been designed in accordance with American National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) regulations, Underwriters Laboratories standards, local regulations, and Factory Mutual global property loss prevention datasheets. The primary components of the fire protection system include a firefighting pump station, an underground main loop with hydrants encircling the plant, hose reel stations, extinguishing systems, a CO2 fire suppression system, as well as detection and alarm systems (Figure 3-30 and Figure 3-31).

## 3.3. SITE VISIT, JANUARY 28, 2026

### 3.3.1. General Power Plant Condition

A walkdown of the combined-cycle power plant was conducted to verify the physical condition of the main equipment, including the gas turbines, steam turbine, generators, HRSGs, main transformer, cooling system, and key balance of plant systems. The inspection focused on visible signs of damage, corrosion, leaks, abnormal vibration or noise, insulation and lagging condition, integrity of supports and foundations, and overall cleanliness and housekeeping. Particular attention was given to rotating equipment seals and couplings, HRSG casing and ductwork, piping and valve condition, cable routing and tray integrity, and the status of safety and fire protection devices.

Moderate local corrosion was observed throughout the plant, consistent with a power plant exposed to a harsh marine environment (Figure 3-35). To counter the problem, Gatún has an ongoing anti-corrosion program using industrial paint to protect equipment and structures (Figure 3-36). In addition, enclosures have been installed on major balance of plant equipment to protect them from the elements (Figure 3-37). No major structural deficiencies, such as damaged insulation, were observed, and this approach was considered acceptable.

## 3.4. ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT AND SYSTEMS

At the end of 1st Quarter 2025 Generadora de Gatún reported an actual overall progress of 99.84% versus 100% planned and declared Mechanical Completion on February 22, 2025 [2]. The Project has been in been in partial commercial operation generating 400 MW in simple cycle (GT-1 and GT-2) since October 01, 2024, to meet commitments with offtakers under the Purchase Power Agreement. The Project declared Substantial Completion on May 22, 2025 [43].

Since there is essentially no deterioration of the electrical equipment, as was observed during the site visit, the following sub-sections provide a brief description of the equipment in the facilities.

## 3.4.1. Generators

The GTs and ST are equipped with generators with ratings as follows:

Table 3-1 — Generator Ratings

|   | Gas Turbine Generators | Steam Turbine Generator  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  Rated Capacity | 265 MVA | 279 MVA  |
|  Rated Voltage | 19 kV  |   |
|  Rated Current | 7,500 A | 8,500 A  |
|  Frequency | 60 Hz  |   |
|  Number of Poles | 2  |   |
|  Rated Speed | 3,600 rpm  |   |
|  Cooling Type | TEWAC  |   |
|  Insulation | Class F with temperature rise corresponding to Class B  |   |
|  Excitation Type | Static  |   |

The generators come equipped with all necessary accessories, including air-to-water coolers, lube oil systems, and current transformers for metering and relaying. Their construction employs state-of-the-art technology, and based on operational experience at other plants, they are expected to deliver reliable, trouble-free performance. The generator capacities are designed to match or exceed the output of the corresponding turbine under all ambient conditions, and their specifications will fully comply with Panamanian regulations.

Sargent &amp; Lundy performed a review of the electrical design information available and did not find any fatal flaws.

## 3.4.2. Generator Step-Up Transformers (GSUTs)

Each GT generator and the ST generator is equipped with a dedicated transformer that increases the voltage from the generator terminal level to 230 kV for connection to the Project substation. These transformers are oil-immersed and utilize natural convection cooling, along with two stages of forced-air cooling. They are also equipped with tap changers for de-energized operation. The transformers are rated as follows:

Table 3-2 — GSUT Ratings

|   | Gas Turbines GSUTs | Steam Turbine GSUT  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  Rated Capacity | 156/208/260 MVA | 174/232/290 MVA  |
|  Rated Voltages | 19 kV-230 kV  |   |
|  Type | Oil-immersed  |   |
|  Cooling Type | ONAN/ONAF1/ONAF2  |   |
|  Frequency | 60 Hz  |   |
|  Taps | +/-2x2.5%  |   |
|  Temperature Rise | 65°C over 40°C maximum ambient temperature (30°C average daily)  |   |

## 3.4.3. Isolated Phase Buses (IPBs) and Generator Circuit Breakers (GCBs)

The connection between each generator and its GSUT is made by means of isolated phase buses made of aluminum, rated 19 kV, 9000 A in the GTs and 10000 A in the ST. The IPBs for the GTs have a Generator Circuit Breaker inserted between each generator and its transformer, while the IPB of the ST is continuous from the generator to the transformer.

All IPBs have taps of lower capacity to feed the excitation transformer (ET) of each generator, and those of the GTs have additional taps to feed the static frequency converters (SFCs) used to start each GTs and the unit auxiliary transformers (UATs) that serve the load of the plant. The taps in the GTs are located between the generator circuit breaker and the main power transformer. The main GSUTs for the GTs remain energized at all times, while the GCB is kept open when the corresponding GT is not in operation. This configuration ensures that the ET, SFC, and UAT transformers for each unit receive power even when the associated GT is not in service. Once started the GT is synchronized to the grid through its GCB.

Based on our site inspection and review of the plant's operational records, the IPBs and GCBs were observed to be in "like new" condition, consistent with the plants near one-year operational age. No signs of physical wear, overheating, corrosion, or abnormal operation were identified during our assessment. Preventive maintenance records indicate that standard manufacturer-recommended inspections have been

## 3.4.4. Unit Auxiliary Transformers (UATs)

The GT generators are each provided with oil-filled, natural cooling and forced-air cooling (ONAN/ONAF) auxiliary transformers rated 15/20 MVA, 18.5-6.9 kV, with on-load tap changers of +/- 8x 1.25 % taps which feed the buses of 6.9 kV distribution switchgear. These transformers are fed from the IPB taps of the GTs at locations between the GCB and the main GSUT, ensuring that each UAT always remains energized, as previously mentioned. This design provides a highly reliable electric supply with exceptional continuity of service to the plant.

## 3.4.5. Medium Voltage Switchgear (MVS) Assemblies

The combined-cycle block is provided with two 6.9-kV switchgear assemblies fed from the auxiliary transformers of the two GTs. These 6.9-kV switchgear assemblies serve as the main power distribution centers for the block and feature a tie breaker at 6.9 kV to interconnect them, allowing for mutual backup in the event of a supply interruption or maintenance of the corresponding UAT. This feature, combined with the very high reliability of the UAT, provides the plant electric self-feeding system with extremely high availability (over 99.9%) since a total interruption of service only happens when there is a whole plant and HV system blackout. The MVS assemblies serve the large loads of the GTs and ST (including the boiler feed pumps, condensate pumps, and others) directly at 6.9 kV, while also servicing secondary unit substations that feed the low-voltage loads.

## 3.4.5.1. Secondary Substations, Motor Control Centers, and Emergency Generator

The 6.9-kV switchgear buses feed two secondary unit substations provided with 6.3 kV–480 V transformers to supply power to the low-voltage equipment of the combined-cycle block. The secondary substations will also serve 480-V motor control centers and low-voltage distribution centers.

An emergency diesel generator is included to service emergency and essential loads of the plant in the event of total loss of alternating-current (AC) power.

## 3.4.6. Gas Insulated Substation (GIS)

The generating units are electrically tied to a 230-kV Gas Insulated Substation (GIS) at the plant. This equipment is arranged in a breaker-and-a-half configuration, with three incoming connections (one for each generator) and three outgoing connections to the grid. Breaker-and-a-half arrangements are frequently used for power generation projects, providing redundant pathways for power delivery. Sargent &amp; Lundy performed a review of the electrical design information available and did not find any fatal flaws.

## 3.5. CIVIL/STRUCTURAL

Sargent &amp; Lundy performed a site visit on May 12–15, 2025 to visually assess the condition of the site. As part of this visit a high-level visual inspection of the foundation concrete condition was performed to determine if any major issues existed. This section discusses the conditions from the site visit as well as the data provided in the testing performed on the soil backfill, concrete strength, and settlement survey. The CTG, HRSG, STG, and Cooling Tower Basin are each discussed. Additional miscellaneous observations and conditions are also discussed at the end of this section.

## 3.5.1. CTG Foundation Condition

Sargent and Lundy's visual inspection of the Gas Turbine Generator foundations did not find any abnormalities or apparent issues. The surface of the concrete appears to be in a like-new condition as no deterioration, major chipping, spalling, or cracking were readily apparent at the time of inspection. Figure 3-40 display the conditions that were present at the time of the visit. The soil backfill compaction testing results for zone 2-2 (area containing the CTG's) [18–21] show that the moisture content was 19.8% with compaction ranging from 91.9% to 100.2%. The data from the settlement survey [11] displays that over the time period from September 28, 2023, to March 7, 2024, a total settlement of 1 mm and 3 mm has been observed for each CTG foundation. S&amp;L does not consider this a risk as minor settlement should be expected in the short-term. The concrete strength tests for the CTG foundations [12 &amp; 13] states that the displayed results show the concrete meeting or exceeding the required concrete strength for all the 28-day breaks.

# 4. OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE

## 4.1. OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE ARRANGEMENTS

### 4.1.1. O&amp;M Overview

The Project will be operated and maintained by Generadora de Gatún S.A. ("Owner") staff managed by AES Latin America, S. de R.L., ("O&amp;M Manager") as per the Operation and Maintenance Management Service Agreement signed on November 16, 2021 ("Effective Date") discussed in this subsection. For major power island equipment such as the gas turbines, HRSG, and steam turbine inspections and maintenance, the Owner has entered into a maintenance agreement, often referred to as a Long-Term Service Agreement (LTSA) with GE for a period of 25 years or 128,000 FFH, which is typical practice. The AES O&amp;M agreement is discussed in subsection 6.1.4.2 and the LTSA is discussed in subsection 6.1.4.3 of this report.

The combined Owner and AES scope includes site management; operations; predictive and corrective maintenance; managing fuel, water, and waste; maintenance of permits, licenses, and approvals; maintenance of O&amp;M manuals; and management of personnel and subcontractors.

Some of the highlights of the O&amp;M Management Staff's scope of work are to:

- Manage the O&amp;M staff to ensure the plant operates within the constraints and goals of the project agreements, such as the PPAs and gas supply agreements.
- Submit monthly operational summaries to the Owner.
- Control the O&amp;M budget.
- Submit a proposed O&amp;M plan and budget to the Owner for the upcoming year. The budget is to contain sufficient detail in each quarter of the year for the Owner's review.
- Recommend to the Owner specialty contractors to be hired by the Owner, as required.
- Monitor the performance of the Owner's maintenance and repair contractors.
- Develop and implement the site's safety and environmental compliance programs and monitor their adherence and effectiveness.
- Recommend plant modifications to the Owner.
- Conduct ongoing staff training.
- Submit to the Owner recommended 3-year capital project plans.
- Manage the dispatch of power and the procurement of gas.

The organizational chart provided by AES for O&amp;M responsibilities is shown in Figure 4-1. While the LTSA personnel are not depicted in the organizational chart, their contract will be managed by the O&amp;M Management Staff. It is important to note that the LTSA contract will be established between GE and the Owner.

## 4.2. MAJOR MAINTENANCE INTERVALS

According to Exhibit C of GE's LTSA [32] scheduled major maintenance for the gas turbines is to be performed every 32,000 factored fired hours (FFH). Based on the capacity factors outlined in Table 4-1 of the LTSA, scheduled maintenance is expected to occur approximately during the program years indicated. Sargent &amp; Lundy opines that this maintenance interval is standard for ensuring optimal performance and reliability of the gas turbines.

Given that the gas turbines are relatively new, no significant maintenance activities are anticipated in the immediate future. The current operational status and performance metrics indicate that the gas turbines are functioning optimally, and routine inspections are expected to suffice for the time being.

As the turbines continue to accumulate operating hours, the O&amp;M team will closely monitor their condition through regular performance assessments and predictive maintenance techniques. This proactive approach will allow for the early identification of any potential issues, ensuring that any necessary maintenance can be scheduled in a timely manner.

## 4.3. GAS TURBINE GENERATOR GTG1 ROTOR INCIDENT, CORRECTIVE ACTION, ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS, AND RETURN TO SERVICE

On January 28, 2026, S&amp;L conducted an independent review of the unit #1 gas turbine generator (GTG1) rotor incident, repair, and return to service and assessed recurrence risk for the affected unit #1 and sister unit #2 gas turbine generator (GTG2) and steam turbine generator (STG). Based on a detailed review of event chronology, diagnostic testing, and the fast-track rotor rewind and reinstallation performed under the EPC equipment warranty program with POSCO's and General Electric the original equipment manufacturer (OEM), S&amp;L finds that GTG1 has been restored to a reliable operational state, with full field rewind, slot-end blending, and enhanced monitoring in place, and that current operating data since its return to service support a low residual risk of recurrence.

## 4.3.1. The GTG1 Rotor Incident and Corrective Action Taken

S&amp;L reviewed and discussed with plant personnel a summary of the sequence of events starting on July 21, 2025, with an alarm during turning gear in a normal shutdown in GTG1 leading to the rotor issue. POSCO the EPC contractor mobilized a generator specialist who was at the plant conducting several diagnostic tests on August 5, 2025, and issued a report concluding that based on the different tests performed, it is likely that the rotor winding or circuit has a failure to ground point that must be analyzed once the rotor is removed for repairs. As a result, the General Electric (GE) engineering department ordered that the rotor be removed and sent to a GE Vernova (GEV) workshop at the Schenectady Service Center

in New York for detailed evaluation and rewinding. This decision triggered a fast-track logistics effort to remove and transport the rotor by land and sea from the Gatún power plant in Panama to GEV in Schenectady, NY.

Once the rotor arrived at the GEV shop, inspections and electrical testing confirmed the field ground condition. During disassembly, debris, copper oxide powder, foreign metallic fragments, slot armor wear, and a crushed amortisseur segment were documented and preserved for analysis. Foreign material was removed, and the insulation sheet was replaced with new material. Retaining ring insulation reassemblies were inspected &amp; validated as per standard process. New amortisseur segments were installed and adjusted. Foreign metallic debris found during the disassembly, removal and inspection were totally removed and cleaned during the rotor rewind. In addition, comprehensive electrical testing was performed throughout. Based on the findings in GE Vernova Service facility, a joint agreement between GE Vernova and the customer confirmed to proceed with a full rewind of the field of GTG1 at the GEV OEM shops using the existing copper. This provided the opportunity to include the enhanced feature of blending the field slot exits as a proactive measure. All required mechanical, electrical, overspeed balance and thermal tests were complete and passed.

The full field rotor rewind took 55 days to complete and on December 15, 2025, the rotor left the port in New York and arrived at Colón, Panama, 15 days later. On January 11, 2026, the rotor reassembly was completed, and at 14:31 hrs., GTG1 was synchronized. On January 13, 2026, at 14:17 hrs., it was declared available for dispatch by the Centro Nacional de Despacho (CND).

## 4.3.2. Corrective Action Taken on GTG2 and STG

Following confirmation of a Field ground condition on GTG1, immediate containment measures were implemented to protect the remaining two units at the Gatún site (GTG2 and STG). GTG1 was kept out of service and preserved in accordance with GE Vernova protocol GEK103616 to prevent degradation and contamination. GTG1 was electrically and mechanically isolated, including the disconnection of the Radial Studs, and the preparations for Field removal. This ensured the elimination of any risk of cross-contamination. Containment measures (as directed by GEV) listed below were implemented to monitor GTG2 and STG units while in operation:

- M&amp;D Watch Alert: Continuous 24/7 monitoring of the EX2K_FLD_OHMS signal.
- Fleet Guidance: Bi-weekly field current measurements.

S&amp;L confirmed with Gatún operations that monitoring and diagnostic (M&amp;D) alert on GTG2 and STG continue, and bi-weekly Field current measurement is ongoing per plan. S&amp;L agrees with this approach as outlined by GE and it is of the opinion that a similar in-depth physical inspection like the one for GTG1 would require disassembly of both units (GTG2 and STG) to extract the rotor and removal of the retaining

## 4.3.3. Incident Root Cause Analysis

GE conducted a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) through an internal structured process to understand potential contributors to the field ground condition. On Feb 6, 2026, GE issued an RCA report based on data collection from the site and corrective actions now complete (Full Field Rewind with existing Copper). Based on findings from the GTG1 rotor rewind in Schenectady, it was concluded that the most likely root cause of the GTG1 field ground was copper slivers from original manufacturing coil-punching residues. Additional machining-related metal debris was considered a medium-probability contributor. Other factors —including copper dust/oxide deposits and site conditions such as high humidity or moisture—were assessed as low-probability contributors, as similar conditions exist across the broader fleet without comparable issues, indicating that the problem is likely manufacturing-specific rather than systemic (Table 4-2). As stated above, foreign metallic debris found during the disassembly, removal and inspection were totally removed and cleaned during the rotor rewind.

Table 4-2 — Most Probable Root Cause to Rotor Event in Gatún GTG1

## 4.3.5. Contractual and Operational Implications – Technical Input Only

Regarding contractual and operational obligations, S&amp;L confirmed that:

- The rotor repair is included in the Warranty Log under item # 173 Doc. No. GAT-W-250173 and covered under existing POSCO EPC / GE-OEM warranties.
- The GTG1 rotor incident and repair does not imply any material changes to the O&amp;M or LTSA obligations, maintenance intervals, or major maintenance planning from a technical standpoint, noting that recurring disassembly of a repaired rotor for inspection is generally not expected in normal practice.
- The GTG1 rotor incident, outage duration, and repair did not present any technical risk to meeting PPA availability obligations and associated penalties.
- There was no material issues regarding minimum take obligations nor send-out ranges under the LNG Supply Agreement (LNGSA) and Terminal Use Agreement (TUA) related to the GTG1 rotor incident and associated outage.

## 4.3.6. Conclusion

S&amp;L understands that, while the final root cause has not yet been conclusively determined, the two root causes with the highest probability (Leading and Mild-Probability) have been identified (Table 4-2) and corrective action implemented. The fact that GE continues to evaluate the remaining “Low Probability” root causes is merely to confirm that they can be discarded. Therefore, it is S&amp;L’s technical opinion that the residual risk of recurrence is low, as supported by the actual operating data shown above [4.3.4], since GTG1 was declared available by CND on January 13, 2026.

## 4.4.2.2. Unit 1 HRSG Inspection

During the GTG1 rotor repair, Generadora de Gatún conducted an inspection of the Unit 1 HRSG. The report documents October 16, 2025, inspection of the HRSG 1 and selected HRSG 1 &amp; 2 pipe supports, which identified multiple findings but no priority issues requiring immediate remedial work before restarting. Key condition concerns include deformation and cracking risk of the bypass stack silencers; debris and damage potential at expansion joints and crawl spaces; localized liner and flashing deterioration; oxidized and broken liner hardware; and various minor casing leaks, hotspots, and warped insulation blankets.

The pipe supports inspection highlighted misaligned or off-center sliding shoes on the HP feedwater and main steam lines and an attemperator drain pot located downstream of elbows with an overextended constant spring hanger, all of which increases the risk of uneven load sharing, overstress, and potential water hammer or support failure if left uncorrected. The main recommendations are to address findings in the near term (current outage if feasible) and plan a structured follow-up for findings with low priorities categorized as 3 and 4 for future inspections. Specifically, the report calls for annual debris removal and possible installation of a removable lower cover at the expansion joint, inspection and repair of deformed bypass stack silencers within the next 1–2 years, repair or replacement of failing sidewall flashing, loose batten bars, oxidized washers, broken studs, warped insulation cladding, casing hot spots, and verification of a potential HP steam stop valve leak using existing thermocouples.

For piping, the report recommends relocating the reheater attemperator drain pot upstream of the first elbow per ASME Section I, performing NDE on affected elbows, recentering, and, if necessary, adjusting misaligned sliding plate supports during a future outage, and continuing close monitoring of all such supports. In conversations with Gatún O&amp;M staff, they confirmed that high-priority HRSG repairs were carried in parallel with the GTG1 rotor repairs and STG outage (Figure 4-6).

# 5. ENVIRONMENTAL, HEALTH AND SAFETY, AND SOCIAL REVIEW

Sargent &amp; Lundy conducted a review of the environmental and social management systems associated with the Project. The main objective of this review was to verify that the Project has been operating in accordance with the requirements established by the Panamanian Ministry of the Environment (MiAmbiente), the Panamanian Ministry of Health, and relevant international standards.

# 5.1. ENVIRONMENTAL

In November 2017, Sargent &amp; Lundy prepared a report addressing the technical, environmental, and social aspects of the Project (Report SL-012550). However, the Project was put on hold before construction began. In late 2020, the Sponsor re-initiated the Project. To facilitate this restart, a revised Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) was completed in April 2021. The Sponsor submitted this EIA to MiAmbiente for review in May 2021. It encompasses various environmental, health, safety, and social programs developed and implemented by the EPC Contractor in collaboration with the Project Sponsor during the construction phase.

MiAmbiente concluded its review of the EIA and granted approval in late August 2021. Sargent &amp; Lundy has since monitored the Project's compliance with the approved EIA during the construction period. This review will concentrate on the operational aspects of the Project, as construction compliance has been addressed in prior construction monitoring reports.

Sargent &amp; Lundy was provided a Monitoring and Surveillance Plan for Environmental Physical Aspects at the 670 MW Combined-Cycle Thermal Power Plant Generadora de Gatún which outlines the environmental monitoring requirements of the Project during operation and maintenance of the Project. The monitoring plan outlines the background, objectives, and monitoring plans for Generadora de Gatún. The Ministry of Environment approved the Environmental Impact Study (EIA) and established an Environmental Management Plan (PMA) that includes a Monitoring and Environmental Follow-up Plan.

The general objective is to carry out environmental and labor monitoring through an accredited laboratory, while specific objectives focus on establishing a structured monitoring plan for the operational phase and identifying required parameters and frequencies in accordance with the PMA.

Table 5-1 provides an overview of the environmental monitoring program.

## 5.1.1. Air Emissions

During its operation, the Project will consistently produce air emissions. To adhere to emissions regulations, the facility will install emissions control equipment, specifically dry low-NOx burners to manage nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions. Additionally, the plant will implement best combustion practices to control carbon monoxide (CO) and particulate matter (PM) emissions. Air quality and emissions will be continuously monitored through Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) installed in the gas unit stacks. These systems provide real-time data on emission levels, and the verification process is overseen from the plant

As shown in Table 5-3, measured $\mathrm{PM}_{10}$ concentrations did not exceed the WHO/IFC 24-hour standard or MiAmbiente limits at any points; however, $\mathrm{SO}_2$ concentrations were above the Panamanian Ministry of Health and WHO/IFC 24-hour limits (as shown in red). During prior construction monitoring site visits, measured $\mathrm{SO}_2$ concentrations have exceeded the WHO/IFC 24-hour standard. The high 24-hour $\mathrm{SO}_2$ concentrations were assumed to be associated with vehicles, machinery, and shipping activity in the surrounding area outside of the NGCC Project Site, as the higher measurements are consistent with daytime work hours. High background $\mathrm{SO}_2$ concentrations were reported in the November 2021 due diligence report and are thus not believed to be associated with the NGCC Project, TL Project, or the Terminal Expansion as none of the projects had begun pre-construction activities [7].

## 5.1.3. Water Quality

The temperature of the water discharged from the plant is also monitored continuously to ensure it remains within the compliance range of $\pm 3^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($\Delta T$). This monitoring is conducted using temperature sensors positioned at both the water intake and discharge points, with oversight maintained at the plant control center. S&amp;L received operational-phase water quality data taken since the performance test held in May 2025 [47]. Daily trend data was provided from May 16 to July 15, 2025, and analyzed by S&amp;L. The analysis did not identify any instances of temperature measurements deviating from the compliance range of $\pm 3^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ ($\Delta T$). S&amp;L will continue to monitor this during the O&amp;M phase.

## 5.1.4. Noise Monitoring

According to the O&amp;M Monitoring and Surveillance Plan noise levels will regularly be recorded at sensitive receptor locations, particularly during specific operations that may produce noise, such as steam blowing activities and steam purity testing. These noise levels will then be assessed by an accredited laboratory at the frequency specified in the Plan and will be compared against local regulations and baseline measurements. During the recent validations related to steam blowing and purity testing, all recorded noise levels were within the limits set by local regulations (Executive Decree No. 1 of 2004 and Executive Decree No. 306 of 2002).

During the site visit, S&amp;L observed numerous positive safety practices in place at the Project, including good housekeeping standards, sufficient spill containment measures, readily accessible first aid kits, and clear signage indicating emergency procedures and muster points. S&amp;L did note some residual construction debris that needs to be cleaned up and mentioned it to the plant manager; however, no other concerns with safety or general housekeeping were noted. Based on these observations, S&amp;L opines that the Project is prioritizing a strong safety culture. Furthermore, the ongoing efforts to enhance safety practices indicate a commitment to improving conditions aimed at mitigating risks and preventing worker injuries.

## 5.3. SOCIAL

Generadora de Gatún has demonstrated a strong commitment to social responsibility and community engagement throughout construction, a trend that S&amp;L expects to continue in the operational phase of the Project. This commitment is evident through various initiatives aimed at fostering sustainable development in Colón and nearby regions. The company prioritizes the well-being of local communities by investing in education, health, and infrastructure projects. For instance, their recent initiatives have included partnerships with local schools to enhance educational resources and promote environmental awareness among students. According to their website, Generadora de Gatún actively encourages employee volunteerism, enabling staff members to engage in community service projects that align with the company's values and mission.

S&amp;L did not receive any recent social management plans or quarterly reports from Generadora de Gatún describing their social work and community engagement during the operational phase of the Project. However, S&amp;L did receive a presentation of the Corporate Affairs for 2025 [45]. The document highlights key social programs Generadora de Gatún plans to implement during the operational phase of the Project in 2025 while also continuing current programs. While it is not a formal plan, it provides important insights into initiatives that will enhance community engagement which include the following:

- Impact Measurement Pilot: This initiative evaluates the social impact of various projects, creating a methodology for effective measurement. It aims to provide verifiable data that can attract funding and improve social strategies based on real-time feedback.
- Women Entrepreneurs Program: This program empowers women in Colón by fostering partnerships and enhancing their skills. Its goals include improving financial management, increasing financial inclusion, and providing access to entrepreneurial capital, with support from stakeholders.
- Casa Esperanza: This program supports vulnerable children and adolescents in Colón through nutritional aid, emotional care, and services to enhance school retention. It targets 100 children to ensure they receive vital support.
- Rain Schools Initiative: This project aims to improve school infrastructure for rainwater collection and use, promoting sustainability and self-sufficiency. It collaborates with government entities and NGOs to strengthen community resilience and environmental responsibility.

These programs demonstrate Generadora Gatún's continuing commitment to social and community engagement. They not only meet immediate needs but also establish a foundation for long-term social impact, aligning with the goals of what would typically be included in an operational social management

Additionally, S&amp;L reviewed the Sixth Monitoring Report on the Environmental Management Plan for the Construction of the Project (Evaluation Period July – December 2024) [10]. The Monitoring Report evaluated the Project's compliance with environmental and social aspects of the Project. At the time the Monitoring Report was prepared, the Project had successfully reached the final commissioning phase, achieving 99.57% completion in its construction without any socioeconomic setbacks.

During the assessment period, various actions were taken to ensure environmental compliance. These included inspecting and maintaining equipment, providing safety and environmental training, and implementing the Dust Control and Waste Management Plan, among other initiatives. Furthermore, the Ministry of Environment approved a request to substitute environmental compensation, committing 457,300 Panamanian Balboa (PAB) to support environmental initiatives.

In terms of social management, relationships with local communities were noted to have been strengthened through educational programs, sports activities, volunteer efforts, and support for local institutions. Additionally, the proper disposal and management of waste have been secured by hiring specialized companies. S&amp;L was also provided with hazardous and nonhazardous waste reports supporting proper waste disposal practices.

The Monitoring Report also noted that stringent operational controls have been put in place for equipment and machinery to ensure optimal safety and functionality. With these developments, the project was noted to be well-prepared to transition to the operational phase, prioritizing sustainability, regulatory compliance, and social responsibility.

The following provides a summary of Sargent &amp; Lundy's assessment of the Project's compliance with these EHS guidelines.

- General EHS Guidelines: The General guidelines address environmental issues (air emissions, ambient air quality, energy use, wastewater and water quality, hazardous and solid waste, noise, and contaminated land); occupational health and safety; community health and safety; and construction and decommissioning.

Generadora de Gatún's EIA indicated that the Project site is located near enough to residents to require noise monitoring during construction and operation every six months. The first noise monitoring measurements occurred in April 2022 and were completed every six months throughout construction. As noted in Section 5.1.4, they are scheduled to occur every six months throughout operation.

In addition, waste materials are logged and removed from the site by either a disposal contractor or a hazardous waste company. Occupational safety procedures for hard-toe shoes, hard hats, gloves, welding goggles, etc., are set by Generadora de Gatún while accident and injury metrics are also tracked, as discussed in Section 5.2.

- EHS Guidelines for Thermal Power Plants: The EHS Guidelines for Thermal Power Plant Projects describe standards related to air emissions, energy efficiency and greenhouse gas emissions, water consumption and aquatic habitat alteration, effluents, solid wastes, hazardous materials and oil, and noise that are applicable to the construction and operations of the plants. The design of the facility was reviewed in Reports SL-012550 and SL-016751 [7, 8]. Sargent &amp; Lundy found that the NGCC and NG pipeline Projects meet the design requirements of the EHS Guidelines for Thermal Power Plants.

- EHS Guidelines for Electric Power Transmission and Distribution: The EHS Guidelines for Thermal Power Plant Projects describe standards related to terrestrial and aquatic habitat alteration, electric and magnetic fields, hazardous materials, live power lines, working at height on poles and structures, and exposure to chemicals that are applicable to the construction and operations of the transmission line. The design of the TL was reviewed in Report SL-016754 and Sargent &amp; Lundy found that the TL Project meets the design requirements of the EHS Guidelines for Electric Power Transmission and Distribution [7].
