There will be two dispatch scenarios that will dictate if the power plant is dispatched or not, based on variable cost vs. spot price as follows:

1. If the variable cost &lt; spot price: the power plant is fully dispatched and will deliver energy on a pro-rata basis of the country on an hourly basis (approximately 65% on average). The remaining portion will be sold on the spot market.
2. If the variable cost &gt; spot price: the plant power plant is not dispatched but will need to deliver energy on a pro-rata basis of the country. Energy will be bought from the spot market and will deliver it at the PPA.

An additional point regarding the need for spot-market purchases, the PPAs do not make provisions for planned and unplanned maintenance. If necessary, deficit capacity will be purchased through reserve capacity and deficit energy would be purchased in the spot market.

It is also worth mentioning that the PPA pricing includes a component that compensates for ETESA's transmission line charges which are in proportion to the installed MW and produced energy at the prices set by ASEP.

The PPAs include the typical terms and conditions found for the sale of power from a combined-cycle plant. The appropriate penalties are in place to ensure the plant will be paid for power delivered to the grids. The guaranteed available power for the plant is 400 MW from October 1, 2024, through July 31, 2028, and 550 MW from August 1, 2028, through September 30, 2044. The Project has been in partial commercial operation generating 400 MW in simple cycle with gas turbines GT-1 and GT-2 since October 1, 2024, to meet the three PPAs with offtakers. S&amp;L observed a net power plant output of about 638 MW on the screen in the control room during the combined-cycle performance test. Also, S&amp;L observed the real-time generation on June 16, 2025, at 6:28 PM when Gatún power plant was generating 603.89 MW (Figure 6-1).

## 6.1.2. Interconnection Agreement (IA)

An Interconnection Agreement (IA) is normally subscribed between a generating plant and the provider of the electrical transmission services that the plant needs, to establish technical requirements, limits of property of the producer's facilities and the grid, the shared facilities, O&amp;M procedures and responsibilities for costs of modifications to the transmission provider's existing grid if needed. IAs normally also establish the connection point(s), firm dates for connection and termination of services, transmission (tolling) rates, delay LDs if one of the parties is affected, and technical requirements for protection for the lines and telecommunications and for supervisory control of the connecting point substation. IAs also establishes the obligations about the national grid reliability and the responsibilities and coordination for operation and maintenance.

Sargent &amp; Lundy reviewed the original Interconnection Agreement (IA) dated September 6, 2017, for the Gatún Project, and the three executed amendments that followed. The purpose of the IA is to define the services that will be provided by the transmission company of Panama (ETESA) to the User Gatún power plant, referred to as "Central Telfers" in the agreement, and contains the typical definitions indicated above. Relevant conditions of the IA and Amendments follow:

- The agreement has a term of 15 years from the Project COD, unless it is terminated by mutual agreement or by petition of the plant, 6 months in advance, by which it renounces to its rights under

## 6.1.3. Fuel Supply Agreements

The fuel gas supply at the power plant interface is provided via three upstream agreements and the expanded Costa Norte LNG Terminal and newly installed pipeline to the Generadora de Gatún power plant.

- LNG Sale and Purchase Agreement (SPA)
- Terminal Use Agreement (TUA)
- Operations Coordination Agreement (OCA) with other offtakers [users] of fuel gas

The LNG SPA between TotalEnergies Gas &amp; Power Limited (TOTAL; Seller) and Generadora de Gatún S.A. (Buyer) is in executed draft form dated November 16, 2021. Under the SPA, an agreed-upon amount of LNG is delivered to the Costa Norte LNG Terminal (Operator).

The LNG Terminal Use Agreement (TUA) between Costa Norte LNG Terminal S. DE R.L. (Operator; Costa Norte) and Generadora de Gatún S.A. (Customer) is an executed draft version dated November 16, 2021. Under the TUA, an agreed-upon amount of LNG is delivered to and managed by Costa Norte, and an agreed-upon amount is re-gasified and delivered via the Operator's fuel gas pipeline to the Generadora de Gatún power plant.

The Operations Coordination Agreement (OCA) between Costa Norte LNG Terminal S. DE R.L. (Operator; Costa Norte) and GANA, Colón LNG Marketing [CLNG], and Generadora de Gatún S.A. (Foundation Customers) is an executed draft version dated November 16, 2021. The OCA adds Generadora de Gatún as a foundation customer to the existing OCA between the terminal operator, Costa Norte, and the existing foundation customers GANA and Colón LNG Marketing and explains the procedures for coordinating the LNG deliveries (received at the terminal) and redeliveries (sent out) for the customers. S&amp;L review of these agreements is summarized below.

### 6.1.3.2.3. LNG Price

The SPA has two pricing formulae for the delivered LNG, depending on the delivery month. They are based on the Henry Hub (HH) natural gas spot pricing for the LNG's scheduled delivery month. The price for each delivery in US$/MMBtu is determined by the formulae presented below. Pricing adjustments are allowed after Year 10 if they are justified by changes in law or if PPA changes cause reduced demand.

**January through April, and November through December**: Contract Price = 1.15 x HH + 2.25 + 0.9 x Consumer Price Index (CPI) adjustment for the applicable contract year.

## 6.1.3.2.4. Measurement and Testing

The quantity and quality of each LNG delivery is determined using standard procedures such as ISO 10976 and GPA 2261. TOTAL is obligated to provide calibration records to Generadora de Gatún. TOTAL and Generadora de Gatún together will select an independent overseer and equally share the cost of their services.

The level gauges on the LNGC tanks are used to determine the volume of LNG being transferred to the LNG terminal. Concurrent with the level readings are LNG pressure and temperature measurements. Procedures are followed to ensure the LNGC piping is in the same condition (full or empty) at both the beginning and the completion of the tank level measurements.

Samples of the LNG being transferred are analyzed to determine the quality of the LNG. The samples are taken from the transfer header, and the analysis is done using a calibrated gas chromatograph. With Costa Norte providing fuel gas to other users, and due to the large storage capacity of standard LNGCs, S&amp;L expects the LNGCs will often deliver additional LNG to Costa Norte. Generadora de Gatún will be charged for their agreed-upon portion. There will be additional metering for the fuel gas sent out to Generadora de Gatún, and this additional metering is addressed in the Terminal Use Agreement.

## 6.1.3.2.5. SPA Review Summary

Overall, the SPA is typical and acceptable compared to other LNG SPAs. The contracted fuel flow ranges in the SPA cover the amount of fuel calculated to be required for meeting the PPAs, using the capacity factors from the financial model. If Generadora de Gatún requires more fuel than the SPA's delivery range, the deficit can be made up by additional LNG purchases.

The TUA is in line with others S&amp;L has reviewed on similar projects. It covers the terminal's handling of the LNG and its regasification and send-out to Generadora de Gatún. ## 6.1.3.4. Operations Coordination Agreement (OCA)

The OCA explains the procedures for coordinating the LNG deliveries (received at the terminal) and redeliveries (sent out) for the customers. The agreement is a revision to the existing OCA between Costa Norte, GANA and CLNG, adding Generadora de Gatún as a Foundation Customer.

## 6.1.3.4.1. LNG and Fuel Gas Delivery Coordination

Every year Costa Norte and each of the customers, following the procedures and limitations in their TUAs, determine the quantity of LNG to be received, stored, managed, and re-delivered by Costa Norte. Consensus is also reached between Costa Norte and each customer on their individual Annual Delivery and Annual Redelivery programs (schedules).

A common annual meeting is held with the relevant parties to determine the Composite Annual Delivery and Redelivery Programs. The foundation customers receive priority in case of conflicts. Conflicts in the annual composite programs among the foundation customers are resolved with Costa Norte giving precedence to the one with the higher annual reception quantity. In addition to the annual schedules, Costa Norte issues a composite 90-day lookahead delivery and redelivery schedule each month. The current 90-

## 6.1.3.4.2. OCA Term, Quality and Price

The term of the OCA is not stated as a number of years, as in the TUA. The term of the OCA mirrors the term of each customer's TUA, as long as there are multiple customers to coordinate. Each customer's part in the OCA terminates when their TUA terminates.

## 6.1.3.4.3. OCA Review Summary

The draft OCA adds Generadora de Gatún as a foundation customer to the existing OCA between the terminal operator, Costa Norte, and the existing foundation customers GANA and Colón LNG Marketing. The OCA has procedures to coordinate the LNG deliveries (received at the terminal) and redeliveries (gas/LNG send-out) for the customers. A joint annual meeting with Costa Norte and the customers is held to develop composite annual delivery and redelivery schedules. Preference is given to the foundation customers in cases of conflicting requests, and if necessary, Costa Norte gives priority to the foundation customer with the greater annual reception quantity. Costa Norte also issues monthly 90-day lookahead schedules for deliveries and redeliveries, which take precedence over the previous schedules, including the annual composite schedules. At the time of this report the 90-day lookahead was not available for review.

The Operations Coordination Agreement is well-defined in its purpose, procedures and handling of requests and conflicts. No issues have been identified in the draft agreement.

### 6.1.4.1. O&amp;M Overview

(O&amp;M Manager), executed on November 16, 2021 [ref 33]. For major power island inspections and maintenance (two gas turbines/generators and the steam turbine/generator), the Owner has entered into a maintenance agreement, often referred to as a Long-Term Service Agreement (LTSA), with GE which is typical practice. ## 6.1.4.4. Liquidated Damages and Bonuses

The contracts specify LDs for failure to meet equivalent reliability factor, inspection duration, capacity, and heat rate. Degradation is unavoidable in a power plant; however, a portion of the performance is recovered through the work done in the outages. With a plant designed to produce 640 (net) MW on natural gas alone, it is extremely unlikely for the plant to degrade to a point where it cannot deliver the 550 (net) MW needed to meet the PPAs after Year 4. Additionally, the plant is less likely to not be able to deliver 400 (net) MW, prior to Year 4.

Table 6-5 summarizes the LTSA LDs and bonus structure. The stated LDs are in line with similar contracts reviewed by Sargent &amp; Lundy. Similarly, if the achieved duration of inspection and/or heat rate degradation for the corresponding year is better than the relevant guaranteed values, the Owner shall pay to the O&amp;M Contractor a bonus in an amount equal to the rate payable in respect of the LDs set forth in the contracts. The LDs and bonuses have identical annual caps.

Table 6-5 — LTSA LDs and Bonuses

| --- | --- | --- |
|  Equivalent Reliability Factor for the combined-cycle island | $100,000 1 per % point | $300,000 1  |
|  Outage Duration Guarantee for Scheduled Inspection | $700 per hour; cap of $300,000 per scheduled inspection | $300,000 for all covered units  |
|  CTG Heat Rate % change (average of both CTGs) | $100,000 LD per 1.0%; cap of $300,000 $300,000 bonus per 1.0%; cap of $300,000 | None  |
|  CTG Output % change (average of both CTGs) | $66,000 per 1.0%; cap of $300,000 | None  |
|  STG Output % change | $100,000 per % point; cap of $150,000 | $300,000 for combined CTG and STG output per outage set  |

1 The reliability LDs and cap will increase if there are consecutive LD years to a maximum of $350,000 per % and a cap of $1,000,000.

The LTSA contains a maximum aggregate LD amount over the term on the contract: $6,000,000 for all the covered units combined.

The LD and bonus terms in the contracts offer sufficient incentive for the O&amp;M Contractor to perform O&amp;M works on time and to keep performance errors to a minimum. Compared to similar projects, the LDs and

## 6.1.5. Generation Permits

The timeline of permits granted by the National Authorities for Public Services of Panama to Generadora de Gatún, S.A. (GdG, the Gatún plant owner) to allow construction and operation of the power plant is as follows:

- The Provisional Permit for construction was issued on November 18, 2020, as Resolution AN No. 19625-Elec. That permit listed all the documentation that that GdG had to present in order to obtain the Definitive Permit. The Gatún power plant is 100% complete except for Punch List items and declared Mechanical Completion in February 2025.
- The Definitive Permit for construction and operation was issued on September 29, 2021, as Resolution AN No. 17156-Elec. This permit established an original Commercial Operation Date (COD) of September 30, 2024. The permit includes conditions such as bonds, insurance, schedule, etc. that are typically required in this type of contract. This permit has a 40-year term and can be extended for an additional 40 years after the proper application to the National Authorities for Public Services. It also describes all obligations that GdG must comply with regarding taxes, payments, reports, performance bond, etc., as well as the penalties due to non-compliances of those terms.
- A modification to the Definitive Resolution was issued on March 25, 2025, as Resolution No. AN No, 20082-Elec to recognize the fact that the Gatún plant was generating power as of that date but still had some pending items before being declared ready for Commercial Operation. The modification allows testing of the plant to start on January 15, 2025, finalizing on March 30, 2025, and COD on April 15, 2025. The actual performance test start date was May 17, 2025, with Substantial Completion declared on May 22, 2025 [43]. Other provisions of the previously issued Definitive Resolution are maintained.

# 7. FINANCIAL MODEL

## 7.1. PRO FORMA ASSUMPTIONS AND FINANCIAL MODEL REVIEW

S&amp;L performed a review of the underlying technical assumptions and inputs within the Project's financial model, dated December 2025, prepared for the Gatún Liquified Natural Gas Project. The intent of the review was to evaluate the reasonableness of the technical input assumptions and to determine if the financial performance forecast for the facility is achievable. Part of this review was to confirm that the financial model is consistent with the plant performance requirements of the Project agreements and the expected capability of the plant.

Overall, S&amp;L finds the financial model to adequately account for the expected technical and operational inputs for a natural-gas-fired combined-cycle project and can perform the revenue and debt calculations accurately.

## 7.2. PROJECT OPERATING PERFORMANCE ASSUMPTION

Table 7-1 outlines the key Project details in the financial model. The Project is modeled with the three power purchase agreement (PPA) off takers, (EDEMET [37], EDECHI [38], and ENSA [39]) for a total of 400 MW of the capacity for Phase I (Oct 2024 – Aug 2028). Phase II capacity contracts 550 MW over (Aug 2028 - Sept 2044) time. These key dates align with the applicable Project agreements, and inputs are consistent within the financial model details.

## 7.2.1. Heat Rate and Availability

The maximum generating capacity in the financial model is assumed to be 640 MW. Plant heat rate average between 2025 and 2044 is modeled at 6,401 kJ/kWh (6,067 Btu/kWh) over the PPA terms with an average availability factor of 93.91%. The heat rate values are conservative when compared to the GE Heat Balances value of 6,254.6 kJ/kWh, guaranteed values of 6,284.6 kJ/kWh listed in the EPC Appendix A Table 7-2 [36]. S&amp;L finds these values to be comparable to other units of comparable size and technology.

The financial model “Build Up” tab contains a CAPEX summary and budgeted line items. This is broken down in Figure 7-3. This includes a total capital expenditure (CAPEX) for the Project of $130,370,000. This does not include any original plant construction costs, only the projected capital from 2025–2050. ## 7.3.3. Project Revenues

The forecasted Project revenues come primarily from the sale of PPA energy and available PPA capacity while excess capacity and energy is sold on the spot market. The financial model considers both capacity and energy revenues attributable to sales under the PPAs from Phase I (October 2024–August 2028) and Phase II from (August 2028–September 2044). Following completion of the PPA term, energy is forecasted to be sold in the wholesale market. The PPAs include a variable energy component and a capacity component. Variable revenues are directly linked to energy sales and capacity revenues are fixed based on the number of megawatts available to the three off takers (see Table 7-1). Figure 7-3 shows the projected annual revenue streams over the life of the Project totaling $11.04 billion.

The majority of the revenues come from the PPA energy sales at 48.30% as shown in Figure 7-4. Energy revenue is variable and based on the forecasted plant generation projections. During the entire 20-year term, the base price of proposed power supply and energy is $18.89 USD/kW-month and $0.088 USD/kWh, respectively, and adjusted using the formulas of the PPA's referenced above. The base pricing and indexing formula adjustments are accounted for in the financial model. S&amp;L finds the revenue projection and provisions of the PPA appear to be adequately formulated within the financial model, and all assumptions used for forecasting variable energy revenue are reasonable for the Project.

## 7.3.4. Debt Service Coverage Ratio and Cash Flow for Debt Service

S&amp;L reviewed the Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) and Cash Flow Available for Debt Service (CFADS) in Table 7-6. The average DSCR of 1.68 is above the critical threshold of 1.0, meaning the Project projects to consistently generate enough cash flow to cover its debt service over the analyzed periods. S&amp;L finds that the Project projections appear to be in good financial health, with a strong cash flow generation relative to debt service obligations and a manageable level of leverage.

## 7.3.5. Generadora Gatún Outputs

Appendix A shows total annual revenues for full years in the range of approximately $380 million to $660 million, primarily from PPA energy and PPA capacity, with additional contributions from spot energy and other revenues. The revenue base remains highly contracted, with contracted revenues generally in the mid-60% to low-80% range over the forecast, and remaining above 60% in all periods, which provides good visibility and stability of cash inflows. After variable and fixed costs, the project generates a robust EBITDA profile consistent with a healthy operating margin. Following deductions for taxes, working capital movements, and maintenance capex, CFADS is positive in every forecast period, ranging from approximately $130 million to just over $200 million for full years, starting in the mid-$100 million range and generally increasing into the low-$200 million range through the mid-forecast years before moderating somewhat as revenues flatten and certain costs and taxes rise; CFADS remains positive in the final, shorter April-September period as well. Appendix A also summarizes the evolution of the bond balance and scheduled principal amortization over the forecast period.

## 7.4. FINANCIAL CONCLUSIONS

Overall, the financial model provided for review is reasonable and appropriate. The major technical and operational assumptions are consistent with the terms in the contractual documents reviewed by S&amp;L.

- S&amp;L finds the projected heat rate based and availability factor values to be comparable to other units of comparable size and technology.
- S&amp;L finds the capital costs for the maintenance and the LTSA to be adequately accounted for in the financial model with a total of $130.37 million not including CapEx to build the plant.
- S&amp;L finds the projected technical O&amp;M costs are increasing, with an average annual inflation rate of 0.90% from 2025 through 2044, with average technical O&amp;M costs of $25.34/kW-yr.
- S&amp;L finds that the revenue projection and provisions of the PPA appear to be adequately formulated within the financial model, and all assumptions used for forecasting variable energy revenue are reasonable for the Project.
- S&amp;L's review of DSCR finds that the Project projections appear to be in good financial health with a strong cash flow generation relative to debt service obligations and a manageable level of leverage.
- The financial profile Gatun appears sound and resilient. The combination of a largely contracted revenue base, solid EBITDA margins, and consistently positive and growing CFADS supports a strong debt service capacity, with LTM DSCR averaging roughly 1.68x and individual yearly DSCRs generally above 1.4–1.5x. This level of coverage provides a comfortable cushion for lenders and suggests the project can withstand moderate adverse movements in costs, dispatch, or market conditions while continuing to meet its debt obligations.

# 8. COUNTERPARTIES REVIEW

## 8.1. COUNTERPARTIES ASSESSMENT

Sargent &amp; Lundy conducted a review of the experience of Generadora Gatún S.A.'s counterparties in meeting their contractual obligations, which include sponsors, suppliers, and operators, as well as their credit ratings. As highlighted in Table 8-1, these counterparties are reputable companies with extensive experience in the energy sector and solid credit ratings.

However, a recent downgrade was noted for ETESA, the electricity transmission company of Panama, which now holds a Long-Term Foreign- and Local-Currency Issuer Default Rating (IDR) of 'B', down from 'BB+', according to Fitch Ratings. This downgrade is related to a delayed coupon payment. Additionally, both the National Long-Term Rating and the national long-term senior unsecured rating have been lowered to 'BB (pan)' from 'AAA (pan)'. This rating action was announced on December 3, 2024.

It is important to note that ETESA is fully owned by the Government of Panama and has a legal monopoly on electricity transmission services within the country. Given these factors, Sargent &amp; Lundy does not view this downgrade as a significant risk to the Project.

(ETESA) is a Panamanian corporation with 100% state capital, responsible for the transmission of high-voltage electrical energy. Its primary function is to transport electricity from generators to distribution companies and large customers. Additionally, ETESA is tasked with system planning, preparing expansion plans for generation and transmission within the National Interconnected Electric System (SENI). The company operates SENI from the National Dispatch Center, ensuring a reliable flow of energy. ETESA also participates as a shareholder in several other companies within the electricity sector, including Interconexión Colombia – Panamá (ICP), Empresa Propietaria de la Red (EPR), and Red Centroamericana de Fibra Óptica (REDCA). As of December 3, 2024, ETESA holds a Long-Term Foreign- and Local-Currency Issuer Default Rating (IDR) of 'B', which was downgraded from 'BB+' by Fitch Ratings. This downgrade is attributed to a delayed coupon payment. The National Long-Term Rating and national long-term senior unsecured rating have also been lowered to 'BB (pan)' from 'AAA(pan)'. Previously, in October 2024, Fitch Ratings had affirmed ETESA's Long-Term Foreign and Local-Currency IDRs at 'BB+' with a Stable Outlook, reflecting the company's strong ties to the Panamanian sovereign rating. However, Fitch subsequently lowered ETESA's Standalone Credit Profile to 'bb' from 'bb+' due to increased leverage and a weakened financial structure. Additionally, Moody's Investors Service revised the outlook on ETESA's "Baa3" (Long-Term foreign currency) credit rating to negative.  |

# EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Generadora Gatún (or the Client), located on Isla Telfers in Colón, Panama, is the largest natural gas-fired power plant in Central America and the Caribbean, with an installed capacity of 670 megawatts (MW). Developed by Grupo Energético Gas Panamá—a partnership between InterEnergy Group (51%) and AES Panamá (49%)—the project required a $1.2 billion investment and was constructed over 36 months. The plant commenced commercial operations on October 1, 2024, initially supplying 440 MW to Panama's electrical grid through two natural gas turbines. A third steam turbine, adding 230 MW, is expected to become operational upon completion of the necessary transmission infrastructure, bringing the total capacity to 670 MW.

During its construction phase, Generadora Gatún employed over 2,100 workers, predominantly from the local Colón community. The company has invested more than $1 million in community and social development projects, benefiting over 42,000 local residents. The plant enhances Panama's energy matrix by providing a cleaner and more reliable power source, which is anticipated to reduce electricity costs for consumers and position the country as a regional energy hub.

This Preliminary Report contains the Power Sector Overview and Regulatory Framework of Panama. This document is organized in three sections that allows the reader to understand the business context of the country's energy sector and to identify opportunities with focus on renewable generation, as desired by the client. This report is based on information available in the public domain.

The first section introduces the reader to the recent evolution of the regional context where the country under analysis is located, including a description of the regional electricity market and its main statistics and agents.

- Current status (2024¹): The Central American region is characterized by peak demands in a range of between 840 MW in Nicaragua to 2122 MW in Guatemala, with El Salvador as a middle size country with a peak demand of 1194 MW. The installed capacity in the countries of the Regional Market (MER) lies between 1600 and 4500 MW. Overall, the electricity generation is predominantly renewable (hydroelectricity and NCRE), but with significant differences among countries: the thermal generation ranges from almost 5% in Costa Rica to 45% in Nicaragua and Honduras.
- In recent years the MER has been one of the regional integration axes, allowing for energy exchanges among interconnected countries in Central America. According to the EOR, the MER has 318 (May 2025) agents registered, Guatemala with 113, Panama with 73, El Salvador with 84, Nicaragua with 44 and Costa Rica and Honduras with only two local agents each². In 2024, the energy purchases positioned Nicaragua first, El Salvador second and Costa Rica third.

# CENTRAL AMERICA GENERAL CONTEXT

## 1. GENERAL CONTEXT

During the early 90s, the power sectors in Central American countries (Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama)³ were basically managed by vertically integrated state-owned utilities that concentrated the production and supply of electric power.


Figure 1: Map of Central America

Like in most Latin-American countries, the main characteristics of the power industry before the sector's restructuring were electric power shortages, vertically integrated state-owned utilities, lack of fresh funds, poorly maintained power plants, and unavailability of public financing resources.

On top of that, consecutive dry years in the Central American between 1991 and 1994 seriously damaged the highly hydro-dependent systems, like Guatemala and Honduras, increasing supply shortages.

In response to this situation, most of the countries underwent a reform of the electricity sector to boost the needed investment in generation and meet the expected demand growth.

Electricity market reform and development have progressed at varying speeds in the six countries. As a result, the region is characterized by a range of market structures and

³ Belize is not considered in the analysis because it is not interconnected with the rest of the countries.

Panamá: Market advisor services for Generadora Gatún

gme

uneven market development.

Broadly speaking, the stage of reform in the region can be divided into two groups:

- Panama, Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua have reformed their generation, transmission and distribution sectors and have competitive generation markets in place. In the same way, Honduras is currently on a reform process to liberalize its electricity market.
- Costa Rica retains a vertically integrated utility, and competition is limited to contracts for generation with the single buyer.

As a member of the more active reform group, Panama has had the most success in terms of attracting private investment (nearly all existing generation was privatized in 2000) and improving operational efficiency. El Salvador implemented a highly deregulated structure which has encountered some difficulties in the context of a small sector and has recently migrated from a bid-based wholesale market towards a cost-based market. Nicaragua has also had some difficulties and private operators have been unable to reduce the high level of electricity losses.

Panama, Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua all have active private sector participation in generation and distribution activities. The ability of these countries to attract and retain private investors is an indicator of their success in creating credible investor protections.

Honduras approved its new General Law of the Electricity Industry (Act. 404-2014). This law provides a legal framework for a new liberalized electricity sector. At present, Honduras is still in a market reform process.

Costa Rica continues operating as a centrally planned system, with the private sector participating in relatively small-sized renewable-based generation, mainly through power purchase agreements (PPAs).

Compared to the situation prior to the reform, most of the countries have improved their energy sectors, succeeding in attracting private investment, increasing efficiency and improving the system's reliability and quality of service.

However, many countries lack the institutional development and human resources necessary to conduct the regulatory oversight that the adopted models require. The condition of open access to the transmission system is crucial for the expansion of generating capacity and the public sector has an active role in the expansion of the transmission grids.

Although the generation segment was, to some extent, open to competition in all these countries, the achievement of strong competition in relatively small markets is still challenging. The trend towards contracting a significant share of the load is a way to minimize excessive market power and to lower price volatility while providing incentives for new investments. # 2. REGIONAL ELECTRICITY MARKET

The original design of the Regional Electricity Market (REM or "MER" in Spanish) consists in a seventh market that coexists with the six existing domestic markets or systems, with independent rules and in contact with them only at the points in the Regional Transmission Grid (RTR) defined as borders between the domestic markets and the regional market. It is operative since July 2013.

Generators and demands located in any of the member countries can freely decide to carry out their energy purchase and sale transactions in the MER or in their own domestic markets. This is how a generator located in any of these countries can sell its production to a demand located in another country.

The so-called SIEPAC project was built so that energy could flow between the countries involved in the transactions at the MER. It consists in a 230 kV circuit with a transmission capacity of 300 MW running through the six member countries.

In practice, the MER operation rules (RMER) has migrated to the setup of a single market with a mandatory 3-steps daily dispatch for the system operators in each country:

1. Isolated pre-dispatch of each domestic system (disregarding regional

Panamá: Market advisor services for Generadora Gatún

gme

interconnections).

2. Regional pre-dispatch: generators that do not participate in the domestic dispatch provide generation supply (injections) in the spot market (MOR) of the MER. The potential demand (withdrawals) in the MOR comprises those generators that were dispatched in step 1 and whose variable cost is higher than generation supply (injections) in the MOR.
3. Final domestic pre-dispatch: the operator of each domestic system adjusts the dispatch carried out in step 1 according to the results of the regional dispatch in step 2: it substitutes local generation (imports) or increases local generation (exports) to comply with the exchanges calculated in step 2 at each border node.

These operation rules (RMER) are currently in force, but certain restrictions apply. Their implementation has proved to be difficult for technical reasons and for other reasons related to security of operation and to the allocation of responsibilities between the operators in each country and the Regional Operator (EOR).

As mentioned, the regulation of the MER allows for opportunity transactions based on price bids as well as the possibility to sign long-term contracts between generation and demand of the different member countries. Restricted, however, in the reality due to the lack of design of long-term firm transmission rights.

Transactions between a MER agent and third countries (non-member countries) are also allowed in the MER if such countries' networks are linked to the regional one, either directly or through the national network of a member country. Mexico is an example of this; Colombia could also be an example if the interconnection project with Panama finally develops.


Figure 3: MER Institutions

The MER is organized into a Regional Contract Market and a Regional Spot Market. The transactions that can be carried out are the following:

- Firm Energy Contracts
- Non-Firm Energy Contracts
- Opportunity Transactions

Panamá: Market advisor services for Generadora Gatún

gme

Firm Energy Contracts imply an obligation⁵ to be performed, meaning the amounts of contracted energy must be injected into and withdrawn from the regional transmission network (RTR) at the nodes indicated by the parties of the contract. Therefore, the amounts contracted under Firm Energy Contracts are not subject to the regional economic dispatch but are dispatched ex-ante.

Firm Energy Contracts may additionally include flexible bids expressed as the price of additional injection to the contracted amount, or withdrawal prices under which firm injection is reduced. Such flexible bids are considered Opportunity Transactions, as described below.

Non-Firm Energy Contracts differ from those above in that there are no Transmission Rights and therefore, the physical amounts contracted may be limited in case of constraints in the Regional Transmission Network.

Finally, opportunity transactions are bids to physically inject and withdraw energy into and from the RTR, made by licensed agents for each market period of the following day (the adopted market period is one hour).

## REGIONAL ELECTRICITY MARKET MAIN BARRIERS

The commissioning of the Regional Electricity Market (MER) evidenced the room for improvement mainly in regulatory aspects that are expected to be incorporated in the Third Protocol of the Framework Treaty of the Central American Electricity Market. The main barriers observed and that should be tackled are:

- Development and full implementation of regional regulation
- Understanding and outreach of regulation: many agents do not understand in depth the regulation of the MER and perceive it as difficult.
- Lack of definition of indicators and market monitoring: There is a need for additional regulatory and technical indicators. The lack of indicators difficult the monitoring and execution of improvements by the institutions and agents of the MER.
- Penalties: It is necessary to adjust the penalties for a strong, coordinated and harmonious development of the MER.
- Short-term transmission right: A harmonized market for fixed transmission rights for long-term power purchase agreements is required. Currently, the firm transmission rights have an annual duration.
- Promote the expansion of regional generation and transmission
- Lack of consolidated regional planning to optimize the use of regional resources.
- Deficient coordination in the expansion of national transmission networks with the maintenance of the regional expansion network.
- Promote the development of a harmonic regulation
- Supremacy of regional rules on MER rules: The rules and regulations published by the CRIE should take precedence over national rules and regulations.
- Expand and improve extra-regional interconnections.

# MARKET OVERVIEW

## 1. COUNTRY PROFILE

Panama, officially the Republic of Panama, is the third smallest country of Central America with an area of 75,420 km². To the north, Panama borders with the Caribbean Sea; on the west, with Costa Rica, on the south with the Pacific Ocean and finally on the east with Colombia. Its capital and largest city is Panama City.



The population is estimated at 4.5 million (2024 estimation⁶) with a density of 60 habitants/km². Most of the population live in the largest cities (68%). GDP per capita is around 17,732 €/cap in 2024, above the region average. It is divided into 10 provinces and 4 comarcas, and sub-divided into about 81 municipalities.

Panama was inhabited by several indigenous tribes prior to settlement by the Spanish in the 16th century. It broke away from Spain in 1821 and joined a union of Nueva Granada, Ecuador, and Venezuela named the Republic of Gran Colombia. When Gran Colombia dissolved in 1831, Panama and Nueva Granada remained joined, eventually becoming the Republic of Colombia. With the backing of the United States, Panama seceded from Colombia in 1903, allowing the Panama Canal to be built by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers between 1904 and 1914. In 1977, an agreement was signed for the total transfer of the Canal from the United States to Panama by the end of the 20th century, which culminated on December 31st, 1999.

Panama's dollar-based economy rests primarily on a well-developed service sector that accounts for more than two thirds of GDP. Services include operating the Panama Canal, logistics, banking, the Colon Free Zone, insurance, container ports, flagship registry, and tourism. Economic growth has been bolstered by the Panama Canal expansion project that began in 2007 and was completed in 2016 at a cost of USD 5.3 billion.

Panama's booming transportation and logistics services sectors, along with aggressive infrastructure development projects, resulting in high growth rates which tended to slow down in the last years (8% average growth from 2004 to 2014, 5% from 2014 to 2017 and around 3% in 2018-2019). Foreign investment, at around 9% of GDP in 2019, has continued to be a source of growth. Strong economic performance has not translated into broadly shared prosperity, as Panama has the third worst income distribution in Latin America. About 13% of the population lives below the poverty line of US$5,5 a day. The US-Panama Trade Promotion Agreement was approved by Congress and signed into law in October 2011 and entered into force in October 2012. Panama also achieved removal from the Organization of Economic Development's gray-list of tax havens by signing various double taxation treaties with other nations⁷.

Tourism in Panama has been growing rapidly. It has maintained its growth over the past years due to government tax and price discounts to foreign guests and retirees. These economic incentives have caused Panama to be regarded as a relatively good place to retire in the world attracting, for example, the interest of real estate developers.

The Panamanian currency is officially the balboa, fixed at a rate of 1:1 with the United States dollar since independence in 1903. However, in practice the country is dollarized: US dollars are legal tender and used for all paper currency, while Panama has its own coinage. Because of the tie to US dollars, Panama's inflation on consumer's prices is rather low (2.2% average since year 2000).

## 2. REGULATORY FRAMEWORK

The Panamanian electricity market is a deregulated mature market; operating as such since 1999 (the reform process and privatization of the electricity sector began in 1997, with Electricity Law No.6-97).

Although the generation segment is organized as a competitive market, there are five major players (together they concentrate over 60% of the total generating capacity): AES, Celsia (previous owner GdF Suez), Americas Generation Corp. (ENEL), Cobre Panama⁸ and InterEnergy Group.

In the last decade, the regulatory framework reinforced the long-term supply contracts, aiming to attract new investment in generating capacity: ETESA (the transmission company), on behalf of the distributors, carries out public tenders periodically to guarantee supply for the regulated market. Generators with firm capacity not yet committed under long-term contracts must bid in ETESA's public auctions.

- Autoridad Nacional de Servicios Públicos (ASEP, regulatory authority) autonomous and independent agency of the Panamanian government in charge of monitoring public services (electricity, water and sewerage, and communications). Its functions include (i) granting power generation and distribution concessions and generation licenses, (ii) establishing the methodologies and formulas for setting tariffs for distribution and transmission services, (iii) issuing regulations and rules applicable to the energy sector, such as the guidelines for the public tenders for contracting energy and capacity, and (iv) imposing sanctions and fines to violators of the energy law and its regulations. Also, it is the ultimate authority in dispute resolution/amendments of PPAs. (www.asep.gob.pa)



- ETESA (Empresa de Transmisión Eléctrica SA) is the state-owned transmission company in charge of the operation and maintenance of the high voltage transmission network. ETESA also elaborates an indicative (non-mandatory) expansion plan of the power system that must be approved by ASEP. Since the enactment of Law No. 57/09, ETESA has coordinated the public auctions to secure supply to regulated customers. (www.etesa.com.pa)
- The National Dispatch Center (CND) centrally coordinates the system's operations and administers commercial transactions between market agents. CND is part of ETESA. (www.cnd.com.pa)

MINISTERIO DE AMBIENTE

# 3. ENERGY POLICY

In 1997, the Government of Panama started a reform process of the power sector, including the privatization of its vertically integrated electricity utility (IRHE). The privatization of IRHE was part of a broader reform program that involved establishing a new regulatory framework, introducing a wholesale electricity market, and adopting a new tariff regulation. IRHE was restructured into four generation companies (Bayano, 192 MW; Bahia Las Minas, 292 MW; Fortuna, 300 MW; and Chiriqui, 222 MW); three distribution companies (EDEMET, ENSA, EDECHI); and one transmission company that would remain in state hands (ETESA).

Law No.6/97 sets the broad parameters underlying the privatization process and the new regulatory guidelines. The new electricity market in Panama began its operations as such in 1999. Generation, transmission, and distribution activities were unbundled. The generation segment was structured as a competitive market while transmission and distribution activities were considered public services and thus regulated.

Panama also participates in the Regional Electricity Market (MER) for Central America, with a trend towards energy exports.

# 3.3.1. Public auctions

Public auctions (does not apply to contracts between private parties): Law No. 57/2009 modified several articles of Electricity Law No. 6/97 to ensure competitive bids in public auctions, secure electric supply to regulated customers and attract new investment in generation. It is mandatory for generators to bid their firm capacity not yet committed in previous public auctions. Although generators cannot enter firm contracts for more than their firm capacity, they can have a combination of firm capacity contracts up to their firm

capacity, and only energy contracts for the period of the year when production is higher, to cover energy surpluses.

ETESA, the transmission company, acts as a single buyer and coordinates the public tenders on behalf of the distribution companies, following the criteria established by ASEP for such auctions. The off takers are the distributors, each one in each proportion that is established in the public tender.

The contract prices that result from public tenders are fully passed through to end user tariffs. Bilateral contracts agreed upon by private parties are passed through to end user tariffs at a price equal to the average price of contracts awarded through public auctions and distributor's energy purchases in the spot market. Such spot purchases must be approved by the regulator.

The seller can terminate the contract if the buyer goes bankrupt and/or fails to honor its monthly payments without a valid cause. In addition, the off taker must keep a guarantee of payment for the amount indicated in the contract, which is usually one month, during the term of the supply contract. This guarantee may be established in cash or in bonds of insurance companies, through bank guarantees or cash from the first month of supply, for annual periods and will remain in force after the end of the contract (usually for 60 days).

# 3.2. Renewable Energy and Climate Change Policy

According to the National Energy Plan 2015-2050, Panama aims to generate 70% of its energy needs using alternative renewable sources. Among the objectives is that the production of 15% to 30% of Panama's electricity derives from renewable and non-hydraulic energy, by 2030 and 2050, respectively.

Energy policy guidelines seek to promote renewable-based projects to reduce dependence on costly fossil fuels. Some laws or decrees have set up incentives for the development of renewable sources:

**Executive Decree No. 45 of June 10, 2009**: "Regime of Incentives for the Promotion of Hydroelectric Generation Systems and other New, Renewable and Clean Sources, contemplated in Law No. 45 of August 4, 2004."

This Decree defines different incentives per category of power plants (up to 500 kW, up to 10 MW, from 10 to 20 MW, more than 20 MW).

- Up to 500 kW and not connected to the distribution network: They do not pay import tax for equipment and spare parts required for the construction and operation of the plants.
- Up to 10 MW: They do not pay transmission or distribution fee. They do not pay import tax for equipment and spare parts required for the construction and operation of the plants. They are entitled to tax incentives. They can contract directly with any distribution company regardless of where the plant is located. They can sell energy in the occasional market. They can sell their firm power to the distributor, to another generator or distributor. They can offer their energy in the Central American market.
- 10 to 20 MW: They have the same benefits as renewable and clean energy plants of up to 10 MW with the following exceptions. They do not pay a transmission fee for the first 10 MW during the first 10 years of commercial operation. They cannot contract directly with the distributor; they have less tax incentives.
- More than 20 MW and up to any power: They have the same benefits as renewable and clean energy plants up to 20 MW but pay normal transmission rate.

In addition to this Decree, the adoption of laws for specific technologies was deemed convenient; they are described below.

**Law 18 of March 26, 2013**: "That modifies and adds articles to Law 44 of 2011¹², relating to wind power plants."

Description: It establishes a legal framework that encourages the development of wind generation activities. Some of the benefits are:

- Allows public tenders for the purchase of energy and/or capacity, exclusive for wind power plants, with contracts for up to fifteen years;
- Exemption from import tax, tariffs, fees, contributions and levies, as well as the Personal

Law No. 38/2016 encourages the import of solar panels, at cost, without taxes, without tariffs or tariff rates, so that end costumers can produce their own electricity.

Additionally, Law 42 of April 20, 2011 establishes the general guidelines of the national policy for the promotion and development of the production and use of biofuels and the generation and/or cogeneration of electrical energy from biomass in the national territory. It offers tax exemptions, payment of license exemptions, distribution and transmission charges exemptions.

It is completed by Law No. 47/2015, which establishes guidelines for the national policy on biofuels and electricity from biomass in the national territory.

## 3.2.1. Strategic Guideline for the Energy Transition 2020-2030

In November 2020, the Panamanian Energy Secretariat issued the Strategic Guideline for the Energy Transition 2020-2030 (Lineamientos Estratégicos Agenda de Transición Energética 2020-2030). The document aims to provide a guide for the execution of national policies in the short, mid, and long-term with the objective of dynamizing the energy sector taking advantage of the new trends observed worldwide, especially the new competitiveness of renewable energies.

The starting point of the analysis performed by SNE considered the increase observed in the last years in the natural gas fired and renewable energy in the power generation mix, with the reduction on the consumption of liquid fuels in the power sector. It expects that in the future the generation mix will be impacted by the development of new solar PV, wind and storage, the digitalization of the grids, and the development of hydrogen (production and consumption).

The document sets the main guidelines for the transition:

- Increase of the renewable generation on the mix (Solar PV, Wind, etc) and the importance of storage to complement it and provide flexibility.
- Introduction of energy efficiency policies with a particular focus on the residential sector.
- Agenda to incorporate electromobility to reduce the increasing emission of the transport sector.
- International interconnections and market integration considering a cost-benefit analysis for each project.
- Decarbonization of the energy sector.

In particular, for the Wholesale Electricity Market, the agenda focuses on:

- Diversifying the generation mix.

- To foment independent commercialization.
- Promoting investment in R&amp;D.
- Promoting pilot projects to develop electromobility (boosting the power demand).

## 3.2.2. National Innovation Strategy of the SIN

In September 2022, the Panamanian Energy Secretariat issued the National Innovation Strategy of the National Interconnected System (SIN) (Estrategia Nacional de Innovación del Sistema Interconectado Nacional - ENISIN). This document is part of the aforementioned Strategic Guideline for the Energy Transition 2020-2030 and focuses in 5 main aspects:

- Flexibility and storage in the SIN;
- Smart transmission and distribution grids;
- Power quality;
- Adjustments in the electricity market;
- Generation infrastructure.

To accomplish these aspects, 4 main goals were set:

- To add storage capacity equal to 5% of the total forecasted demand by 2030.
- To reduce the SAIFI and SAIDI indicators by 50% compared to the 2002 levels by 2030.
- To achieve active participation of the demand of at least 30% of the total energy consumption (Demand Side Management).
- To encourage the contribution of non-conventional renewables energies, from generation plants connected to the SIN and at distributed level, to achieve at least 20% of the energy consumption by 2030.

It is worth pointing out that the fulfillment of **flexibility and storage in the SIN** shall be achieved by:

- Creation of a complete market of ancillary services.
- Incorporation of evaluation mechanism for monitoring and performance of flexibility within the current norms.
- Incorporation of storage technologies in the entire industry chain.

## 3.2.3. Specific regulatory framework for BESS Technologies

In December 2020, ASEP's Resolution 16564-Elec was published. This resolution modifies the operative rules of the Wholesale Electricity Market in order to modernize the regulatory framework and incorporate Storage technologies.

The resolution covers diverse topics regarding the inclusion of these technologies:

- Definitions: adds "Sistema de Almacenamiento de Energía basado en Baterías (SAEB)" (Battery based Energy Storage Systems) to the definitions included in the norm.

Battery-based Energy Storage System (SAEB): Equipment capable of storing, injecting and withdrawing energy from the grid to quickly compensate, through electronic controls, and maintain it for a predetermined time, within all acceptable ranges of voltage and frequency of the SIN, in addition to providing various auxiliary services that help increase the reliability of the system and use of the assets of a national interconnected system.

Panamá: Market advisor services for Generadora Gatún

gme

- The development of BESS facilities must be linked to a generation unit (operative or future). The development of a storage facility will require the adaptation of the license, concession or certificate of the agent.
- BESS facilities can participate in the provision of rotating reserves (primary frequency regulation).
- BESS must declare to CND the required technical data y order to operate the facility and include it in the planning process of the system.

As observed in this resolution, the objective was to allow BESS facilities to be developed but with a focus on potentially modifying the injection of a power plant to capture better spot prices or participating in the provision of reserves and in particular rotating reserves. But it did not include concepts like the recognition of firm capacity to a BESS facility, operations of standalone batteries for energy trading, and development of BESS facilities within the transmission or distribution business.

In April 2024, ASEP's Resolution 19112-Elec was published. This resolution intended to modify the commercial rules of the Wholesale Electricity Market in order to consider the use of SAEBg as complement in the calculation of firm capacity of renewable generation and to include the possibility of use of BESS facilities within the transmission business.

The resolution adds the following definitions to the commercial rules:

- Battery-based Energy Storage System (SAEB, or "Sistema de Almacenamiento de Energía con Baterías"): is a technological equipment capable of transforming electrical energy and storing it for future use in order to improve the operation of the system to which it belongs.
- Battery-based Energy Storage System of a generator (SAEBg or "Sistema de Almacenamiento de Energía con Baterías de un generador"): it is a system capable of transforming electrical energy into another form of energy, storing it, and subsequently using it as electrical energy for the use of the Participant Producer. The SAEBg includes components such as battery systems, connection devices, and a user interface to monitor its operation.
- Battery-based Energy Storage System for the Transmission System (SAEBt or "Sistema de Almacenamiento de Energía con Baterías para el Sistema Principal de Transmisión") is an installation of a set of batteries, along with their corresponding connection, fuses, and protection equipment, used for the temporary storage of energy and its subsequent delivery to the system.

The resolution presents a series of modifications to the considerations of long-term firm capacity, the main ones are presented below:

- Photovoltaic power plants are now considered in the calculation of long-term firm capacity, solar irradiance must be taken into consideration in its calculation.
- SAEBg capacity must be considered in the calculation of long-term firm capacity of power plants.
- The capacity of the SAEBg will be considered based on the real availability of the system in terms of power energy, taking into account factors such as unavailability, degradation due to charge and discharge cycles, and other technical operational variables that may affect its functioning or capacity.

The resolution also adds the Transmission companies as market participants in order to be able to consider in the WEM energy balances the injection and withdrawals of energy due to the charge and discharge of SAEBt.

# 4. WHOLESALE MARKET

Commercially speaking, the wholesale electricity market (WEM) consists of two markets, a relatively small one accounting for opportunity exchanges (spot market) and another for contracts.

Distribution Companies must contract 100% of their expected peak capacity (including regulatory reserve) and energy needs one year in advance, to guarantee the supply of their regulated customers. This obligation percentage is reduced for the following years (Res. AN 991 and amendments). Contract prices are passed through to end user tariffs. Distribution companies can self-generate up to 15% of their demand.

Two products are traded in the wholesale market: energy (hourly) and capacity (daily and yearly through the long-term reserve service). A generator receives the hourly spot price (short run marginal cost of the system) for energy produced during each hour. If it is not dispatched, it does not receive energy payments. In addition, if a generator participates in the long-term reserve service (where the traded product is capacity), it receives a capacity payment whether it is being dispatched or not.

Large users (over 100 kW) can either purchase their energy needs in the wholesale market (through bilateral contracts and/or on the spot market) or they can be supplied by the Distributor at a regulated tariff (Res. 5864/06 and Res. 961/2007). Those large users who decide to purchase their energy needs in the spot market must also purchase firm capacity in the long-term reserve service, to secure their supply. In other words, if there is a portion of the large user's demand that is not contracted, such portion must be considered in the demand to be secured by the long-term reserve service, annually auctioned by the system operator for the year ahead (LTRS).

The long-term reserve service represents a one-year firm capacity contract awarded through public auctions. The system operator aggregates all demands not yet contracted for the year ahead (both of distributors and large users) and carries out a public auction for the generators to offer their firm capacity (not yet committed in contracts). There is a cap price for the capacity offered, which is the regulated capacity price, currently at 8.96 USD/kW-month¹³.

At present, Resolution AN No. 961-ELEC of June 2007 establishes the criteria and procedures to sell energy and capacity to large customers. Some of the most relevant aspects of this Resolution are stated below:

- The Large Customer opting to buy directly in the WEM will need a supply contract with a participating producer to guarantee its energy demand.
- Said supply contract will contain, at least:
- a) the prices of energy, capacity, and other services, if any, (charges, compensations, fines, discounts, etc.);
- b) the party responsible for paying forced generation overruns.
- c) the duration of the contract;
- d) the method to adjust price while the contract is effective;

¹³ See Resolution AN No. 3037-Elec (price indicated in Balboas, 1 Balboa=1 USD).

## 4.1. Organization

The Wholesale Market in Panama started its operations in 1999. It operates mainly as a contract market after Res. AN 991/ 2007 and its amendments in which Distribution Companies must contract in advance a given percentage of their total demand for the years ahead.

Large users (over 100 kW) can either purchase their energy needs in the wholesale market (through bilateral contracts and/or on a spot basis) or they can be supplied by Distributors at a regulated tariff (Res. 961/2007). Those large customers who choose to purchase their energy needs in the spot market must also pay for the system's long-term reserve service.

The Wholesale Electricity Market is administered by the National Dispatch Center (CND), in charge of operating and dispatching generation plants at the lowest possible cost, determining spot prices and settlement procedures between agents.

The Panamanian wholesale electricity market comprises the following markets and products:

- Contract market (90.5 % of total energy supplied): this is a long-term market, where Distribution companies (and large users) seek to guarantee supply to their regulated clients. The contract market stabilizes prices and promotes investment in new capacity, which, in turn, guarantees long-term supply. Contracts usually have a constant capacity payment for committed firm capacity and a variable energy payment based on the energy delivered. In general, revenues for the power plants are largely based on the payment received from long-term contracts.

- Long Term Reserve Service (LTRS or SARLP in Spanish "Servicio Auxiliar de Reserva de Largo Plazo"): once a year, usually between October and December, the system operator (CND) computes the portion of the projected demand not yet committed under long term contracts and conducts a tender among generators to bid in the so-called Long-Term Reserve Service (LTRS). The purpose of this service is to guarantee the supply to all customers not yet covered under long-term contracts. Any generator can participate in such tender by bidding a price for the firm capacity not committed yet. The system operator ranks the bids in ascending price order until they meet the system's long-term reserve capacity requirement. The highest-priced accepted bid defines the price of firm capacity in the LTRS. All the generators whose bid has been accepted are recognized this price. The price bid has a cap defined by regulation (same cap as for the daily capacity deviation market, currently 8.96 USD/kW-month).

- Hourly energy spot market (9.5 % of total energy supplied): opportunity market, intended to compensate deviations between hourly energy contracted and actual hourly consumption. Whenever a generator sells its production in the spot market, it receives the hourly spot price (short run marginal cost of the system) for the energy produced.

- Daily capacity compensation market: it compensates short-term deviations between committed firm capacity and actual capacity. Pursuant to present commercial rules, each market agent with a capacity surplus can bid a price at which it is willing to sell said capacity surplus. It is a market for opportunity exchanges, and it is not intended to represent a significant source of income for a

Panamá: Market advisor services for Generadora Gatún

gme

generator. The bidding price cannot exceed the maximum price set by the CND for each day, estimated as the maximum capacity price of long-term supply contracts that are passed through to end user tariffs. In addition, the Regulatory Authority can enforce the regulated price cap (8.96 USD/kW-month). The average price in the daily compensation market is around 0.5 USD/kW-month, evidencing a supply surplus in the market.

## 4.1.1. Long Term Contracts

The merit order of dispatch of the power units is not influenced by contractual commitments, which are financial. In each hour, if the generator produces more energy than the amount committed under contracts (long position), it sells the energy surpluses in the spot market. If the generator delivers less energy to the grid than the amount committed (short position), it must purchase this energy shortage in the spot market.

Commercial rules allow for three types of financial supply contracts:

- Capacity and Energy contract: Seller commits a certain amount of firm capacity and associated energy (in general, it follows the demand load curve). The Buyer has priority of supply if the seller can honor its commitment with its own generation. In a rationing situation, the CND will consider this contract as a physical contract and will deliver the energy produced by the Seller to the Buyer.
- Capacity contract: The product traded is firm capacity. The Seller commits a maximum amount of firm capacity to be available when the Buyer needs it to comply with regulatory obligations. In exchange, the Buyer will pay for the contracted capacity, whether it generates or not.

Panamá: Market advisor services for Generadora Gatún

gme

- Energy contract: The Seller commits itself to deliver a certain amount of energy to the Buyer.

## 4.1.2. Reserve contracts

The chapter 4.5 of the Commercial Rules set the main rules for the Reserve Contracts. The reserve contracts are private contracts between generators in which they trade energy and capacity.

A generator can buy capacity and/or energy from another generator through Reserve Contracts to sell on the market and/or to back up commitments under supply contracts in which they are the seller.

A generator may sell surplus power and/or energy to another generator through Reserve Contracts.

A generator may sell contracts to other participants according to its "Potencia Máxima para compromisos de Productores (Producers Maximum capacity for Commitments)" calculated as the sum of the actual output of the generator, minus the power sold by supply contracts to other consumers.

When signing a contract, a generator must keep in mind that can only sell firm power that is not yet committed in another contract and that is installed for the duration of the contract.

## 4.1.3. Hourly energy spot market

The National Dispatch Center (Centro Nacional de Despacho, CND) centrally operates the interconnected system in real time and runs the economic dispatch model, minimizing the system's variable cost of production in each hour. CND is part of the transmission company, ETESA.

The CND is responsible for short to medium-term operation and its optimization, aiming to fulfill the expected demand at minimum cost. CND computes a water value for each reservoir so that energy resources are optimally allocated (the economic dispatch generally uses the water of reservoirs during peak hours when the supply cost is higher).

**Regulations related to the declaration of variable costs:** the variable cost for dispatch is set by the variable operation cost of the thermal and self-generation units, the "water value" for hydroelectric power plants with reservoir, the assigned price for imports and zero variable cost for cogeneration, wind, and solar plants, as well as run of river hydro plants. The variable cost declared by the thermal generators for the merit order dispatch includes the variable fuel cost and O&amp;M variable costs.

Generators declare costs (excluding transmission costs), and not prices, to compete for dispatch. The variable production costs of thermal plants are auditable.

## 4.1.4. Capacity market

In the Panamanian market, Distributors are obliged to contract their DMG ("Demanda Máxima de Generación" or maximum generation demand) in advance. The commercial rules establish three ways in which capacity requirements and capacity offers are balanced.

- Capacity Contracts: supply and reserve contracts
- Long Term Reserve Service (LTRS or SARLP - Servicio Auxiliar de Reserva de Largo Plazo): It's an annual tender designed for the distributors to contract their capacity requirements not already covered by the current contracts for the

Panamá: Market advisor services for Generadora Gatún

gme

next year. The cap price is set by the regulated capacity.

- Daily capacity market: a daily market in which the participants settle the capacity positions. In this market, the consumers and generators trade capacity in the hour of maximum generation of the day. Consumers buy the demand not covered by the contracts or the LTRS. Generators purchase the contracted capacity that has not been backed with contract or the generators availability. In the last years, prices were 0.5 USD/kW-month on average.

In the first two markets (contracts and LTRS), generators can offer capacity until they reach their long-term firm capacity. The long-term firm capacity is defined as the capacity that the generator is capable of guaranteeing in maximum requirement conditions. For example, in the case of hydroelectric power plants it is calculated for a P95 condition of energy output (dry hydrology) during peak hours.

In the third market (daily capacity compensation), generators can offer capacity until they reach their Maximum Commercial Capacity, defined as the maximum capacity that the generator can provide for a maximum period of 15 minutes considering the operative restrictions of the unit (own restrictions, fuel constraints in case of thermal plants and transmission restrictions). In the case of a hydroelectric unit, depending on the hydroelectric conditions, the available capacity for the daily compensation market may be higher than the long-term firm reserve. Only in a very dry condition, will the long-term firm capacity equal the commercial capacity.

It is worth mentioning that wind and solar PV power plants are not recognized any firm capacity nowadays, although this matter is being analyzed by the system operator CND and may change in the upcoming future.

With respect to the regulated capacity price, it is calculated by the regulator. Since 2010, it is set as 8.96 USD/kW-month. The following figure shows the different capacity prices as explained above.


Figure 8: Historical capacity prices, 2009-2025

## 4.1.5. Long Term Firm capacity for Thermal assets

In the case of a thermal power plant, the long-term firm capacity is the capacity that is capable of guaranteeing under conditions of maximum requirement, and it is based on its technical and operational characteristics, the regulated reliability requirement, and the

Panamá: Market advisor services for Generadora Gatún

gme

commitment assumed by the Generator.

According to the regulations, the Long-term Firm Capacity of a thermal generator is the effective capacity minus the unavailability of the power plant (measured in the last three years).

The Long-term Firm Capacity of each unit is calculated every year by CND in the "Informe de Potencia Firme de Largo Plazo", fixing a value for each week of the year.

## 4.2. Payments Among Market Participants

The system operator (CND) commercially administers the hourly energy spot market, the daily capacity market, and the ancillary services (including the long-term reserve service and other ancillary services). Commercial transactions are monthly settled. The economic transactions are between debtors and creditors, where debtors owe all creditors.

With respect to bilateral contracts between private parties, CND does not commercially administer such contracts. It only provides physical information (energy and capacity amounts) to the parties involved to compute commercial transactions.

Relative to transmission charges, CND provides all market participants with the physical information necessary to compute transmission charges to be paid to the transmission company.

# ELECTRICITY SECTOR

## 1. SUPPLY

Panama's installed generation capacity has a high hydroelectricity component (the rainy season runs from May to October). Fortuna (ENEL Group, 300 MW) and Bayano (AES, 260 MW) are the two main hydroelectric plants of the generation park with regulation capacity (reservoir). Together, they produce about 30% of the total hydroelectric generation, in average conditions. Thermal power plants were historically based on liquid fuels and coal. Since the entry into operation of Costa Norte CCGT in 2018, LNG is also part of the fuel mix of thermal power plants. Furthermore, with the commissioning of Gatun in late 2024, the installed capacity based on LNG reached around 62% of the entire thermal capacity. In 2025, LNG contributed 23% of total generation.

From 2000 to 2009, the system's reserve margin has been closed to 40% on average. Since 2010, it has a growing tendency, recently reaching values over 140%. This high reserve margin is explained by the large participation of hydro and renewable resources in the generation mix. During the dry season, the availability of hydro resources (firm energy) is low, and there is the need to complement with thermal generation in order to guarantee enough supply to meet demand. In the last five years, the addition of wind and solar projects also contributed to an increase in the reserve margin measured in terms of installed capacity (although their firm energy is much lower). On the other hand, the decommissioning of thermal units has resulted in a generalized reduction in the reserve margin; still high though.

Electricity prices rise when hydro generation diminishes. This happens mainly during the dry season (January to May). In these months it is necessary to dispatch costly thermal generation to meet demand.

The supply curve is affected by hydrological conditions; during dry years hydroelectricity diminishes and viceversa. In this respect, maximum demand in Panama reached 1,915 MW in 2025 while total installed capacity of hydro power plants was near 1,847 MW. However, this does not mean that demand can be supplied mainly by hydro resources all the time. In fact, during 2014, there was rationing because available capacity was not enough to meet demand (due to very dry weather and low water inflows).

Figure 13 presents the seasonality of hydroelectricity generation: there is a dry season (from Jan to May) and a rainy season. This weather pattern influences on the electricity spot prices. Thus, during the dry season spot prices tend to be higher than in the rainy season because it is necessary to call to dispatch costlier thermal units to supply the demand.

Bayano (260 MW) and Fortuna (300 MW) are the only hydroelectric plants with regulating capacity, they have a seasonal reservoir which enables them to store water during the rainy season to produce energy during the dry season. The rest of the hydro power plants in the system are run-of-river, with no significant regulating capacity.

The wholesale power market in Panama is a "marginal market": the spot price of electricity is determined by the variable costs of the last unit called to dispatch. The system operator (CND) centrally dispatches all the available power units in the generation fleet by ranking them in ascendant order of their variable costs, thus assuring the supply of the demand at the minimum possible cost all the time conforming the so-called merit order dispatch. It is worth mentioning that variable costs of renewable-based projects are very low, therefore they rank first in the merit order dispatch (dispatch priority vis a vis thermal generation and hydro power plants with reservoirs).

## 1.1. Renewable energy potential

### 1.1.1. Hydroelectric Potential

Panama has an available potential for hydroelectric capacity of 2382.7 MW distributed in 53 potential sites. These projects have an estimated potential of 11879 GWh/year.

It also has identified 42 sites with development potential for small hydro projects under 1 MW of capacity, which are aimed mainly at rural communities. Together they add up to 6.4 MW.

The biggest potential lies in the Bocas del Toro province.

### 1.1.2. Wind Power Potential

Panama has sites with very good wind development capabilities, mostly located in the Caribbean coast and along the central mountain range. These sites have wind speeds of up to $10\mathrm{m / s}$ and estimated dispatch factors of up to $35\%$.

Nowadays, Panama has 336 MW of installed wind capacity, witch account for $8\%$ of total installed capacity.
